Whether a person becomes a hero or a coward may depend partly on circumstances they did not choose.

Constitutive luck concerns the kind of person we are: our temperament, talents, and character traits, which are shaped by genetics, upbringing, and experience. Some people are naturally patient, while others struggle with anger. If our character results largely from factors we did not control, how much credit or blame do we deserve for acting in accordance with it?

Taken to its extreme, the argument seems to threaten the very idea of moral responsibility. If luck influences everything, perhaps nobody truly deserves praise or blame. Most philosophers resist this conclusion, but they disagree about how to reconcile responsibility with luck.

Some argue that we should judge people mainly by their intentions and choices, not by outcomes. Others accept that outcomes matter, at least for practical purposes such as compensation and legal punishment. Still others suggest that recognizing the role of luck should make us more humble and compassionate in our judgments.
Perhaps that is the most valuable lesson. When we condemn others for their failures or celebrate our own successes, it is worth remembering how much depended on circumstances nobody chose.

title: The Meaning of a Good Life
paragraphs: What makes a life good? The question is ancient, yet it remains as urgent as ever. People make decisions about careers, relationships, and values based on implicit answers to it, often without examining those answers carefully. Philosophers have offered many competing views, and each captures something important about human experience.

One influential tradition holds that a good life is a happy life, filled with pleasure and free from pain. Ancient thinkers such as Epicurus argued that wisdom lies in seeking lasting tranquility rather than intense but fleeting pleasures. Contrary to popular belief, Epicurus recommended simple living, friendship, and moderation rather than luxury. Later philosophers in the utilitarian tradition also emphasized happiness, though they focused on the well-being of society as a whole.

A second view emphasizes desire satisfaction. According to this perspective, a life goes well when people get what they want. This approach respects individual differences, since people value very different things. However, it faces difficulties. People sometimes desire things that harm them, or desire things based on false information. Satisfying every desire does not necessarily produce a flourishing life.

A third tradition, associated especially with Aristotle, focuses on flourishing. For Aristotle, a good life involves developing and exercising virtues such as courage, generosity, wisdom, and justice. It is not merely a feeling but a way of living. Human beings flourish when they realize their capacities as rational and social creatures, participating in communities and pursuing worthwhile activities.

Some modern philosophers emphasize meaning. A meaningful life may involve commitment to projects, relationships, or causes that extend beyond oneself. The philosopher Susan Wolf has suggested that meaning arises when subjective attraction meets objective worth, in other words, when people are passionately engaged in activities that are genuinely valuable.

These views are not necessarily incompatible. Many people seek a life that contains pleasure, satisfies important desires, develops their abilities, and connects them to something meaningful. The difficulty lies in balancing these elements. A life devoted entirely to pleasure may feel empty, while a life devoted entirely to duty may feel joyless.

Perhaps the question cannot be answered once and for all. Our understanding of a good life may change as we age, face challenges, and learn from experience. Yet asking the question regularly is itself valuable. It encourages us to live deliberately rather than simply following the expectations of others.

title: Free Will in an Age of Neuroscience
paragraphs: Most people feel that they make free choices. They decide what to eat for breakfast, which job to accept, and whether to apologize after an argument. This sense of agency is central to how we understand ourselves and others. We praise people for good decisions, blame them for harmful ones, and organize legal systems around the idea that individuals are responsible for their actions.

Yet neuroscience has raised challenging questions about this familiar picture. If every thought and decision corresponds to physical processes in the brain, governed by the laws of nature, in what sense are our choices truly free? Could our feeling of deciding be merely a story the brain tells after the real work has already been done?

Some of the most discussed evidence comes from experiments conducted by the neuroscientist Benjamin Libet in the nineteen eighties. Participants were asked to make a simple movement whenever they felt like it and to report when they became aware of the intention to move. Libet found that brain activity associated with preparing the movement began before participants reported the conscious decision. Some commentators interpreted this as evidence that unconscious processes determine our actions before we are aware of choosing.

Later research has complicated this interpretation. Critics have pointed out that the experiments involved trivial, spontaneous movements rather than meaningful decisions. Others have argued that the measured brain activity may reflect general readiness or random fluctuations rather than a specific decision. Some studies have suggested that people may still be able to cancel an action after the early brain activity begins.

Philosophers have long debated free will, and neuroscience has not settled the question. Many philosophers are compatibilists, meaning they believe free will is compatible with a world governed by natural laws. For them, freedom does not require escaping causation. It requires acting according to one's own reasons, values, and deliberation, without external coercion.

Others argue that genuine freedom requires something more, and that if our choices are fully determined by prior causes, traditional notions of moral responsibility must be revised. Some even suggest that abandoning belief in free will could lead to a more compassionate justice system focused on prevention and rehabilitation rather than retribution.

Whatever the answer, the debate has practical consequences. It affects how we think about addiction, mental illness, criminal responsibility, and personal growth. Understanding the brain does not necessarily eliminate freedom, but it does invite us to think more carefully about what freedom means.

title: The Tyranny of the Inbox
paragraphs: For many office workers, the day begins and ends with email. Before breakfast, they check their phones to see what has arrived overnight. Throughout the day, notifications interrupt meetings, conversations, and concentrated work. In the evening, they glance at their inbox one last time before sleep, hoping that nothing urgent has appeared. Email was supposed to make communication easier. For many people, it has become a source of constant pressure.

The problem is not email itself but the way it is used. Messages are easy to send and cost nothing, so they multiply rapidly. People copy colleagues on conversations to keep them informed, reply to everyone instead of a single person, and send quick questions that could have been answered with a moment of independent research. Each message seems small, but together they create an overwhelming flow of information.

Research on attention suggests that frequent interruptions can be costly. When people switch from a demanding task to check a message, they often need time to regain their previous level of concentration. Some studies have found that workers who check email constantly report higher stress than those who check it at scheduled times. The habit of responding immediately may create an illusion of productivity while preventing deeper work.

Workplace culture plays an important role. In some organizations, fast replies are treated as evidence of commitment. Employees may feel that they must answer messages late at night or during holidays to demonstrate reliability. Over time, this expectation can blur the boundary between work and private life, contributing to exhaustion and burnout.

Some companies and governments have tried to address the problem. In France, a law has given many employees what is often described as a right to disconnect, requiring larger employers to negotiate policies about after-hours communication. Some organizations limit internal emails outside working hours, while others encourage teams to use shared documents and project management tools instead of endless message threads.

Individuals can also develop healthier habits. Turning off notifications, checking email at specific times, and writing clearer, shorter messages can reduce unnecessary communication. Before sending a message, it may be worth asking whether it is truly necessary, who actually needs to receive it, and whether a brief conversation would be more effective.

Email is unlikely to disappear. It remains a useful tool for sharing information across distances and time zones. But tools should serve people, not the other way around. Regaining control of the inbox may begin with a simple realization: not every message deserves an immediate reply.

title: Remote Work and the Lost Hallway
paragraphs: When millions of office workers suddenly began working from home, many discovered unexpected benefits. They no longer spent hours commuting, could organize their days more flexibly, and enjoyed quieter environments for focused tasks. Surveys showed that large numbers of employees wanted to continue working remotely at least part of the time. For many, returning to the office full time seemed unnecessary, even absurd.

Yet as remote work became routine, some people began to notice what was missing. They missed the casual conversations that happened in hallways, kitchens, and elevators. They missed overhearing colleagues discuss problems, asking quick questions without scheduling a call, and meeting people from other departments by chance. These small interactions had seemed trivial at the time, but they turned out to play an important role in working life.

Researchers sometimes describe such encounters as weak ties: relationships with acquaintances rather than close colleagues. Weak ties can be surprisingly valuable because they connect people to new information, ideas, and opportunities. A chance conversation with someone from another team may reveal a solution to a problem or lead to a new collaboration. Some studies of large companies found that remote work tended to make communication networks more static and isolated, reducing these cross-team connections.

Younger employees may be particularly affected. Much professional learning happens informally, by watching experienced colleagues handle difficult situations, listening to how they speak with clients, or asking for advice in casual moments. In remote settings, such learning requires deliberate effort, and newcomers may hesitate to interrupt busy colleagues with questions.

At the same time, offices were never perfect. Open-plan environments often made concentration difficult, and spontaneous interactions sometimes favored people who were already well connected. Remote work has allowed some employees, including those with disabilities or caregiving responsibilities, to participate more fully than before.

Many organizations now use hybrid arrangements, combining days at home with days in the office. The challenge is to use office time intentionally, focusing on collaboration, mentoring, and relationship building rather than tasks that could be done anywhere. Some companies organize team days, informal events, or virtual spaces designed to imitate casual encounters.

The lost hallway reminds us that work is not only a series of tasks. It is also a social environment in which people learn, connect, and develop a sense of belonging. Designing the future of work requires paying attention to those invisible moments that once happened simply because people shared the same space.

title: Digital Detox Weekends
paragraphs: On a Friday evening, a group of strangers arrives at a remote cabin in the countryside. Upon entering, each of them places their phone in a small locked box. For the next two days, they will have no internet access, no social media, and no messages from work. Instead, they will hike, cook meals together, play games, read books, and sit around a fire talking. They have paid for the privilege of being disconnected.

Digital detox retreats have become increasingly popular as people grow concerned about the role of technology in their lives. Many describe feeling tired, distracted, and anxious after hours of scrolling through news and social media. Smartphones offer enormous benefits, but their constant notifications and endless content can make it difficult to rest, concentrate, or enjoy the present moment.

Participants often report that the first hours without their phones are uncomfortable. They reach instinctively for their pockets, feel anxious about missing important messages, and struggle with moments of boredom. Some describe a kind of phantom vibration, imagining that a phone is buzzing even when it is not there.

As the weekend continues, many people notice changes. Conversations become longer and more attentive. Meals are eaten slowly, without interruptions. Participants observe the landscape more carefully and sleep more deeply. Some say they feel calmer and more connected to the people around them.

Scientific research on digital detoxes is mixed. Some studies have found that reducing social media use can improve mood or reduce feelings of loneliness and anxiety. Others have found small or inconsistent effects, and some people experience increased stress when cut off from important communication. The impact appears to depend on the individual, the context, and how technology is normally used.

Critics also question whether short retreats address the underlying problem. A weekend without phones may feel refreshing, but if people return to the same habits on Monday morning, the benefits may disappear quickly. Some argue that technology companies, rather than individuals, should take greater responsibility for designing products that respect users' attention.

For many participants, the most valuable outcome is not the break itself but the reflection it encourages. Without the constant presence of their phones, people notice which digital habits genuinely enrich their lives and which simply consume time.

A digital detox does not need to involve an expensive cabin. Leaving the phone in another room during dinner or taking a walk without headphones can offer a small version of the same experience: a moment of attention returned to the physical world.

title: The Culture of Busyness
paragraphs: Ask someone how they are doing, and there is a good chance they will reply with a single word: busy. The answer is often delivered with a sigh, but sometimes also with a hint of pride. In many modern societies, busyness has become more than a description of how people spend their time. It has become a symbol of importance, ambition, and value.

Historically, leisure was associated with high status. Wealthy people demonstrated their privilege by not having to work, spending their time on travel, hobbies, and social events. The economist Veblen famously described this behavior as conspicuous leisure. Today, the relationship seems to have reversed in some circles. Being busy suggests that a person is in demand, that their skills are valuable, and that others depend on them.

Researchers have explored this shift. In one series of studies, participants evaluated people described as working long hours with little free time. In the American samples, these busy individuals were often perceived as having higher status than people with more leisure. The effect was weaker or even reversed in some European samples, suggesting that cultural values shape how busyness is interpreted.

Technology contributes to the problem. Smartphones allow work to follow people everywhere, making it difficult to separate professional obligations from private life. Social media encourages people to display productivity, travel, achievements, and constant activity. Even free time can begin to feel like another set of tasks, as people schedule exercise, hobbies, and social engagements with the same intensity as work meetings.

Yet constant busyness has costs. It can lead to stress, exhaustion, and poorer health. It may reduce the time available for reflection, creativity, and meaningful relationships. Some people find that they are always occupied but rarely feel that they are making progress on what truly matters to them.

There is also a difference between being busy and being productive. Many activities that fill our days, such as answering unnecessary messages or attending unfocused meetings, create the appearance of effort without producing much value. Recognizing this difference can help people protect time for deeper work and genuine rest.

Some thinkers have begun to argue for a different ideal, one that values slowness, attention, and balance. Instead of asking how much we can fit into a day, they ask what kind of life we actually want to lead.
The next time someone asks how you are, it might be interesting to answer with something other than busy. The response could open a more honest conversation.

title: Why We Photograph Our Food
paragraphs: In restaurants around the world, a familiar ritual takes place before many meals begin. Plates arrive, conversation pauses, and diners raise their phones to photograph their food. They adjust the angle, move a glass out of the frame, and sometimes stand on a chair to capture the perfect overhead shot. Only after the picture has been taken does the eating begin.

To some observers, this habit seems absurd. Food is meant to be eaten, not documented. Yet the impulse to photograph meals reflects deeper human motivations involving memory, identity, and social connection.

Food has always been more than nutrition. It is tied to culture, celebration, family traditions, and personal experiences. A meal can represent a special occasion, a successful cooking experiment, or a memorable trip abroad. Photographing it helps preserve the moment and share it with others. Long before smartphones, people kept recipe books, wrote about memorable dinners in diaries, and gathered around tables for celebratory photographs.

Social media has amplified these traditions. Platforms built around images reward attractive presentations, and food photography has become a popular genre. Restaurants have responded by designing dishes, lighting, and interiors that look appealing in photographs. Some chefs even consider how a dish will appear on a small screen when developing new recipes.

Psychologists have explored whether photographing food changes the experience of eating. Some studies suggest that taking pictures before a meal may increase enjoyment, perhaps because the ritual builds anticipation and focuses attention on the food. However, this effect may depend on the type of food and on how many photographs are taken. Spending too much time arranging the perfect picture could also distract people from the meal and their companions.

The habit can also reveal social pressures. Online images often present carefully selected, idealized versions of daily life. Seeing a constant stream of beautiful meals may make some people feel that their own ordinary food is somehow inadequate. Others worry that the desire to document every experience prevents people from fully enjoying the present.

Yet food photography can also be creative and communal. Home cooks share recipes, travelers discover local cuisines, and small restaurants attract customers through images posted by satisfied diners. A photograph can spark conversation, inspire someone to cook, or preserve a memory that might otherwise fade.
Perhaps the best approach is moderation. Take the picture if it matters to you, then put the phone away and enjoy the meal while it is still warm.

title: The Quiet Rebellion of Hobbies
paragraphs: In a culture that values productivity, it can feel strangely difficult to do something simply for enjoyment. Many people feel pressure to turn every interest into an achievement. A person who enjoys baking is encouraged to start a business. Someone who likes writing is asked when their book will be published. Even exercise is tracked, measured, and shared, transforming relaxation into another form of performance.

Against this background, hobbies pursued purely for pleasure can seem almost rebellious. Knitting, gardening, birdwatching, playing an instrument badly, or building model ships may produce nothing of economic value. Yet these activities offer something increasingly rare: time spent without the pressure to optimize, compete, or monetize.

Research suggests that hobbies can provide significant psychological benefits. Engaging in creative or absorbing activities is associated with reduced stress, improved mood, and greater life satisfaction. Hobbies can offer a sense of competence and progress that may be missing from other parts of life, particularly when work feels repetitive or uncontrollable.

Many hobbies also encourage the kind of deep concentration that psychologists call flow. When people become absorbed in carving wood or solving a complex puzzle, they often lose track of time and forget everyday worries. This immersive focus can be restorative, especially in a world filled with constant interruptions.

Social connection is another benefit. Clubs, classes, and online communities bring together people who share interests, regardless of age, profession, or background. A choir may include students, retirees, and office workers who would rarely meet otherwise. Shared enthusiasm creates natural opportunities for friendship.

Interestingly, being mediocre can be part of the pleasure. Hobbies allow people to practice skills without needing to be excellent. Mistakes become less threatening when nothing important depends on the outcome. For adults accustomed to being evaluated at work, this freedom can feel liberating.

Of course, hobbies can sometimes become sources of pressure themselves. Expensive equipment, competitive communities, and social media comparisons may transform a relaxing activity into another arena for status. The key is to remember why the hobby began in the first place.

Perhaps the greatest value of hobbies lies in their uselessness. They remind us that human beings are not machines designed solely for productivity. We are also curious, playful, and creative creatures who need time to make things, learn things, and enjoy them simply because they bring us joy.

title: Living Alone by Choice
paragraphs: For most of human history, living alone was rare. People lived with extended families, servants, lodgers, or members of religious communities. Solitary living was often associated with poverty, widowhood, or social isolation. Today, however, single-person households have become common in many countries, and for a growing number of people, living alone is a deliberate choice rather than an unfortunate circumstance.

Several social changes have contributed to this trend. Rising incomes have made independent living more affordable for many people. Women have gained greater economic independence, and marriage has become less universal and often occurs later in life. People live longer, which means more older adults live alone after the death of a partner. Urban environments also offer services and social opportunities that make solitary living more practical.

The sociologist Eric Klinenberg, who has studied this phenomenon extensively, argues that living alone does not necessarily mean being lonely. Many people who live by themselves maintain active social lives, spending time with friends, family, colleagues, and communities. Having a private home allows them to choose when to socialize and when to rest.

For some, living alone offers valuable freedom. They can arrange their space according to their own tastes, keep their own schedules, and pursue interests without negotiating with others. Solitude can provide time for reflection, creativity, and self-discovery. Some people find that living alone helps them better understand their needs and preferences.

Nevertheless, living alone can also present challenges. Without regular contact with others, some people may become isolated, particularly if they lose mobility, employment, or social networks. Practical difficulties also arise, such as managing household tasks alone, coping with illness, or handling emergencies without immediate help.

Cities and governments are beginning to respond to the needs of single-person households. Some housing projects include smaller private apartments combined with shared kitchens, gardens, or common rooms. These designs allow residents to enjoy privacy while still having opportunities for community.

Cultural attitudes are changing as well. Once viewed with suspicion or pity, people who live alone are increasingly recognized as making legitimate life choices. Their experiences challenge the assumption that a fulfilling life must follow a single traditional pattern.

Living alone is not inherently better or worse than living with others. Its value depends on personal circumstances, preferences, and social connections. What matters most may not be whether someone shares a home, but whether they feel connected to people who care about them.

title: My Morning
paragraphs: I get up at seven o'clock every day. First, I open the window and look at the sky. Then I wash my face and brush my teeth. I put on my clothes and go to the kitchen.
For breakfast, I eat bread with butter and drink a cup of hot tea. My cat sits next to me and waits for milk. I give her a little milk in a small blue bowl.
At eight o'clock, I take my bag and walk to the bus stop. The bus is often late, but I am never in a hurry. I like my quiet mornings.

title: My Family
paragraphs: My name is Sam, and I am ten years old. I live in a small house with my family. There are five people in my family: my mom, my dad, my two sisters, and me.
My mom is a teacher. She is kind and very funny. My dad is a cook in a big restaurant. He makes great pizza on Sundays.
My sisters are Lucy and Kate. Lucy is twelve, and Kate is six. Lucy likes books, and Kate likes dolls. We play games together in the evening. I love my family.

title: The Red Bike
paragraphs: Tom has a new bike. It is red and shiny, and it has a small bell. Tom is very happy. He rides his bike in the park every afternoon.
One day, Tom sees a little girl in the park. She is sad because she has no bike. Her name is Mia. She watches the other children and does not smile.
Tom stops and rings his bell. "Do you want to ride my bike?" he asks. Mia smiles. She rides around the park two times. Now Tom and Mia are friends, and they share the red bike.

title: At the Market
paragraphs: On Saturday morning, Anna goes to the market with her grandmother. The market is big and busy. There are many people and many colors. Some people sell fruit, and some people sell fresh flowers.
Anna and her grandmother buy apples, bananas, and tomatoes. They also buy a big piece of cheese. The cheese man is friendly. He gives Anna a small piece to try. It is delicious.
At the end, Anna's grandmother buys yellow flowers for the kitchen table. They walk home slowly with two heavy bags. Anna loves Saturday mornings at the market.

title: My Dog Max
paragraphs: I have a dog, and his name is Max. He is three years old. Max is big and brown, and he has long ears. He is very friendly, and he loves people.
Every morning, I take Max for a walk. We go to the park near my house. Max runs fast and plays with a ball. He likes other dogs, but he does not like cats.
In the evening, Max sleeps on the floor in the living room. Sometimes he sleeps on my bed, but my mom does not like that. Max is my best friend.

title: A Rainy Day
paragraphs: Today it is raining. The sky is gray, and the streets are wet. I can hear the rain on the window. It is cold outside, so I stay at home.
I make a cup of hot chocolate and sit on the sofa. I have a good book and a warm blanket. My little brother plays with his cars on the floor.
In the afternoon, the rain stops. The sun comes out, and there is a rainbow in the sky. My brother and I put on our boots and go outside. We jump in the big puddles and laugh.

title: My Room
paragraphs: My room is small, but I like it very much. The walls are light green, and there is a big window. From the window, I can see a tall tree and the street.
There is a bed, a desk, and a chair in my room. On the desk, there is a lamp and my computer. I do my homework here every day. There are many books on the shelf.
I have a soft carpet on the floor. It is blue and white. My favorite thing in my room is a photo of my grandparents. It is on the wall next to my bed.

title: Lunch at School
paragraphs: At school, we have lunch at twelve o'clock. The lunchroom is big and noisy. All the students sit at long tables and talk with their friends.
Today there is chicken, rice, and green beans. There is also an orange and a glass of milk. I don't like green beans, but I eat them because they are good for me.
My friend Leo has a sandwich from home. His mom makes very good sandwiches. Sometimes he gives me half, and I give him my orange. After lunch, we go outside and play soccer for twenty minutes.

title: The New Neighbor
paragraphs: There is a new family on our street. They live in the white house next to us. They have a boy and a big black dog. The boy's name is Daniel.
On Sunday, my mom makes a cake. "Let's take this cake to our new neighbors," she says. We walk to the white house and knock on the door. Daniel's mother opens it. She is surprised and very happy.
Daniel and I play in the garden with his dog. He is from another city, and he doesn't have friends here. Now he has one friend, and that is me.

title: My Favorite Food
paragraphs: My favorite food is soup. I like many kinds of soup, but tomato soup is the best. My dad makes it on cold days. He uses fresh tomatoes, onions, and a little garlic.
We eat the soup with warm bread. Sometimes we put cheese on top. It smells very good, and the kitchen is warm and happy.
My sister does not like soup. She likes pasta with red sauce. My mom likes fish and salad. We all like different things, but we always eat dinner together at the big table.

title: A Day at the Beach
paragraphs: In summer, my family goes to the beach. The beach is one hour from our town by car. We leave early in the morning, and we take sandwiches, water, and fruit.
The sand is hot, and the water is blue and cold. My dad and I swim in the sea. My mom reads a book under a big umbrella. My little sister builds a sand castle.
In the afternoon, we eat ice cream. Then we walk on the beach and look for shells. We go home in the evening. We are tired, but very happy.

title: My Best Friend
paragraphs: My best friend is Rosa. She is eleven, like me. We are in the same class at school. Rosa has long black hair and big brown eyes. She is tall and very smart.
Rosa loves music. She plays the piano, and she sings very well. I can't sing, but I can dance. Sometimes she plays the piano, and I dance in her living room.
We talk every day. We walk to school together, and we eat lunch together. When I am sad, Rosa always makes me laugh. She is a great friend.

title: The Lost Cat
paragraphs: Lily has a small white cat called Snow. One evening, Snow is not at home. Lily looks in the kitchen, in the bedroom, and in the garden. The cat is not there.
Lily is very sad. She makes a poster with a photo of Snow. She puts it on a tree in the street. Her dad helps her. They walk around the town and call, "Snow! Snow!"
The next morning, Lily hears a sound at the door. She opens it, and there is Snow. The cat is dirty and hungry, but she is fine. Lily gives her food and a big hug.

title: My Weekend
paragraphs: I love the weekend. On Saturday, I don't go to school, so I sleep late. I get up at nine o'clock and eat pancakes with my family.
In the afternoon, I play basketball with my friends. We play in the park near my school. I am not very tall, but I am fast. After the game, we drink cold water and talk.
On Sunday, I visit my grandparents. My grandmother makes a big lunch, and my grandfather tells funny stories. In the evening, I read a book and go to bed early. The weekend is always too short.

title: In the City
paragraphs: I live in a big city. There are tall buildings, busy streets, and many cars. There are also parks, museums, and lots of cafes. The city is never quiet.
Every day, I go to work by train. The train is fast, but it is often full. I listen to music and look out the window. I can see the river and the bridges.
On the weekend, I like to walk in the old part of the city. The streets there are small and pretty. I sit in a cafe, drink coffee, and watch the people.

title: The Birthday Party
paragraphs: Today is my brother's birthday. He is seven. We have a party at our house in the afternoon. There are balloons in every room, and there is a big chocolate cake on the table.
Ten children come to the party. They play games in the garden and run around. My mom takes many photos. My dad plays music, and everybody dances.
At five o'clock, we sing "Happy Birthday." My brother blows out the seven candles on the cake. He opens his presents. His favorite present is a toy train. It is a very happy day.

title: My Job
paragraphs: My name is Carlos, and I am a nurse. I work in a big hospital in the city. I start work at seven in the morning and finish at three in the afternoon.
I help sick people every day. I give them medicine, and I talk to them. Some people are scared, so I am always kind and calm. The doctors and nurses in my hospital are a good team.
My job is hard, and I am often tired. But I love it. When a patient smiles and says "thank you," I feel very happy.

title: Winter
paragraphs: In my town, winter is very cold. It snows a lot, and the streets are white. The days are short, and the nights are long. The trees have no leaves.
I wear a warm coat, a hat, and gloves every day. My hands and my nose are always cold. At home, I drink hot tea and sit near the window.
But winter is also fun. On the weekend, my friends and I go to the hill near the school. We slide down on the snow and make a big snowman. Then we go home for hot soup.

title: At the Cafe
paragraphs: There is a small cafe on my street. It is open every day from eight o'clock. The cafe has six tables and big windows. It is warm and bright inside.
I go there on Friday after work. I usually order a coffee with milk and a piece of apple cake. The waiter is a young man called Ben. He knows my name, and he always says hello.
Sometimes my friend Nina comes with me. She drinks green tea, and she eats a cookie. We sit by the window and talk for an hour. It is my favorite place in town.

title: Grandpa's Garden
paragraphs: My grandpa has a big garden behind his house. There are flowers, vegetables, and three apple trees. He works in the garden every morning. He says it makes him happy and strong.
In spring, I help him. We plant carrots, potatoes, and beans. I water the plants with a green watering can. Grandpa shows me the small birds in the trees.
In autumn, we pick the apples. Some are red, and some are yellow. Grandma makes apple pie, and we eat it together in the kitchen. Food from the garden tastes the best.

title: The Bus Driver
paragraphs: Mr. Lee is a bus driver. He drives the number ten bus in our town. He starts work very early, at six o'clock in the morning. He drives from the train station to the hospital and back again.
Mr. Lee knows many of the people on his bus. He says good morning to everybody. He helps old people with their bags, and he waits for children who are late.
At lunchtime, Mr. Lee stops at a small park. He eats a sandwich and feeds the birds. Then he drives again until four o'clock. He likes his job and his town.

title: A Picnic in the Park
paragraphs: It is a sunny Sunday, and my friends and I have a picnic in the park. We meet at eleven o'clock under a big tree. Everybody brings some food.
Emma brings sandwiches and a bottle of orange juice. Jack brings chips and grapes. I bring a chocolate cake. We put a big blanket on the grass and sit down. The food is very good.
After lunch, we play a game with a ball. Then we lie on the blanket and look at the clouds. One cloud looks like a rabbit. We stay in the park all afternoon.

title: My Grandmother
paragraphs: My grandmother is seventy-five years old. She has short white hair and blue eyes. She wears glasses, and she always smiles. She lives in a small house near the river.
Every day, my grandmother walks for one hour. Then she reads the newspaper and drinks coffee. She loves cooking. Her cookies are the best in the world.
I visit her every Wednesday after school. We sit in her kitchen and talk. She tells me stories about her life when she was young. I love my grandmother very much.

title: New Shoes
paragraphs: My old shoes are too small, so today my mom and I go to the shoe store. The store is in the shopping center. It is big, and there are hundreds of shoes.
I try on black shoes, but they are not comfortable. Then I try on white sports shoes. They are soft and light, and I can walk and run in them. I love them.
The shoes are not cheap, but my mom says yes. I wear them out of the store. On the way home, I look at my feet all the time. They look great.

title: A Trip to the Zoo
paragraphs: Today my class goes to the zoo. We go by bus with our teacher. The zoo is big, and there are animals from all over the world.

First, we see the lions. They sleep in the sun. Then we see the monkeys. They are funny, and they jump from tree to tree. The children laugh at them. The giraffes are very tall, and they eat leaves from the top of the trees.
My favorite animals are the penguins. They are small and black and white. They swim very fast in the cold water. I want to come back to the zoo with my family.

title: A Letter to a Friend
paragraphs: Dear Paul, How are you? I am fine. I am in a new city now, and I have a new school. My school is big, and my teacher is nice. I have two new friends. Their names are Mark and Julia.
Our new apartment is on the fifth floor. From my window, I can see the park and the river. My room is small, but it is bright.
I miss you and our old street. Do you still play soccer every Friday? Please write to me soon and tell me your news. Your friend, Mike

title: Cooking with Dad
paragraphs: Every Friday evening, my dad and I cook dinner together. My mom works late on Fridays, so it is our job. We look in the fridge and choose something to make.
Tonight, we make pasta with vegetables. I wash the tomatoes and the peppers. My dad cuts the onions because they make me cry. We cook the pasta in a big pot of water.
At seven o'clock, my mom comes home. The table is ready, and dinner is hot. She tries the pasta and says, "This is delicious!" My dad and I are very proud.

title: The Library
paragraphs: There is a library near my house. It is a big old building with tall windows. Inside, it is very quiet. People read, study, and use the computers.
I go to the library every Tuesday. I can take five books home for three weeks. I like books about animals and stories about other countries. The librarian helps me find good books.
There is also a room for children. On Saturday mornings, a woman reads stories to the little kids. My little brother goes there with my mom. He loves the stories and the pictures.

title: My Teacher
paragraphs: My English teacher is Ms. Green. She is young, and she has curly red hair. She is very kind, and she is never angry. All the students like her.
In her lessons, we sing songs and play games. We read short stories and talk about them. Sometimes we watch funny videos in English. Her lessons are never boring.
When I make a mistake, Ms. Green helps me. She says, "That's OK. Try again." Now English is my favorite subject. I want to be a teacher like Ms. Green one day.

title: The Magic Hat
paragraphs: Ella finds an old hat in her grandmother's house. It is black and tall, and it has a red ribbon. Ella puts the hat on her head and looks in the mirror.

Suddenly, a small white rabbit jumps out of the hat. Ella is very surprised. She takes off the hat and looks inside. There is nothing there. She puts it on again, and now there are flowers in her hands.
Ella runs to the kitchen. "Grandma, this hat is magic!" she says. Her grandmother laughs. "Yes," she says. "It was my hat when I was a girl. Now it is yours."

title: Spring
paragraphs: I love spring. After the long, cold winter, the days are warm again. The sun is bright, and the sky is blue. There are new green leaves on the trees.
In spring, there are flowers everywhere. In my garden, there are red, yellow, and purple flowers. Birds sing in the morning, and I can hear them from my bed.
On spring days, I walk to school, and I don't need a big coat. After school, I ride my bike with my friends. We stay outside until dinner time. Spring is the best season.

title: A Busy Mom
paragraphs: My mom is always busy. She gets up at six o'clock and makes breakfast for us. Then she drives my sister and me to school. After that, she goes to work at an office.
In the evening, my mom cooks dinner and helps us with our homework. She also cleans the house and washes our clothes. I help her a little. I wash the dishes and take out the trash.
On Sunday, my mom rests. She sits in the garden and reads a magazine. We bring her tea and cake. She says Sunday is her favorite day.

title: The Train Trip
paragraphs: Today we go to the mountains by train. The trip is three hours long. We have big bags, sandwiches, and water. The train is clean and comfortable.
I sit by the window. First, I see the city and the tall buildings. Then I see fields, cows, and small villages. After two hours, there are big mountains with snow on the top.
My little brother sleeps, and my dad reads a book. My mom and I play cards. When the train stops, we get off and breathe the cold, fresh air. It is beautiful here.

title: My Computer
paragraphs: I have a computer at home. It is on my desk in my bedroom. I use it every day for my homework. I write my stories on it, and I find information for school.
I also use my computer to talk to my cousins. They live in another country. We talk on video every Sunday. I can see their faces, and they can see mine.
Sometimes I play games on my computer, but only for one hour. My parents say too much time on the computer is bad for my eyes. They are right, so I go outside too.

title: The Hungry Bear
paragraphs: In a big forest, there is a brown bear. It is spring, and the bear is very hungry. He walks through the trees and looks for food.

He finds some berries, but they are not ready. He finds a river, but he can't catch a fish. Then he smells something sweet. It is honey in a tall tree. The bees are angry, and they fly around the bear.
The bear climbs the tree and takes the honey. The bees sting his nose, but he doesn't care. The honey is delicious. Now the bear is happy, and he goes to sleep.

title: My Street
paragraphs: I live on a quiet street in a small town. There are twelve houses on my street. Most of the houses are white, and they have small gardens. There are tall trees on both sides.
At the end of my street, there is a bakery. It opens at seven o'clock, and the street smells of fresh bread. Next to the bakery, there is a small shop with fruit and vegetables.
The people on my street are friendly. In summer, we have a party in the street. Everybody brings food, and the children play together until late.

title: Sports Day
paragraphs: Today is sports day at my school. There are no lessons, and all the students are outside. The weather is sunny and warm. Our parents come to watch us.
There are many races. I run in the hundred meter race, and I come third. My friend Ana wins the long jump. Our class also plays in a big game of tug of war. We pull very hard, and we win.
At the end of the day, the teachers give us medals. I am tired and hot, but I am very happy. I love sports day.

title: At the Doctor's
paragraphs: Today I am sick. I have a headache and a sore throat, and I am very hot. I don't go to school. My mom takes me to the doctor.
The doctor is a tall woman with a friendly face. She looks in my mouth and listens to my heart. "You have a cold," she says. "Drink a lot of water, and stay in bed for two days."
At home, I lie in bed and sleep. My mom makes me chicken soup and honey tea. After two days, I feel much better. I am ready for school again.

title: My Hobby
paragraphs: My hobby is drawing. I draw every day after school. I have a big book of white paper and many colored pencils. I draw animals, people, and houses.
My favorite thing to draw is horses. I like their long legs and their beautiful faces. Sometimes I draw my cat, but she doesn't sit still. She always walks away.
My drawings are on the walls of my room. My aunt is an artist, and she gives me lessons on Saturdays. She says my drawings are very good. One day, I want to be an artist too.

title: The Snowman
paragraphs: It snows all night, and in the morning, the garden is white. Ben and his sister Amy put on their coats and boots. They run outside and make a big snowman.
The snowman has two black stones for eyes and a carrot for a nose. Amy gives him her old red scarf. Ben puts his dad's hat on the snowman's head. "He is perfect," says Amy.
That night, Ben looks out of the window. The snowman is still there in the moonlight. Ben waves at him. In the morning, the sun is warm, and the snowman is very small. Ben is a little sad.

title: The Fish Tank
paragraphs: In my classroom, there is a big fish tank. There are eight fish in it. Some are orange, some are yellow, and one is blue. The blue fish is the biggest, and we call him King.
Every week, two students take care of the fish. They give them food in the morning and look at the water. This week, it is my job with my friend Omar.
The fish are beautiful. When we are tired, our teacher says, "Look at the fish for one minute." We watch them swim, and we feel calm again.

title: Feeding the Ducks
paragraphs: There is a small lake in the park near my house. Many ducks live on the lake. On Sunday afternoons, my grandfather and I go there to see them.
We take some old bread and some seeds in a bag. When the ducks see us, they swim very fast to the side of the lake. They are noisy and hungry. The baby ducks are small and yellow.
My grandfather sits on a bench and watches. I give the food to the ducks, and they eat it all. Then we walk around the lake and go home for tea.

title: My House
paragraphs: I live in a house with my parents and my brother. Our house has two floors. Downstairs, there is a living room, a kitchen, and a bathroom. Upstairs, there are three bedrooms.
The kitchen is my favorite room. It is big and sunny, and it has a round table. We eat all our meals there. My mom has many plants on the windows.
Behind the house, there is a garden with green grass and a tall tree. My dad makes a swing for us on the tree. In summer, we eat dinner in the garden.

title: Pizza Night
paragraphs: Friday is pizza night in our family. We don't buy pizza. We make it at home. Everybody helps, and the kitchen is always a little dirty after.
My mom makes the dough in the afternoon. Then we put tomato sauce on it. My dad likes mushrooms and peppers on his pizza. My sister likes only cheese. I like pizza with ham and pineapple.
We cook the pizzas in the hot oven for fifteen minutes. Then we sit in the living room and eat them in front of a movie. It is the best night of the week.

title: The Mail Carrier
paragraphs: Every morning at ten o'clock, Mrs. Brown comes to our street. She is a mail carrier, and she brings letters and packages. She walks to every house with a big blue bag.
Mrs. Brown walks about fifteen kilometers every day. She works in the sun, in the rain, and in the snow. She says the job keeps her strong.
All the children on our street know her. She always says hello, and she knows the names of all the dogs. In December, we give her a card and a box of chocolates.

title: The Little Boat
paragraphs: Jack makes a little boat from paper. It is white with a small blue flag. He takes it to the river near his house and puts it on the water.
The boat sails slowly down the river. Jack walks next to it. The boat goes past a big rock and a tall tree. A duck swims next to it and looks at it.
Then the boat goes under a bridge. On the other side, a little girl sees it. She picks it up out of the water and smiles. Jack waves at her, and she waves back. Now they are friends.

title: A Summer Vacation
paragraphs: In July, my family goes on vacation. This year, we go to a small town by a lake. We stay in a wooden house with a big garden. There are mountains all around the lake.
Every day, we swim in the lake. The water is cold, but it is clean and clear. In the afternoon, we walk in the forest or ride our bikes. My dad likes fishing.
In the evening, we cook dinner outside and eat in the garden. We look at the stars in the sky. There are many stars here, more than in the city. I love this place.

title: My Uncle
paragraphs: My uncle Peter is my mom's brother. He is forty years old, and he is very tall. He has a black beard and a loud laugh. He lives on a farm with his wife and their three children.
On the farm, there are cows, sheep, chickens, and two horses. My uncle gets up at five o'clock every morning. He works outside all day. He is never tired.
Every summer, I stay with my uncle for two weeks. I help him with the animals, and I ride the horses. I love the farm, and I love my uncle.

title: At the Supermarket
paragraphs: On Thursday evenings, I go to the supermarket. I always have a list, because I forget things. Today I need milk, eggs, bread, rice, and some fruit.
The supermarket is big and bright. I take a cart and walk down the long rows. I find the milk and the eggs first. Then I look for the rice. The fruit is near the door. I buy apples and a melon.
At the end, I stand in line and pay. The woman at the checkout is friendly. She puts my things in two bags. I carry them to my car and drive home.

title: Bedtime
paragraphs: At nine o'clock, it is bedtime in our house. I put on my pajamas and brush my teeth. Then I go to my bedroom and get into bed.
My dad comes into my room and sits on my bed. Every night, he reads a story to me. Tonight the story is about a dragon and a little girl. It is exciting, and I don't want it to stop.
After the story, my dad turns off the light. "Good night," he says. "Sleep well." I close my eyes and think about the dragon. Soon I am asleep.

title: On the Farm
paragraphs: Maria lives on a farm with her parents. There are many animals on the farm. There are cows, pigs, goats, and lots of chickens. There is also an old dog called Rex.
Every morning before school, Maria helps her mother. She gives food to the chickens and looks for eggs. Sometimes she finds ten eggs, and sometimes she finds twenty.
After school, Maria plays with the baby goats. They are small and funny, and they jump everywhere. In the evening, she sits on the steps with Rex and watches the sun go down.

title: The Guitar Lesson
paragraphs: Every Monday, I have a guitar lesson. My teacher is an old man called Mr. Stone. He has long gray hair, and he plays the guitar very well.
The lesson is one hour long. First, I play some easy songs. Then Mr. Stone shows me something new. Today, I learn a new song. It is hard, and my fingers hurt a little.
At home, I practice every day for thirty minutes. My family listens to me. My little sister sings with my music. Next month, I play in a small concert at my school.

title: The Yellow Umbrella
paragraphs: Kim has a yellow umbrella. It is big and bright, and she loves it. One morning, it is raining, and she takes it to the bus stop.
At the bus stop, there is an old man with no umbrella. He is wet and cold. Kim stands next to him and holds her umbrella over his head too. "Thank you," says the man.
The next week, Kim sees the old man again. He has a present for her. It is a small yellow raincoat. "Now you can be dry too," he says. Kim laughs and puts it on.

title: My Phone
paragraphs: I have a phone, and I use it every day. I call my parents, and I send messages to my friends. I also take photos with it. My phone has a good camera.
In the morning, my phone wakes me up at seven o'clock. On the bus, I listen to music and read the news. At work, I check my calendar on it.
But in the evening, I put my phone in the kitchen. I don't take it to my bedroom. I read a book before bed, and I sleep much better.

title: The Swimming Pool
paragraphs: There is a big swimming pool in my town. It is open every day from seven in the morning to nine at night. I go there with my friend Lucas on Saturdays.
The water is warm, and the pool is very clean. We swim for one hour. Lucas is a good swimmer, and he is very fast. I am slow, but I can swim for a long time.
After swimming, we are always very hungry. We go to the cafe next to the pool and eat hot fries. Then we take the bus home. We are tired, but we feel great.

title: The New Baby
paragraphs: We have a new baby in our family. She is my little sister, and her name is Grace. She is two weeks old. She is very small, and she has a lot of black hair.
Grace sleeps a lot. When she is awake, she cries, and she is hungry. My mom and dad are always tired. I help them. I bring the clean clothes, and I sing to the baby.
When I sing, Grace stops crying. She looks at me with her big dark eyes. My mom says Grace loves my songs. I think I am a good big brother.

title: Autumn
paragraphs: In autumn, the weather is cool and windy. The days are shorter, and it often rains. The leaves on the trees are red, orange, and yellow. Then they fall to the ground.
I like walking in the park in autumn. The leaves make a sound under my feet. My little dog runs in the leaves and plays. The air smells fresh and clean.
In autumn, we eat warm food. My mom makes pumpkin soup and apple cake. In the evening, we sit together in the living room and drink hot tea. Autumn is cozy.

title: The Old Clock
paragraphs: In my grandfather's house, there is a very old clock. It is tall and brown, and it stands in the hall. Every hour, it makes a loud sound. Bong, bong, bong!
One day, the clock stops. My grandfather is very sad. "This clock was my father's clock," he says. He tries to fix it, but he can't.
The next day, we take the clock to a small shop in town. An old woman looks at it for a long time. Then she opens it and fixes a small part. Bong! The clock works again, and my grandfather smiles.

title: The Baker
paragraphs: My aunt Sophie is a baker. She has a small bakery in the center of our town. She starts work at four o'clock in the morning, when everybody is asleep.
She makes bread, cakes, and cookies. Her bakery smells wonderful. People come every morning to buy fresh bread for breakfast. Her chocolate cake is very popular.
My aunt finishes work at two o'clock in the afternoon. Then she goes home and sleeps for two hours. She says her job is hard, but she loves it. I want to work in her bakery one day.

title: A Walk in the Forest
paragraphs: On Sunday, my family takes a walk in the forest. The forest is near our town. It is big and green, and it is very quiet. We walk on a small path between the tall trees.
We see many things. There are birds in the trees and small flowers on the ground. My brother finds a big beetle. Then we see a deer. It looks at us and runs away.
After two hours, we stop near a small river. We sit on the rocks and eat our sandwiches. The water is very cold. Then we walk back home.

title: Moving Day
paragraphs: Today is moving day. My family and I go to a new apartment in another part of the city. There are boxes everywhere. There are boxes in the kitchen, in the hall, and in my room.
A big truck comes at nine o'clock. Two strong men carry our furniture down the stairs. They carry the sofa, the beds, and the big table. My dad helps them, and my mom carries the plants.
The new apartment is bigger than the old one. My new room has a balcony. In the evening, we eat pizza on the floor because the table is still in a box.

title: The Dentist
paragraphs: I go to the dentist two times a year. Today is my appointment. I am a little scared, but my mom comes with me. We sit in the waiting room and read magazines.
The dentist is a young man with a big smile. I sit in a big chair, and I open my mouth. He looks at all my teeth with a small mirror. "Your teeth are very good," he says.
He tells me to brush my teeth two times a day and eat fewer sweets. Then he gives me a new toothbrush. It is green, my favorite color.

title: Games at Home
paragraphs: It is a rainy weekend, and we can't go outside. My cousins come to our house. There are six children, and we are all bored. Then my aunt has an idea.
She brings old board games from the closet. We play a game with cards and a game with a small house and money. My cousin Tim wins every game, and he is very happy.
Later, we build a big tent in the living room. We use blankets and chairs. We sit inside it with flashlights and tell scary stories. It is the best rainy day.

title: The Kite
paragraphs: Leo has a new kite. It is red and yellow, and it looks like a big bird. It is a windy day, so Leo and his dad go to the top of the hill.
Leo runs, and the kite goes up into the sky. It flies high above the trees. Leo holds the string very tight. Suddenly, the wind is very strong, and the string breaks.
The kite flies away over the hill. Leo is sad. But the next day, a farmer comes to his house with the kite. "Is this your bird?" he asks with a smile.

title: Fruit and Vegetables
paragraphs: I love fruit and vegetables. They have so many colors. Tomatoes and strawberries are red. Bananas and lemons are yellow. Carrots and oranges are orange. Grapes can be green or purple.
Every day, I eat fruit for breakfast. I usually have a banana or an apple. At lunch, I eat a big salad with lettuce, tomatoes, and cucumbers.
My favorite vegetable is the potato. I like potatoes in soup, and I like them hot from the oven. My favorite fruit is the mango. It is sweet and soft.

title: The Taxi Driver
paragraphs: Ahmed is a taxi driver in a big city. He works at night, from seven in the evening to five in the morning. He drives a yellow car, and he knows every street in the city.
Many different people take his taxi. Some go to the airport, and some go home after a party. Some people are quiet, and some talk a lot. Ahmed likes to listen to their stories.
In the morning, Ahmed goes home. His children are going to school, and he is going to bed. He sleeps all day. He doesn't see his family very much, and that is hard.

title: My Cat Luna
paragraphs: My cat is called Luna. She is black with green eyes. She is five years old. Luna is very lazy. She sleeps for about sixteen hours every day.
Luna loves the sun. In the morning, she sleeps by the kitchen window. In the afternoon, she moves to the living room, because the sun is there. She always finds the warm places.
At night, Luna is not lazy. She runs around the house and plays with her toys. Sometimes she jumps on my bed at three o'clock in the morning. I love her, but I want to sleep.

title: The Museum
paragraphs: On Saturday, my dad and I go to the city museum. It is a very big building with white walls. Inside, there are old things from many countries and many years.
We see old coins, old clothes, and beautiful paintings. My favorite room has dinosaur bones. There is a very big dinosaur in the middle of the room. It is taller than a house.
We stay in the museum for three hours. Then we eat lunch in the museum cafe. I buy a small dinosaur toy in the shop. I want to come back next month.

title: Camping
paragraphs: This summer, my family goes camping. We drive to a big forest near a lake. We put up our tent between two tall trees. It is green and has space for four people.
In the day, we walk in the forest and swim in the lake. My dad shows me how to make a fire. In the evening, we cook sausages on the fire and eat them with bread.
At night, it is very dark, and I can hear many sounds. I hear owls and the wind in the trees. I am a little scared, but I am warm in my sleeping bag.

title: My Week
paragraphs: On Mondays and Wednesdays, I go to the gym after work. On Tuesdays, I have a Spanish lesson. On Thursdays, I meet my friends for dinner. I am busy all week.
On Fridays, I am always tired. I go home, cook a simple dinner, and watch a movie. I usually go to bed at ten o'clock.
On Saturdays, I clean my apartment and go shopping. On Sundays, I visit my parents. My mother makes a big lunch, and we talk all afternoon. Then the week starts again.

title: The Lost Key
paragraphs: Every day, Mr. Brown puts his key in his coat pocket. But today, when he comes home from work, the key is not there. He looks in all his pockets and in his bag. It is not there.
He sits on the steps in front of his house. It is cold, and it is getting dark. He calls his wife, but she is at work until nine o'clock.
Then his neighbor's little boy comes out. "Mr. Brown, is this your key?" he asks. "It is in the street near the bus stop." Mr. Brown is very happy, and he gives the boy some chocolate.

title: The Hotel
paragraphs: We are on vacation, and we stay in a hotel by the sea. It is a big white hotel with a swimming pool. Our room is on the fourth floor, and it has a balcony with a view of the sea.
Every morning, we have breakfast in the hotel restaurant. There is fruit, bread, eggs, and pancakes. I eat too much every day.
The people who work in the hotel are very friendly. The man at the front desk helps us with a map of the town. The hotel is perfect, and I don't want to go home.

title: Learning to Swim
paragraphs: I am thirty years old, and I can't swim. This year, I want to learn. So every Tuesday evening, I go to a swimming lesson for adults.
There are six people in my class. Our teacher is a young woman called Sara. She is very patient. In the first lesson, we only put our faces in the water. It is not easy for me.
Now it is my eighth lesson. I can swim from one side of the pool to the other. It is only twenty-five meters, but I am very proud. Next summer, I want to swim in the sea.

title: The Tall Tree
paragraphs: In the middle of our village, there is a very tall tree. It is more than two hundred years old. It is taller than all the houses, and its branches are very long.
In summer, the tree gives us shade. Old people sit on the benches under it and talk. Children play around it. Birds make their nests in its branches.
Every winter, the people of the village put lights on the tall tree. In the evening, it is bright and beautiful. Everybody loves the tree. It is the heart of our village.

title: My Classroom
paragraphs: My classroom is on the second floor of my school. It is big and bright, with four big windows. There are twenty-four desks and chairs for the students.
At the front of the room, there is a big whiteboard and the teacher's desk. On the walls, there are maps and posters. There are also pictures by the students.
At the back of the classroom, there are shelves with books and games. There is also a small plant on the window. Every week, one student waters it. This week, it is me.

title: The Ice Cream Shop
paragraphs: In summer, there is a long line in front of the ice cream shop on our street. The shop has thirty different flavors. There is chocolate, strawberry, lemon, and many more.
My favorite flavor is mint with chocolate chips. My brother always gets vanilla. My mom likes coffee ice cream, and my dad likes everything.
The man in the shop is called Tony. He is from Italy, and he makes all the ice cream himself. He says the secret is fresh milk and lots of love. His ice cream is the best in town.

title: The Sleepy Owl
paragraphs: In a tall tree, there lives an owl. In the day, the owl sleeps. In the night, he flies through the forest and looks for food. That is the life of an owl.
But one day, a woodpecker comes to the tree. Knock, knock, knock! The woodpecker is very loud, and the owl can't sleep. "Please stop," says the owl. But the woodpecker doesn't stop.
That night, the owl is very tired. He can't see well, and he can't find food. The next morning, he finds a new tree, far from the woodpecker. Finally, he can sleep.

title: Mrs. White
paragraphs: Mrs. White lives in the apartment under my apartment. She is eighty years old, and she lives alone. Her husband died many years ago, and her children live in other cities.
Mrs. White is very active. She walks in the park every morning and goes to an art class on Thursdays. She has many beautiful plants on her balcony.
On Saturdays, I go shopping for her. I carry her heavy bags up the stairs. Then she makes tea for me, and we talk. She tells me interesting stories about the city long ago.

title: Our Car
paragraphs: Our car is old and blue. It is fifteen years old, and it is very small. There is space for four people, but only two big bags. My dad loves it.
Every morning, my dad drives the car to work. On the weekend, we go to the lake or to the mountains. The car is slow, and it makes a lot of noise.
Sometimes the car doesn't start, and my dad is angry. My mom wants a new car, but my dad says no. "This car is part of our family," he says.

title: A Snow Day
paragraphs: This morning, there is a lot of snow. The snow is very deep, and the buses can't go. There is no school today. My sister and I are very happy.
We eat breakfast and put on our warm clothes. We go outside and play in the snow. We make snow angels and throw snowballs at our dad. He throws snowballs at us too.
After two hours, our hands and feet are cold. We go inside, and our mom makes hot chocolate. We sit by the window and watch the snow. It is still falling.

title: The Flower Shop
paragraphs: Julia has a small flower shop near the train station. The shop is full of color. There are roses, tulips, and sunflowers. There are also small plants for the home.

Julia opens the shop at eight o'clock. Many people buy flowers on their way to work. Some flowers are for birthdays, and some are for a mother or a friend. Some people buy one flower, and some buy a big bunch.
Julia loves her job. She says flowers make people happy. At the end of the day, she takes the old flowers home and puts them on her kitchen table.

title: The Park
paragraphs: There is a big park near my home. It has green grass, tall trees, and a small lake. In the middle of the park, there is a playground for children.
In the morning, people run and walk their dogs in the park. At lunchtime, office workers sit on the grass and eat sandwiches. In the afternoon, children come from school and play.
I go to the park every evening after work. I walk around the lake two times. It takes about thirty minutes. Then I sit on a bench and watch the ducks. It is very relaxing.

title: The Big Game
paragraphs: Today my team plays in a big soccer game. We play against a team from another town. Many parents and friends come to watch. My mom and dad sit in the front.
The other team is very good. After the first half, they have one goal, and we have zero. Our coach says, "Don't stop. Work together." We go back on the field and try very hard.
In the second half, my friend Pedro scores a goal. Then, two minutes before the end, I score a goal. We win! Everybody shouts and jumps. It is the best day.

title: A New Student
paragraphs: Today there is a new student in my class. Her name is Aiko, and she is from Japan. She is quiet, and she doesn't know anybody. She sits alone at lunch.
I go to her table and sit down. "Hi, I'm Sophie," I say. Aiko smiles. Her English is good. She tells me about her old school and her city. I tell her about our town.
After lunch, I show her the library and the gym. Now we sit together every day. Aiko teaches me some Japanese words, and I help her with math.

title: The Present
paragraphs: It is Anna's birthday next week. Her brother Tom wants to buy her a present, but he has only five dollars. He goes to many shops, but everything is too expensive.
Then Tom has an idea. He takes some paper and colored pencils. He works on his present every evening in his room. He doesn't show it to anybody.
On Anna's birthday, Tom gives her a small book. It is full of his drawings and funny stories about them. Anna reads it and laughs. "This is the best present," she says, and she hugs him.

title: Breakfast
paragraphs: People eat many different things for breakfast. In my house, we all like different food. My dad eats eggs and toast. My mom has only coffee and a small piece of fruit.
My little brother eats cereal with milk every day. He never wants anything else. I like yogurt with fruit and honey. Sometimes I eat pancakes on the weekend.
My grandmother says breakfast is the most important meal of the day. She eats a big breakfast every morning at seven o'clock. She is eighty-two, and she is very healthy, so maybe she is right.

title: The White Horse
paragraphs: There is a white horse in the field near my school. She is beautiful and very big. Every day, I stop at the fence and look at her. Sometimes she comes to the fence.
One day, a farmer is in the field. "Do you like my horse?" he asks. "Her name is Star." He gives me a carrot. I give it to Star, and she eats it from my hand. Her nose is very soft.
Now I bring a carrot or an apple every day. Star knows me. When she sees me, she runs to the fence. She is my friend.

title: The Old Photo
paragraphs: In my grandmother's house, there is an old photo on the wall. It is black and white. In the photo, there is a young man and a young woman. They are standing in front of a church.
"Who are these people?" I ask my grandmother. She laughs. "That is me, and that is your grandfather," she says. "It is our wedding day." I am very surprised. They look so young.
My grandmother tells me about the wedding. There were a hundred people and a big cake. In the evening, everybody danced. She smiles when she talks about it.

title: Sunday Bread
paragraphs: Every Sunday morning, my dad goes to the bakery. He leaves the house at eight o'clock, and he always takes me with him. We walk there together. It takes ten minutes.
There is always a line in front of the bakery. We wait and talk with our neighbors. The smell of fresh bread is wonderful. When we go inside, it is very warm.
My dad buys a big loaf of bread and some croissants. The baker gives me a small cookie. We walk home, and my mom makes coffee. Then we eat breakfast together.

title: My Office
paragraphs: I work in an office in the city center. My office is on the tenth floor of a tall building. From my desk, I can see the river and the old bridge.
There are twelve people in my team. We work on computers all day. We write emails, answer the phone, and have many meetings. My boss is a woman called Mrs. Lopez. She is strict, but fair.
At lunch, I eat with my colleagues in the kitchen. We talk about our weekends and our families. I finish work at five o'clock and take the bus home.

title: The River
paragraphs: A big river goes through my town. It is long and wide, and the water is green. There are three bridges over it. The oldest bridge is made of stone.
In summer, people swim in the river and sit on the grass next to it. Some people go fishing, and some people go out in small boats. Children throw stones into the water.
In winter, the river is cold and gray. Sometimes there is ice on it. But I still like to walk next to it. The river is always beautiful, in every season.

title: At the Airport
paragraphs: Today I am at the airport. I am going to visit my sister in another country. My flight is at eleven o'clock, so I am here at nine. The airport is big and very busy.
First, I give my big bag to a woman at the desk. Then I go through security. I take my phone and my keys out of my pockets. After that, I find my gate.
I have one hour, so I buy a coffee and a book. Then I sit by the big window and watch the planes. At half past ten, I get on the plane.

title: The Clever Crow
paragraphs: It is a hot summer day, and a crow is very thirsty. He flies around and looks for water. Then he finds a tall jar in a garden. There is a little water in the bottom.
The crow puts his head into the jar, but he can't drink. His beak is too short. He thinks and thinks. Then he has an idea.
He picks up a small stone and drops it into the jar. Then another stone, and another. Slowly, the water comes up. Finally, the crow can drink. He is very happy, and very clever.

title: A Day Off
paragraphs: Today I don't go to work. It is my day off. I don't set my alarm, and I sleep until nine o'clock. The sun is shining through the window.
I make a big breakfast with eggs, toast, and orange juice. I eat it on my balcony. Then I call my friend Nina. We go for a long walk by the river and have lunch in a nice restaurant.
In the afternoon, I read a book on the sofa and take a short nap. In the evening, I cook a good dinner and watch a movie. It is a perfect day.

title: After the Rain
paragraphs: It rains all morning. The sky is dark, and the wind is strong. We can't play outside, so my sister and I sit by the window and wait.

At two o'clock, the rain stops. The clouds move away, and the sun comes out. Then my sister shouts, "Look! A rainbow!" There is a big rainbow over the hills. It has many colors: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple.
We run outside to see it better. Our neighbors come out too. Everybody looks at the sky. After ten minutes, the rainbow goes away. But we still remember it.

title: My Favorite Season
paragraphs: My favorite season is summer. In summer, the days are long and hot. There is no school, and I have a lot of free time. I can stay outside until nine o'clock in the evening.
In summer, I go to the beach with my family. I swim in the sea and eat ice cream. I also ride my bike and play with my friends in the park every day.
My brother doesn't like summer. He says it is too hot. His favorite season is winter, because he loves snow. We are very different, but we are good brothers.

title: The Painter
paragraphs: Mr. Hill is a painter, but he doesn't paint pictures. He paints houses. He paints walls, doors, and windows. He works with his son, and they have a small white van.
This week, they are painting our house. The old color is brown. The new color is light yellow. They start at eight o'clock every morning and work all day. They listen to the radio and sing.
After four days, the house is finished. It looks new and bright. My mom is very happy. She makes coffee and cake for Mr. Hill and his son.

title: The Concert
paragraphs: Tonight I am going to a concert with my best friend. The band is our favorite band. The concert is in a big hall in the city. It starts at eight o'clock.
We arrive at seven, and there are already many people. Everybody is excited. When the band comes on, everybody shouts. The music is very loud. We sing all the songs and dance.
The concert is two hours long. At the end, my ears are ringing, and my feet hurt. But I am very happy. We talk about the concert all the way home.

title: Visiting Grandpa
paragraphs: My grandfather is in the hospital. He has a problem with his heart, but the doctors say he is getting better. Today, my mom and I visit him.
We bring him flowers, grapes, and a newspaper. His room is clean and quiet. He is in bed, but he is happy to see us. He says the food in the hospital is terrible.
We stay for two hours. We talk, and I tell him about school. Before we go, he says, "Next week, I am going home." I hug him, and he smiles.

title: Two Friends
paragraphs: Jack is a big dog, and Pip is a small gray mouse. They live in the same old farmhouse. Jack sleeps by the fire, and Pip lives in a little hole in the wall.
One cold night, a cat comes into the house. The cat sees Pip and runs after her. Pip is very scared. She runs to Jack and hides under his big ear.
Jack opens his eyes and makes a loud sound. The cat is scared, and it runs away. Pip comes out and says, "Thank you, Jack." From that night, Jack and Pip are best friends.

title: My First Job
paragraphs: When I was sixteen, I got my first job. I worked in a small cafe near my school on Saturdays and Sundays. I washed the dishes, cleaned the tables, and sometimes made coffee for the customers.
The first day was terrible. I dropped three cups, and I forgot two orders. I went home and cried. I wanted to stop, but my mother said, "Go back next weekend. It will be easier." She was right.

After a few weeks, I knew all the regular customers and their favorite drinks. An old man came every Sunday at ten o'clock and always ordered black coffee and a piece of lemon cake. He always left a big tip and told me jokes.
I worked at that cafe for two years. The money wasn't very good, but I learned a lot. I learned to work hard, to be polite, and to stay calm when it was busy. Those lessons are still useful today.

title: A Weekend in the Mountains
paragraphs: Last month, my friends and I went to the mountains for the weekend. We left early on Saturday morning and drove for four hours. The roads were narrow and full of curves, and my friend Tom felt sick.

We stayed in a small wooden house near a lake. It didn't have a television or the internet, but it had a big fireplace and a beautiful view. On the first evening, we cooked dinner together and played cards until midnight.

On Sunday, we climbed to the top of a mountain. It was harder than we expected. The path was steep and rocky, and it took us three hours. But the view from the top was amazing. We could see lakes, forests, and small villages far below us.
We were very tired when we got home on Sunday night, but everybody agreed it was a great trip. We are going to go back in the winter, when there is snow.

title: The Lost Wallet
paragraphs: One evening, Daniel was walking home from work when he saw a brown wallet on the sidewalk. He picked it up and looked inside. There was a lot of money, two bank cards, and a driver's license with a woman's photo.
Daniel thought about the money for a moment. He needed a new bike, and nobody saw him. But then he looked at the photo again. The woman looked kind, and she probably needed her cards.

The address was on the license, so Daniel walked there. It was a small yellow house on the other side of the park. An old woman opened the door. When she saw the wallet, she started to cry. "My husband's pension is in there," she said. "Thank you so much."
The next week, Daniel received a letter. Inside, there was a thank you card and a small cake. He didn't get any money, but he felt happier than he expected.

title: Healthy Habits
paragraphs: Many people want to be healthier, but they don't know where to start. Doctors say that small changes are often better than big ones. You don't need to change your whole life in one day.
