paragraphs: One night in winter, a fire started in the old bakery on Main Street. It was two o'clock in the morning, and everybody in the street was asleep. Only one person was awake: a teenage boy called Josh, who couldn't sleep and was looking out of his window.

Josh saw smoke coming from the bakery. He knew the baker and his family lived above the shop. He called the fire department, and then he ran outside and started knocking on doors and shouting. The neighbors woke up and came out.

The baker, his wife, and their two small children came down the stairs just in time. A few minutes later, the fire trucks arrived. The firefighters worked for two hours and stopped the fire. The bakery was badly damaged, but everybody was safe.
The next day, the whole town talked about Josh. The mayor gave him a special award. And the baker promised him free bread for the rest of his life.

title: My Art Class
paragraphs: Last autumn, I started an art class at a community center near my home. I haven't painted since I was a child, and I was nervous on the first day. But the teacher, Anna, made everybody feel welcome.

There are ten people in the class. Some are students, some are retired, and one is a doctor. We meet every Tuesday evening for two hours. In the first lessons, we drew simple things, like fruit, bottles, and flowers. Then we started to use paint. Anna showed us how to mix colors and how to paint light and shadow.
At first, my paintings were not very good. But Anna always found something positive to say. "Look at this color," she said, or "I like the shape of this apple." Every week, I learned something new.
At the end of the year, the class had a small exhibition. My painting of the river near my house was on the wall, next to the others. My family came, and my mother bought it.

title: Selling at the Market
paragraphs: Every Sunday, my wife and I sell our homemade jam at a market in the town square. We started three years ago as a hobby. Now it is a small business.

We make the jam at home during the week. In summer, we use strawberries, raspberries, and cherries. In autumn, we use apples, plums, and figs. We buy the fruit from local farmers. Each batch takes about three hours, and the kitchen is always hot and sticky.

On Sunday mornings, we get up at five o'clock and load the car. At seven, we put up our small table and our tent. We always give customers a taste of the jam on a small piece of bread. Many people come back every week, and some of them are now our friends.
We don't make a lot of money, but we enjoy it very much. Last month, a small shop in the city asked to sell our jam. Maybe one day, this hobby will be our full-time job.

title: Energy from the Sun
paragraphs: Last year, my parents put solar panels on the roof of their house. Solar panels use the light from the sun to make electricity. They are flat and dark blue, and they face the south, where the sun is strongest.

At first, my father was not sure. The panels were expensive, and he didn't know if they would work in our country, where it often rains. But they work even on cloudy days. They make less electricity, but they still make some.

In summer, the panels make more electricity than my parents need. The extra electricity goes to the town's power network, and the electricity company pays them for it. In winter, they make less, so my parents still buy some electricity. But overall, their electricity bill is much lower than before.
My father now talks about the panels all the time. He checks an app on his phone every evening to see how much electricity they made. He says it is better than television.

title: My First Opera
paragraphs: Last month, my friend Sophie invited me to the opera. I have never been to an opera before, and I didn't think I would like it. I thought it was boring music for old, rich people. But Sophie had two free tickets, so I said yes.

The opera house was beautiful, with red seats, golden walls, and a huge light in the ceiling. Everybody was dressed nicely. The opera was in Italian, but there were English words on a small screen above the stage.

When the music started, I was surprised. The orchestra was amazing, and the singers had incredible voices. They sang so loudly without a microphone! The story was about two young people in love, but their families hated each other. It was very sad, and at the end, I cried a little.
The opera lasted three hours, but it didn't feel long. On the way home, I told Sophie I wanted to go again. I was wrong about opera. It isn't boring at all.

title: Cleaning the Beach
paragraphs: Every year in September, our town organizes a beach clean-up day. Hundreds of volunteers come to the beach on a Saturday morning to collect trash. This year, I went for the first time with my two children.

We got big bags and gloves at the meeting point. Then we walked along the beach and picked up everything that didn't belong there. We found plastic bottles, bags, old shoes, fishing nets, and many small pieces of plastic. My son even found a broken toy car and an old phone.
After three hours, we filled six big bags. In total, the volunteers collected more than two tons of trash. The organizers told us that most of it came from the sea, not from people on the beach.

My children were shocked. "Why do people throw things in the sea?" my daughter asked. It was a good question. On the way home, we talked about how we can use less plastic at home. It was a good lesson for all of us.

title: The Best Advice
paragraphs: When I was twenty, I was very unhappy. I didn't like my studies, I didn't have much money, and I didn't know what I wanted to do with my life. One day, I talked to my grandfather about it.

He listened quietly for a long time. Then he said something I will never forget. "You don't have to know everything now," he said. "Just take one small step. Then take another one. The path will appear when you start walking."

At the time, I didn't really understand. But I followed his advice. I left my studies and got a job in a bookstore. I loved it. After a year, I started studying literature in the evening. Then I got a job at a publishing company. Today, I edit books for a living, and I love my work.
My grandfather died five years ago. But whenever I have a difficult decision, I remember his words. One small step, then another one.

title: Is a Four-Day Week the Future?
paragraphs: For more than a hundred years, most office workers have worked five days a week. But in recent years, some companies have started to try something different: a four-day week. Employees work four days instead of five, but they receive the same salary.

At first, this sounds like a bad idea for businesses. If people work less, surely they will produce less? However, the results of several experiments have been surprising. In many companies, employees got the same amount of work done in four days. They spent less time in long meetings, took fewer breaks, and concentrated better because they knew they had a three-day weekend.

Workers in these experiments also reported many personal benefits. They felt less stressed and slept better. They had more time for their families, hobbies, and exercise. Some said they finally had time to do everyday jobs, like going to the doctor or repairing things at home, without taking a day off work.

Of course, the four-day week doesn't work for every job. Hospitals, schools, and shops need people every day of the week, so they would need to hire more staff. Some critics also worry that people will try to fit five days of work into four, and that they will end up working very long, exhausting days.

Still, the idea is becoming more popular. If the experiments continue to be successful, it is possible that in twenty years, a five-day week will seem as old-fashioned as working on Saturdays does today.

title: The Man Who Planted Trees
paragraphs: In the late nineteen seventies, a teenager called Jadav Payeng was living near a large river in northeast India. Every year, the river flooded and washed away the land on a big sandy island in the middle of it. After one terrible flood, Jadav found hundreds of dead snakes on the sand. There were no trees to protect them from the heat.

The scene shocked him. He asked the older people in his village what he could do, and they told him to plant trees. So he did. He started with twenty small bamboo plants. Then he planted more, and more. Every day for the next forty years, he went to the island to plant and water trees.

Slowly, the empty sand became a forest. Today, the forest covers more than five hundred hectares, which is bigger than many city parks. It has become home to deer, rabbits, monkeys, birds, and even tigers and a group of elephants that visit every year. The trees also help to protect the island from the floods.

For many years, nobody outside the area knew about Jadav. Then, in two thousand seven, a journalist discovered the forest by accident and wrote about it. Jadav became famous, and people started calling him "the Forest Man of India." He has received many awards, but he still lives a simple life near his forest.

His story shows that one person, working patiently every day, can make an enormous difference. When people ask him why he did it, he simply says that nature gives us everything, so we should give something back.

title: The Art of Saying No
paragraphs: Do you find it difficult to say no? Maybe a colleague asks you to help with a project when you are already busy, or a friend wants you to come to a party when you really need to rest. Many people say yes because they don't want to disappoint others, and then they feel stressed and unhappy.

Psychologists say that this is very common. We are social animals, and we want people to like us. Saying no can feel rude or selfish, especially in some cultures where it is important to be polite and helpful. But if you always say yes, you will have no time or energy for the things that really matter to you.

The good news is that saying no is a skill, and you can learn it. Experts suggest starting with small things. You don't have to give a long explanation. A short, friendly answer is usually enough, for example: "Thank you for asking, but I can't this time." It is also useful to give yourself time to think. Instead of answering immediately, you can say, "Let me check my calendar and get back to you."

Another good strategy is to offer an alternative. If a colleague asks for help, you could say, "I can't do it today, but I could help you on Thursday morning." This shows that you care, but that your time is also important.
Learning to say no won't make people like you less. In fact, many people will respect you more. And when you do say yes, it will really mean something.

title: Stuck in the Elevator
paragraphs: It was nearly midnight when Rachel finally left the office. She had been working on a report all evening, and she was exhausted. The building was empty and silent as she got into the elevator on the fourteenth floor and pressed the button for the ground floor.

The elevator had just passed the ninth floor when it suddenly stopped with a loud bang. The lights went off, and a moment later a small emergency light came on. Rachel pressed the alarm button, but nothing happened. She took out her phone. There was no signal.

At first, she tried to stay calm. She told herself that somebody would come soon. But after half an hour, she started to feel scared. It was getting hot, and she was thirsty. She sat on the floor and thought about her family, her cat, and all the things she had planned to do.

Then she heard a voice. "Hello? Is anybody in there?" It was the night security guard, an old man called Frank. He had noticed the elevator wasn't working on his computer screen. "Don't worry," he said through the doors. "The repair company is on its way. I'll stay here and talk to you until they come."

And he did. For the next hour, Frank told Rachel stories about his years as a sailor, and she found herself laughing. When the doors finally opened, she hugged him. The next day, she brought him a big box of chocolates. They have been friends ever since.

title: Why Do We Need Sleep?
paragraphs: We spend about a third of our lives asleep. If you live to be ninety, that is around thirty years of sleeping. For a long time, scientists didn't really understand why we need so much sleep. Today, we know much more, and the answers are fascinating.

One of the most important jobs of sleep is to help our memory. During the day, our brain collects huge amounts of information. While we sleep, the brain sorts this information. It decides what is important, saves it in our long-term memory, and deletes what we don't need. That is why students who sleep well after studying usually remember more than students who stay up all night.

Sleep also cleans the brain. Scientists have discovered that while we sleep, a special liquid moves through the brain and washes away waste products. Some of these waste products are connected to diseases like Alzheimer's. Without enough sleep, they can build up over time.

The body uses sleep to repair itself too. During deep sleep, the body produces hormones that help muscles grow and heal. Sleep also helps our immune system to fight illnesses. People who regularly sleep less than six hours a night catch colds more often than people who sleep seven or eight hours.

So, if you want to stay healthy, sleep is not a waste of time. In fact, it may be one of the most important things you do every day. Next time you feel guilty about going to bed early, remember that your brain is doing important work.

title: A Year Without Shopping
paragraphs: Two years ago, I made an unusual decision. I decided not to buy anything new for a whole year, except for food, medicine, and things for my hygiene. No new clothes, no new books, no new gadgets. My friends thought I wouldn't last a month.

I had several reasons. I was spending too much money, and I had a credit card debt that was making me anxious. My apartment was full of things I didn't use. I also felt guilty about the environment, because I knew that producing all these things uses a lot of energy and creates a lot of waste.

The first three months were the hardest. I didn't realize how often I bought things without thinking. When I was bored or sad, I used to go shopping online. Now I had to find other ways to feel better. I started going for walks, calling friends, and reading books from the library.

Something interesting happened. I started to appreciate the things I already had. I repaired a jacket instead of buying a new one, and I discovered that I really liked it. When I needed something, like a tent for a camping trip, I borrowed it from a neighbor. I also sold or gave away many of the things I didn't need.

At the end of the year, I had paid off my debt and saved a good amount of money. But the biggest change was in my mind. I learned that buying things doesn't make me happy for very long. Today I still shop, but much less, and I always ask myself first: do I really need this?

title: The Story of Chocolate
paragraphs: Today, chocolate is one of the most popular sweets in the world. But for most of its history, it wasn't sweet at all. It was a bitter drink, and it was so valuable that people used it as money.

Chocolate comes from the seeds of the cacao tree, which grows in hot, wet places in Central and South America. More than three thousand years ago, people in this region started making a drink from the seeds. They roasted them, crushed them, and mixed them with water, chili, and spices. The Maya and the Aztecs believed the drink was a gift from the gods, and they used it in important ceremonies.

In the sixteenth century, Spanish explorers brought cacao back to Europe. At first, Europeans didn't like the bitter taste, but then somebody had the idea of adding sugar and honey. Hot chocolate became a fashionable drink for rich people, and chocolate houses opened in cities like London and Paris.

Solid chocolate, the kind we eat today, was only invented in the nineteenth century. New machines made it possible to produce chocolate cheaply, and soon chocolate bars were available to everybody. A Swiss inventor discovered how to add milk, and milk chocolate quickly became the most popular type.

Today, most of the world's cacao is grown in West Africa, not in Central America. Sadly, many cacao farmers are very poor, even though chocolate companies earn billions of dollars. That is why some people now choose to buy fair trade chocolate, which pays farmers a better price.

title: The Power of Walking
paragraphs: When people decide to get fit, they often think they need to join an expensive gym or start running long distances. But many doctors say that one of the best forms of exercise is also the simplest: walking.

Walking has a long list of benefits. Regular walking makes your heart and lungs stronger and helps to control your weight. It reduces the risk of many serious illnesses, such as heart disease and diabetes. It also strengthens your bones and muscles, which is especially important as you get older. And unlike running, it is gentle on your knees and back.

The benefits are not only physical. Research has shown that walking is very good for mental health. A thirty-minute walk can reduce stress and improve your mood. Walking in nature, such as in a park or a forest, seems to be even more effective. Many people also find that walking helps them think. Some famous writers and scientists used to go for long walks every day to find new ideas.

So how much should you walk? Many people try to walk ten thousand steps a day, which is about seven or eight kilometers. But recent studies suggest that even fewer steps, around seven thousand, can bring big health benefits. The most important thing is to walk regularly.

The best part is that walking is free, and you can do it almost anywhere. You can walk to work, take the stairs, or go for a walk after dinner with your family. It may be the easiest healthy habit you will ever start.

title: Starting a New Life Abroad
paragraphs: Five years ago, my husband got a job offer in Portugal. We had always dreamed of living abroad, so we decided to go. We sold our car, packed our lives into twelve boxes, and moved to Lisbon with our two young children. It was the most exciting and the most difficult thing we have ever done.

The first months were full of challenges. We didn't speak Portuguese, so even simple things like opening a bank account or going to the doctor were stressful. The paperwork seemed endless. I remember crying in a government office because I didn't understand what the woman was asking me. I felt lonely, and I missed my family and friends terribly.

The children adapted much faster than we did. Within six months, they were chatting in Portuguese with their new friends at school and correcting my pronunciation. Watching them gave me the motivation to try harder. I took evening classes and forced myself to speak, even though I made many mistakes.

Slowly, things got better. We made friends with our neighbors, who invited us to family dinners and taught us about local traditions. I found a job at an international school. We started to love the city: the bright light, the sea, the delicious food, and the relaxed way of life.

Today, Lisbon feels like home. Moving abroad taught us to be patient, flexible, and brave. It wasn't always easy, but I have never regretted our decision. If you ever get the chance, I would say: go for it.

title: The Honest Robot
paragraphs: In the near future, many homes may have robots that help with daily tasks. They could clean the house, cook dinner, and look after older people. But this raises an interesting question: should robots always tell the truth?

Imagine a robot that helps an old woman who lives alone. One day, she asks it, "Do I look nice in this dress?" The dress is old and doesn't fit her well. An honest robot would say no. A kind human might say yes, to make her happy. Which answer is better?

Scientists who design robots and artificial intelligence are thinking seriously about questions like this. Most people agree that robots should not lie about important things, such as medicine or safety. If a robot told an old man that he had taken his pills when he hadn't, the results could be dangerous. People also need to trust machines, and that trust would disappear quickly if robots lied.

However, human communication is complicated. People tell small lies every day to be polite or to protect other people's feelings. We say "I'm fine" when we are tired, or "What a lovely present!" when we don't really like it. A robot that is always completely honest might seem rude or cold.

Some researchers think robots should learn to be honest but kind, like a good friend. Instead of saying "That dress looks bad," a robot could say "I think the blue dress suits you even better." Teaching machines this kind of social skill is one of the biggest challenges in technology today.

title: My Grandmother's Kitchen
paragraphs: When I think about my childhood, the first thing I remember is my grandmother's kitchen. It was small and always warm, with a big wooden table in the middle and a window that looked out over her vegetable garden. There was always something cooking on the stove, and the room smelled of bread, onions, and herbs.

My grandmother never used recipes. She cooked everything from memory, using a little of this and a pinch of that. When I asked her how much flour to use, she would say, "Enough." When I asked how long to cook the soup, she would say, "Until it's ready." As a child, this drove me crazy. Now I understand that she cooked with her senses: she looked, smelled, and tasted all the time.

She taught me to cook when I was about eight. My first job was peeling potatoes, and I wasn't very good at it. Later, she showed me how to make bread, how to roll pasta, and how to tell when a cake was done by touching it gently. While we worked, she told me stories about her own childhood, during difficult times when food was scarce and nothing was ever wasted.

My grandmother died when I was twenty-two. A few years later, I tried to write down her recipes so I wouldn't forget them. It was impossible to get them exactly right. But I realized that her recipes were not really about the amounts. They were about patience, attention, and love.
Today, I cook for my own children in my own kitchen. And when they ask me how much salt to use, I hear myself say: "Enough."

title: A Volunteer Firefighter
paragraphs: In many small towns and villages, there is no full-time fire department. Instead, the town depends on volunteer firefighters: ordinary people with normal jobs who are ready to help in an emergency at any time of the day or night. Tom Harris, a forty-five-year-old electrician, has been one of them for twenty years.

Tom carries a special pager with him everywhere he goes. When there is an emergency, it beeps loudly, and he has to leave whatever he is doing and drive to the fire station. "I've left in the middle of dinner, at my daughter's birthday party, and once even at the dentist," he laughs. "My family is used to it now."

The volunteers deal with much more than fires. They respond to car accidents, floods, and storms. They rescue people trapped in cars, help with medical emergencies, and sometimes even rescue animals. To do this, they need a lot of training. Tom spends two evenings a month practicing with the team, and he has taken courses in first aid and rescue techniques.

The job can be frightening and emotionally difficult. Tom has seen terrible accidents, and some nights he can't sleep afterward. But he says the team supports each other, and they often talk about difficult experiences together.

Why does he do it, without being paid? "This is my community," he says simply. "These are my neighbors. If my house was on fire, I'd want somebody to come. So I think I should be that somebody for other people."

title: The Statues of Easter Island
paragraphs: Easter Island is one of the most isolated places on Earth. It is a small island in the Pacific Ocean, more than three thousand five hundred kilometers from the coast of Chile. But it is famous all over the world because of its huge stone statues, called moai.

There are almost a thousand moai on the island. Most of them are about four meters tall, but the largest one is almost ten meters tall and weighs more than eighty tons. They were carved from volcanic rock between about seven hundred and five hundred years ago by the Rapa Nui people, who had arrived on the island by canoe many centuries earlier.

For a long time, the statues were a mystery. How did people without machines, metal tools, or large animals move such heavy objects across the island? Some people suggested strange theories, even saying that aliens had helped. But scientists have found a simpler answer. Experiments have shown that a small group of people with ropes could "walk" a statue by rocking it from side to side. Local legends say that the moai walked to their places, so the old stories may have been true in a way.

Another mystery is what happened to the island's society. When Europeans arrived in the eighteenth century, the forests had disappeared, and the population was much smaller. Some scientists blame the islanders for cutting down too many trees. Others believe that rats and diseases brought by Europeans caused most of the damage.
Today, the moai are protected as a World Heritage Site, and they remind us of the skill and determination of the people who made them.

title: How to Spot Fake News
paragraphs: Every day, we see hundreds of news stories on our phones and computers. Some of them are true, but some are false or misleading. These are often called "fake news." They can spread very quickly on social media, sometimes faster than real news, because they are often shocking or emotional.

Why do people create fake news? Some do it to make money, because shocking stories get a lot of clicks, and clicks bring money from advertising. Others do it for political reasons, to make people angry or to influence their opinions. And sometimes, people simply share stories without checking them, because they believe them or because they think they are funny.

So how can you tell if a story is true? First, look at the source. Is it a well-known news organization, or a website you have never heard of? Check the address of the website carefully, because some fake sites copy the names of real ones. Second, read more than the headline. Headlines are often exaggerated, and the real story may be quite different.

Third, check the date. Sometimes old stories are shared again as if they were new. Fourth, search for the story on other websites. If something important has really happened, many news organizations will be reporting it. Finally, be careful with photos. Pictures can be edited or taken from a completely different event.

The most important thing is to stop and think before you share. If a story makes you very angry or very excited, that is a good moment to check it. We all have a responsibility to stop false information from spreading.

title: The Violinist in the Subway
paragraphs: On a cold morning in January two thousand seven, a young man stood in a subway station in Washington and played the violin. It was rush hour, and over the next forty-five minutes, more than a thousand people walked past him on their way to work.

Very few of them stopped. A few threw some coins into his violin case without looking at him. A small boy tried to stop and listen, but his mother pulled him away. In total, the musician earned about thirty-two dollars. When he finished, nobody clapped.

What the commuters didn't know was that the violinist was Joshua Bell, one of the most famous classical musicians in the world. Just a few days earlier, he had played to a full concert hall where tickets cost about a hundred dollars each. And his violin was worth several million dollars.

The event was an experiment organized by a newspaper. The journalists wanted to find out whether people would recognize beauty in an unexpected place, when they were busy and not expecting it. The answer, it seemed, was mostly no.

The story became very famous, and people still discuss what it means. Some say it shows that modern life is too busy, and that we don't notice the beautiful things around us. Others say it is not fair to judge the commuters, because they had to get to work on time. Interestingly, the people who were most likely to stop were children. Perhaps we can learn something from them.

title: Taking a Gap Year
paragraphs: In some countries, it is quite common for young people to take a "gap year" between finishing school and starting university. During this year, they might travel, work, volunteer, or learn new skills. For many, it is a chance to discover more about the world and about themselves.

Supporters of gap years say they have many benefits. After years of exams and studying, students often feel tired and unsure about what they really want to do. A year away from education gives them time to rest and to think about their future. Many come back more mature and more motivated. Some even change their plans completely after discovering a new interest.

Traveling and working abroad can also help young people become more independent. They learn to manage money, solve problems on their own, and communicate with people from different cultures. These are skills that employers value highly. Volunteering can give them practical experience and a better understanding of social problems.

However, gap years also have disadvantages. Traveling can be expensive, and not every family can afford it. Some students worry that they will forget what they learned at school, or that they will lose the habit of studying. There is also a risk that a gap year will become a wasted year, if a student doesn't plan it carefully and spends most of the time doing nothing.

In the end, a gap year is a personal decision. Experts say the most important thing is to have a clear plan and a purpose. A well-planned gap year can be one of the most valuable experiences of a young person's life.

title: The Last Letter
paragraphs: When Helen's father died, she had to empty his house. It was a small house in the countryside where he had lived alone for many years since her mother's death. Helen hadn't visited very often. They had argued a lot when she was young, and they had never really been close.

On the third day, she was clearing out his desk when she found a wooden box at the back of a drawer. Inside, there were dozens of letters, all addressed to her. None of them had been sent. The first was dated twenty years ago, the week she had left home after a terrible argument.

Helen sat on the floor and began to read. In the letters, her father wrote about his life: the garden, the weather, his loneliness after her mother died. But mostly, he wrote about her. He wrote about how proud he was when he heard she had become a doctor. He wrote about how much he regretted the angry words he had said. In every letter, he asked her to forgive him.

The last letter had been written only a month before he died. "I know I am not good at saying these things," it said. "I have tried to send these letters many times, but I was always afraid. I hope one day you will read them and know that I always loved you."
Helen read the letters until it was dark. Then she went into the garden and sat under the apple tree that her father had planted when she was born. For the first time in years, she cried for him.

title: The Bicycle
paragraphs: Today, there are more than a billion bicycles in the world, about twice as many as cars. They are cheap, healthy, and good for the environment. But the bicycle we know today took a long time to develop.

The first machine that looked a little like a bicycle was invented in Germany in eighteen seventeen. It was made of wood and had two wheels, but no pedals. To move, the rider pushed against the ground with their feet, like a child on a balance bike. It was called a "running machine," and for a short time it was quite fashionable.

About fifty years later, inventors in France added pedals to the front wheel. These bicycles were very uncomfortable, because the wheels were made of wood and iron. People called them "boneshakers." Later came the famous "penny-farthing," with a huge front wheel and a tiny back wheel. It was fast, but very dangerous, because riders sat high above the ground and often fell off.

The modern bicycle appeared in the eighteen eighties. It had two wheels of the same size, a chain connected to the back wheel, and, soon after, air-filled rubber tires. It was safe, comfortable, and easy to ride. Suddenly, bicycles became very popular, especially with women, because they gave them a new kind of freedom.
Today, many cities are building bike lanes and encouraging people to cycle instead of drive. After two hundred years, the simple bicycle may be more important than ever.

title: Learning from Failure
paragraphs: Nobody likes to fail. When we fail an exam, lose a job, or make a mistake at work, we often feel embarrassed and disappointed. Many of us are afraid of failure, so we avoid taking risks. But some psychologists believe that failure is one of the best ways to learn.

Think about how a baby learns to walk. It falls down hundreds of times, but it doesn't give up. Each fall teaches it something about balance. Adults, however, often stop trying after one or two failures, because they worry about what other people think.

Many successful people have experienced big failures. The writer J. K. Rowling was rejected by twelve publishers before her first Harry Potter book was accepted. The inventor Thomas Edison made thousands of attempts before he created a light bulb that worked. When people asked him about his failures, he reportedly said, "I have not failed. I've just found ten thousand ways that won't work."

Psychologists talk about a "growth mindset." People with a growth mindset believe that their abilities can improve with effort and practice. When they fail, they ask, "What can I learn from this?" People with a "fixed mindset" believe their abilities cannot change, so failure feels like proof that they are not good enough.

The good news is that we can develop a growth mindset. One simple way is to change the way we talk to ourselves. Instead of saying "I'm bad at this," we can say "I'm not good at this yet." That small word, "yet," can make a big difference.

title: Living in Amsterdam
paragraphs: Amsterdam, the capital of the Netherlands, is famous for its canals, bicycles, and narrow old houses. I moved there for work three years ago, and I still feel like a tourist sometimes when I walk along the water on a sunny evening.

The city center was built in the seventeenth century, when Amsterdam was one of the richest cities in the world. Merchants built tall, thin houses along the canals, because taxes were based on the width of the house. Many houses lean forward slightly, and they have hooks at the top. These were used to lift furniture up and in through the windows, because the stairs inside are very steep and narrow.

The most surprising thing for me was the bicycles. There are more bikes than people in Amsterdam, and everybody cycles, from businesspeople in suits to parents with three children in a box at the front. At first, I was terrified of the busy bike lanes, but now I can't imagine life without my bike. It is the fastest way to get around.

Life in Amsterdam is not perfect. Housing is very expensive, and it can be hard to find an apartment. The weather is often gray and wet, and the wind can be very strong. In summer, the city center is crowded with tourists.

But I love the relaxed atmosphere, the beautiful architecture, and the way people enjoy life. On summer weekends, people sit on their boats or by the canals with friends, and the whole city seems to be having a picnic.

title: Working from Anywhere
paragraphs: Not long ago, working from home was unusual. Most companies expected their employees to come to the office every day, and people who worked from home were often seen as less serious. Then, almost overnight, millions of people around the world had to start working from their kitchens and bedrooms. Many of them have never gone back.

For many workers, remote work has clear advantages. They no longer spend hours every week traveling to and from work, which saves time, money, and stress. They can organize their day more freely, for example by taking a walk at lunchtime or starting early and finishing early. Parents often find it easier to combine work and family life.

Some people have taken this freedom even further. They have become "digital nomads," living and working in different countries while they travel. As long as they have a laptop and a good internet connection, they can work from a beach in Thailand or a mountain village in Spain.

However, remote work is not perfect. Many people feel lonely and miss the social contact of the office. It can be harder to separate work from free time, and some people end up working longer hours than before. Young employees, in particular, may find it difficult to learn from more experienced colleagues when everybody is at home.

That is why many companies now offer a mix of both, known as hybrid work. Employees might spend two or three days in the office and the rest at home. For many people, this seems to be the best of both worlds.

title: The Boy Who Caught the Wind
paragraphs: In two thousand one, the small African country of Malawi was hit by a terrible drought. There was no rain, the crops died, and millions of people went hungry. William Kamkwamba was fourteen years old at the time. His family were farmers, and they could no longer pay for him to go to school.

William was disappointed, but he didn't give up on learning. He started going to a small library in his village, where he read every science book he could find. One day, he found a book with a picture of a windmill on the cover. He learned that windmills could produce electricity and pump water. He had an idea: if he could build one, his family could water their fields even when there was no rain.

He had no money and no proper materials, so he collected what he could find in a local scrapyard. He used an old bicycle frame, a tractor fan, plastic pipes, and pieces of wood. The people in his village thought he was crazy. Some even said he was using magic.

But after months of work, his windmill was ready. When the wind blew, the blades turned, and a small light bulb in his house came on. His neighbors were amazed. Soon, people were coming to charge their phones, and William later built a windmill to pump water for the fields.

William's story spread around the world. He was given the chance to return to school and later studied at a university in the United States. He wrote a book about his experience, and it was made into a film. Today, he works on projects that help young people in Africa solve problems in their own communities.

title: The Clever Octopus
paragraphs: The octopus is one of the strangest animals on our planet. It has eight arms, three hearts, and blue blood. It can change the color of its skin in less than a second, and it can squeeze its soft body through a hole as small as a coin. But perhaps the most surprising thing about the octopus is its intelligence.

Scientists have discovered that octopuses can solve complex problems. In experiments, they have learned to open jars to get food inside, and some have even learned to open them from the inside. They can find their way through mazes and remember the solution later. Some octopuses in the wild collect coconut shells and carry them around to use as a portable home.

Octopuses also seem to have individual personalities. Some are shy, while others are curious and bold. In aquariums, they can recognize different people. Some octopuses have been known to squirt water at keepers they don't like. One famous octopus in New Zealand escaped from its tank at night, crossed the floor, and slid down a pipe into the sea.

What makes octopus intelligence so interesting is that it developed in a completely different way from ours. Octopuses are more closely related to snails than to humans. Most of their brain cells are not in their head, but in their arms. This means each arm can taste, touch, and even make simple decisions on its own.
Studying octopuses helps scientists understand that intelligence can take many different forms. It also makes many people think again about how we treat these remarkable animals.

title: An Unexpected Guest
paragraphs: It was a stormy night in November, and Martha was alone in her farmhouse. Her husband was away visiting his sister, and the nearest neighbor lived three kilometers down the road. She was sitting by the fire with a book when she heard a knock at the door.

Martha froze. Nobody ever came to the farm at this time of night. The knock came again, louder this time. She picked up the phone, ready to call for help, and walked slowly to the door. "Who's there?" she called.

"I'm very sorry to bother you," said a man's voice. "My car has broken down on the road, and my phone has no signal. I've been walking for an hour. Could I use your phone?" Martha hesitated. Then she looked through the window and saw a young man, soaking wet and shivering, with a little girl in his arms.

She opened the door immediately. She gave them towels and dry clothes, made hot soup, and let them sit by the fire. The man, whose name was David, called a mechanic, but nobody could come until the morning. So Martha made up the spare bed for them.

The next morning, the storm had passed. David's car was repaired, and before he left, he thanked her again and again. Three weeks later, Martha received a parcel. Inside was a beautiful painting of her farmhouse in the storm, with a light shining in the window. On the back, it said: "Thank you for opening your door. From David and Lily."

title: Why Boredom Is Good for You
paragraphs: When was the last time you felt really bored? For many of us, it is hard to remember. Today, whenever we have a free moment, while waiting for a bus or standing in a line, we take out our phones and start scrolling. We are never more than a few seconds away from entertainment.

Most people think boredom is something bad that we should avoid. But some psychologists believe that a little boredom can actually be good for us. When our brain has nothing to focus on, it starts to wander. We begin to daydream, to think about our lives, and to make connections between different ideas. This is often when we have our most creative thoughts.

In one famous experiment, researchers asked people to do a very boring task: copying numbers from a phone book. Then they asked them to think of as many uses as possible for a plastic cup. The people who had done the boring task came up with more creative ideas than people who hadn't.

Boredom can also motivate us. When we feel bored, it is often a sign that we need a change. It can push us to try a new hobby, learn a new skill, or look for more meaningful work. Children who have time to be bored often invent their own games and stories.

So the next time you feel bored, try not to reach for your phone immediately. Look out of the window, go for a walk without headphones, or simply sit and let your mind wander. You might be surprised by what you discover.

title: The Tiny House Movement
paragraphs: Over the last twenty years, houses in many countries have become bigger and bigger. But a growing number of people are choosing to go in the opposite direction. They are moving into tiny houses, homes that are often smaller than twenty square meters.

A tiny house usually has everything a normal house has, just in a much smaller space. There is a kitchen, a bathroom, and a living area. The bed is often in a loft, which you reach by a ladder. Every centimeter is used cleverly. Stairs might have drawers inside them, tables fold away into the wall, and sofas turn into beds.

People choose tiny houses for different reasons. For many, the main reason is money. Houses in many cities have become extremely expensive, and a tiny house costs a fraction of the price. Some owners can buy their home without a loan, which gives them a lot of financial freedom. Others are attracted by the idea of a simpler life, with fewer possessions and less cleaning.

Tiny houses are also better for the environment. They need much less energy to heat and cool, and they are often built with recycled materials. Some have solar panels and collect rainwater. Many tiny houses are built on wheels, so their owners can move them to a new place whenever they like.

But living in a tiny house is not for everyone. There is very little storage space, and it can be difficult to share such a small home with a partner or children. In many places, laws also make it hard to find somewhere to park one legally. Still, for some people, less space really does mean more freedom.

title: How Music Affects the Brain
paragraphs: Music is part of every human culture in the world. People sing to their babies, dance at weddings, and listen to music when they are happy, sad, or bored. But why does music have such a strong effect on us? Scientists have been studying this question for many years.

When we listen to music we enjoy, our brain releases dopamine. This is the same chemical that is released when we eat delicious food or fall in love, and it makes us feel good. Interestingly, the brain releases dopamine not only at the best part of a song, but also just before it, while we are waiting for it. This is why the moment before a song's chorus can feel so exciting.

Music also has a strong connection with memory. A song can take us back to a particular summer or a special person in an instant. Doctors have found that people with serious memory problems, such as Alzheimer's disease, can often remember the words of songs from their youth, even when they have forgotten many other things. Some care homes now use music to help patients feel calmer and more connected.

Learning to play an instrument seems to be especially good for the brain. Studies suggest that children who learn music often become better at languages, mathematics, and concentration. For older people, playing music may help keep the brain healthy.

Music can even affect our bodies. Slow, calm music can lower our heart rate and reduce stress, while fast music can give us energy during exercise. It is no surprise that so many people go running with headphones on.

title: A City Center Without Cars
paragraphs: In nineteen ninety-nine, the city of Pontevedra in northern Spain made a bold decision. It banned private cars from its city center. At the time, many people thought the plan would destroy the local shops and make life difficult for residents. Today, the city is often held up as an example for the rest of the world.

Before the change, the streets were full of traffic, noise, and pollution. Parked cars covered the sidewalks, and children rarely played outside. The mayor believed that streets should be for people, not cars. So the city closed the center to traffic, built large free parking areas on the edge of town, and turned roads into pedestrian areas with trees and benches.

The results were remarkable. Air pollution fell dramatically, and the number of traffic accidents dropped. The center became quiet enough to hear birds singing. Families returned to live in the old town, and children began walking to school on their own again. Instead of closing, many small shops and cafes did better business, because more people were walking past them.

Of course, there are still some cars in the center. Delivery vans, emergency vehicles, and people with disabilities can still drive there, but only slowly. Everybody else walks or rides a bike. Since the city is small, most places can be reached on foot in about fifteen minutes.

Not every city can copy Pontevedra exactly, especially very large ones. But many cities, from Oslo to Paris, are now taking similar steps to reduce cars in their centers and give more space back to people.

title: An Unlikely Friendship
paragraphs: Animals of different species don't usually become friends, especially when one of them normally hunts the other. But every now and then, a story appears that surprises everybody. One of the most famous happened at a wildlife park in Russia.

In two thousand fifteen, the park workers gave a live goat to a Siberian tiger called Amur. The goat was supposed to be his dinner. Tigers in the park were regularly fed live animals so they could practice their hunting skills. But this goat, which was later named Timur, didn't seem to understand that he was in danger. Instead of running away, he walked straight up to the tiger and stood his ground.

Amur seemed confused. He didn't attack. Over the next few days, the two animals began spending time together. They walked around the enclosure side by side, and Timur even started sleeping in Amur's shelter, while the tiger slept outside on the roof. The park workers couldn't believe what they were seeing.

The story quickly spread around the world. People watched videos of the pair online, and thousands of visitors came to the park to see them. Scientists offered different explanations. Some said the goat's lack of fear had confused the tiger. Others pointed out that Amur was well fed and simply wasn't hungry.

The friendship lasted for a few months until Timur became too bold and began to annoy the tiger, who finally lost patience and threw him off a hill. Timur was hurt but survived, and he lived for several more years in a separate enclosure.

title: The Secret of a Long Life
paragraphs: In a few places in the world, people live much longer than average. Many of them reach the age of one hundred, and they often stay healthy and active until the end of their lives. Researchers call these places "Blue Zones," and they have been studying them to find out what their residents have in common.

The Blue Zones include the island of Okinawa in Japan, a mountain region on the Italian island of Sardinia, and a small town in California. The people who live there have very different cultures, but their lifestyles share some important features.

First, they don't do intense exercise, but they move naturally all day. They walk, work in their gardens, and do physical jobs at home. Second, they eat mostly plants, such as beans, vegetables, and whole grains, and only small amounts of meat. Many of them also stop eating before they feel completely full. In Okinawa, people have a saying that reminds them to stop eating when they are about eighty percent full.

But the secrets are not only about diet and exercise. People in Blue Zones usually have strong connections with their family and community. They spend time with friends and often belong to a religious or social group. They also have a clear sense of purpose. In Okinawa, there is a word for this, "ikigai," which means a reason to get up in the morning.
Of course, genes play a role in how long we live. But researchers believe that lifestyle is even more important. The good news is that many of these habits are simple and free.

title: Saving a Language
paragraphs: There are around seven thousand languages spoken in the world today. But experts believe that about half of them could disappear by the end of this century. Every two weeks or so, the last speaker of a language dies, and that language is lost forever.

Languages usually disappear when a community starts using a more powerful language, such as English, Spanish, or Chinese. Parents decide to speak the dominant language with their children, because they think it will give them better opportunities. Within a few generations, only old people speak the traditional language, and then nobody does.

When a language dies, much more than words is lost. Every language contains a unique way of looking at the world. It holds stories, songs, jokes, and knowledge about plants, animals, and medicine that may not exist anywhere else. Some languages have words for ideas that other languages cannot easily express.

Fortunately, some languages have been brought back from the edge. One famous example is the Welsh language in Britain. In the middle of the twentieth century, the number of speakers was falling fast. Then Welsh began to be taught in schools, and there are now Welsh television channels and radio stations. Today, hundreds of thousands of people speak it. In New Zealand, the Maori people created "language nests," where young children spend their days with older people who speak only Maori.
Technology can help too. Linguists are recording the last speakers of endangered languages, and some communities are creating apps and online courses to teach their language to young people.

title: The Dog with an Amazing Nose
paragraphs: Dogs have been helping humans for thousands of years. They have guarded our homes, herded our sheep, and kept us company. Today, they are also doing some surprising jobs, thanks to one special ability: their amazing sense of smell.

A dog's nose is incredibly powerful. While humans have about six million smell receptors in their noses, some dogs have around three hundred million. The part of a dog's brain that analyzes smells is also much larger than ours. Scientists believe that dogs can smell some things at concentrations a hundred thousand times lower than we can.

Because of this, dogs are trained to do many important jobs. At airports, they sniff bags to find drugs, explosives, or food that people are not allowed to bring into the country. After earthquakes, rescue dogs search through buildings to find people trapped under the ruins. Other dogs help to find people who are lost in forests or mountains.

Even more surprisingly, some dogs can detect illnesses. Researchers have trained dogs to recognize the smell of certain types of cancer, sometimes before doctors can find it with tests. Other dogs live with people who have diabetes. They can smell when their owner's blood sugar is dangerously low and warn them before they feel ill.

Training a dog for this kind of work takes a long time, often more than a year. Not every dog is suitable. The best ones are curious, energetic, and love to play. For them, finding a smell isn't work at all. It is a game, and the reward is usually a favorite toy.

title: Small Acts of Kindness
paragraphs: Most of us like to think of ourselves as kind people. But in our busy lives, it is easy to forget about the small things we can do for others. Research suggests that these small acts of kindness are good not only for the people who receive them, but also for the people who do them.

In one study, psychologists gave people some money and asked them to spend it. Half of the group had to spend it on themselves, and the other half had to spend it on somebody else. At the end of the day, the people who had spent the money on others felt happier, even though the amount was small.

Doing something kind for others can also reduce stress and improve our health. When we help somebody, our brain releases chemicals that make us feel good and calm. Some scientists call this the "helper's high." People who volunteer regularly often report feeling more satisfied with their lives.

Kindness can also spread. When someone is kind to us, we are more likely to be kind to the next person we meet. A simple smile, a thank you note, or holding a door open can start a chain of positive actions. In one coffee shop in the United States, a customer paid for the drink of the person behind them in line. That person did the same, and the chain continued for more than a hundred people.
You don't need to do something big. Calling a lonely relative, helping a neighbor with their shopping, or listening to a friend who is having a bad day can make a real difference.

title: First Day Nerves
paragraphs: Daniel had been looking for a job for eight months when he finally got an offer from a small design company. He was thrilled, but also extremely nervous. The night before his first day, he hardly slept. He kept imagining all the things that could go wrong.

He arrived at the office thirty minutes early, wearing his best shirt. The receptionist smiled and told him to wait. While he was sitting there, he spilled coffee all over his pants. He rushed to the bathroom and tried to clean them, but it only made things worse. When he came out, there was a large wet stain on his leg.

His new manager, a woman called Grace, came to meet him. Daniel was so embarrassed that he started explaining immediately. Grace laughed. "On my first day here, I locked myself out of the building and had to climb through a window," she said. "Don't worry. Coffee is the least of your problems."

The rest of the day went much better than Daniel had expected. His colleagues were friendly and patient, and they showed him how everything worked. At lunchtime, they took him to a small restaurant around the corner and asked him lots of questions about himself. By the afternoon, he was already working on his first project.

When he got home that evening, his girlfriend asked how it had gone. Daniel thought for a moment. "Terrible start," he said with a smile. "But I think I'm going to like it there." Two years later, he still works at the same company, and every new employee hears the story of the coffee.

title: The Great Wall of China
paragraphs: The Great Wall of China is one of the most famous structures in the world. Every year, millions of tourists visit it, walking along its ancient stones and admiring the views of the mountains around it. But there are many myths about the wall, and its true history is even more interesting.

First of all, the Great Wall is not a single wall. It is a series of walls built over a period of more than two thousand years by different Chinese dynasties. The earliest parts were built around the seventh century before Christ. Most of the wall that tourists see today was built during the Ming Dynasty, between the fourteenth and seventeenth centuries.

The wall was built mainly to protect China from attacks by groups from the north. It had watchtowers where soldiers could look out for enemies. When they saw danger, they lit fires or sent smoke signals to warn the next tower. In this way, a message could travel hundreds of kilometers in just a few hours.

Building the wall was extremely hard work. Millions of soldiers, farmers, and prisoners worked on it, often in terrible conditions. Many of them died during the construction. In the mountains, workers had to carry heavy stones up steep slopes by hand.

One popular myth says that the Great Wall can be seen from the Moon. This is not true. Astronauts have said that it is very difficult to see even from a low orbit around the Earth, because it is narrow and has a similar color to the land around it.

title: Coffee Around the World
paragraphs: Coffee is one of the most popular drinks on the planet. People drink more than two billion cups of it every day. But the way people drink coffee is very different from one country to another.

The coffee plant probably came from Ethiopia, in East Africa. According to a popular legend, a goat herder noticed that his goats became very energetic after eating red berries from a certain bush. In Ethiopia today, coffee is still part of an important ceremony. The beans are roasted, ground, and boiled in a special pot in front of the guests. The ceremony can take more than an hour, and it is a time for talking and friendship.

In Italy, most people drink espresso, a small, strong coffee. Italians usually drink it standing at the bar, and it is finished in a minute or two. Many Italians believe that you should never drink a cappuccino, which contains a lot of milk, after about eleven o'clock in the morning.

In Turkey, coffee is boiled with sugar in a small pot and served without being filtered, so the coffee grounds stay at the bottom of the cup. In Vietnam, a popular drink is iced coffee with sweet condensed milk. Some cafes there also serve egg coffee, which is topped with a sweet, creamy egg foam.

In the United States, people often drink large cups of filter coffee, and many take their coffee with them to drink on the way to work. Whatever the style, coffee brings people together in almost every culture.

title: The Message in a Bottle
paragraphs: Ten-year-old Ethan was walking along the beach with his grandfather when he saw something shining in the sand. It was an old green bottle with a cork in the top. Inside, there was a rolled-up piece of paper.

Ethan's grandfather helped him pull out the cork. The paper was yellow and fragile, and the handwriting was faded, but they could still read it. "My name is Anna," it said. "I am nine years old, and I live in a small town in Norway. If you find this bottle, please write to me." There was an address at the bottom. The letter was dated more than fifty years ago.

Ethan was fascinated. "Do you think she is still alive?" he asked. "She would be an old woman now," his grandfather said. "But let's try." That evening, they wrote a letter and sent it to the address, not really expecting an answer.

Six weeks later, a letter arrived from Norway. It was from Anna's granddaughter. She explained that her grandmother still lived in the same town and was now sixty-three. She remembered throwing the bottle into the sea from her father's fishing boat, and she was amazed that it had traveled so far.

Ethan and Anna started writing to each other regularly. They sent photos and told each other about their lives. Two summers later, Ethan's family traveled to Norway, and Ethan met Anna in person. She took him out on a boat, and together they threw a new bottle into the sea.

title: What Makes Us Happy?
paragraphs: Everybody wants to be happy, but what actually makes us happy? Many people believe that money, success, or a beautiful house will make them happier. But according to researchers who study happiness, the truth is a little more complicated.

Money does matter, up to a point. People who don't have enough money for food, housing, and healthcare are usually less happy, because they live with constant stress. But once people have enough to live comfortably, extra money doesn't increase their happiness very much. A person who earns twice as much as their neighbor is not usually twice as happy.

One of the longest studies of happiness began at an American university in the nineteen thirties. Researchers followed hundreds of men for more than eighty years, and later their children too. The most important finding was clear: the people who were happiest and healthiest in old age were the ones with good relationships. Close friendships and a strong family were more important than money, fame, or career success.

Other research has shown that we often get used to good things quickly. When people buy a new car or move to a bigger house, they feel happy for a while, but soon it becomes normal. Experiences, such as traveling or learning something new, tend to give us more lasting happiness than possessions.

Experts also say that small daily habits can make a difference. Spending time outside, exercising regularly, getting enough sleep, and helping others can all improve our mood. Some people also find it helpful to write down three things they are grateful for every evening.

title: The Island That Appeared from the Sea
paragraphs: In November nineteen sixty-three, fishermen near the south coast of Iceland noticed something strange. Black smoke was rising out of the sea. At first, they thought a ship was on fire. But when they got closer, they saw that it was something much more unusual. A volcano was erupting under the water.

Over the next few days, the eruption grew stronger. Huge clouds of ash and steam rose kilometers into the sky. Then, a few days later, a small black island appeared above the waves. The volcano continued to erupt for more than three years, and by the end, the new island was more than two square kilometers in size. It was named Surtsey, after a giant from old Icelandic stories.

Scientists immediately realized that Surtsey was a unique opportunity. Here was a completely new piece of land, with no plants or animals at all. They could watch how life arrived and developed on it, from the very beginning. To protect the island, the government made it a nature reserve. Only a small number of scientists are allowed to visit it.

Life arrived surprisingly quickly. Within two years, the first plant was growing on the beach. Its seeds had probably been carried there by the sea. Birds started to visit, bringing more seeds on their feet and in their droppings. Today, dozens of plant species grow on Surtsey, and many birds nest there.
However, the sea is slowly eating away at the island. Scientists think that in a hundred years, much of Surtsey may disappear back under the waves.

title: Can You Make Real Friends Online?
paragraphs: Twenty years ago, if you told people that your best friend was somebody you had met on the internet, they might have thought it was strange. Today, it is very common. Millions of people have friends they met through online games, social media, forums, or language exchange apps.

Online friendships have some clear advantages. The internet allows us to connect with people who share our interests, even if those interests are unusual. If you love old science fiction films or a rare type of music, you might not find anybody in your town who shares your passion. Online, you can find thousands. For people who are shy, live in isolated places, or have health problems that make it hard to go out, online friends can be especially important.

Some people also find it easier to be honest online. Without seeing the other person's face, they feel less judged, so they share their thoughts and feelings more openly. Many online friendships become very deep.

However, there are also risks. It is easy for people to pretend to be someone they are not. Some people spend so much time online that they neglect their friends and family in real life. And some research suggests that online communication, while valuable, cannot completely replace the experience of being with people face to face.

Many friendships that start online eventually move offline. Friends meet at concerts or events, or travel to visit each other. Perhaps the most important thing is not where a friendship begins, but how much care and honesty both people put into it.

title: The Library of Things
paragraphs: How often do you use a drill? According to some estimates, the average drill is used for only about thirteen minutes in its whole life. Most of the time, it just sits in a cupboard. The same is true of many other things we own, such as ladders, tents, sewing machines, and party decorations.

This is the idea behind a new kind of library that is appearing in cities around the world: the library of things. Instead of books, these libraries lend out everyday objects. Members can borrow a vacuum cleaner, a projector, a camping stove, or a set of gardening tools for a few days, usually for a small fee.

The benefits are clear. Borrowing is much cheaper than buying, especially for things you only need once or twice a year. It also saves space at home, which is important for people who live in small apartments. And it is better for the environment, because fewer things need to be produced, transported, and eventually thrown away.

Many libraries of things also offer workshops where people can learn to repair objects or use new tools. Volunteers check that everything is clean and working before it is lent out again. Some libraries have become important meeting places, where neighbors get to know each other and share skills.

Of course, the idea depends on trust. Borrowers have to look after the things they take and return them on time. But so far, most libraries report very few problems. As one organizer said, "People are generally good. When you trust them, they usually respect that trust."

title: Climbing Everest
paragraphs: At almost eight thousand nine hundred meters, Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world. For a long time, many people believed it was impossible to climb. Then, in nineteen fifty-three, Edmund Hillary from New Zealand and Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa from Nepal, finally reached the top.

Since then, thousands of people have climbed Everest, but it is still extremely dangerous. At the top, the air contains only about a third of the oxygen that it does at sea level. Most climbers use bottles of oxygen to breathe. Without it, the brain and body begin to fail. Climbers can become confused, make bad decisions, and even lose consciousness.

The weather is another serious danger. Temperatures can fall below minus thirty degrees, and winds can be strong enough to knock a person off the mountain. Climbers also face avalanches and deep cracks in the ice. Every year, some climbers die on the mountain.

In recent years, Everest has also faced new problems. Climbing it has become a business, and hundreds of people now attempt it every season. On good days, long lines of climbers form near the top, waiting in the freezing cold for their turn. The mountain is also polluted with tons of trash, such as empty oxygen bottles, old tents, and food packages left behind by expeditions.

The government of Nepal has introduced new rules to protect the mountain and its visitors. Climbers now have to bring their trash back down. Still, many people believe that more needs to be done to protect the highest place on Earth.

title: Leonardo da Vinci
paragraphs: When people hear the name Leonardo da Vinci, most of them think of the Mona Lisa, one of the most famous paintings in the world. But Leonardo was much more than a painter. He was also a scientist, an engineer, an inventor, and a musician. Many people consider him one of the greatest minds in history.

Leonardo was born in a small town in Italy in fourteen fifty-two. As a teenager, he went to Florence to work for a famous artist, where he learned to paint, draw, and make sculptures. He quickly became known for his extraordinary talent. But he was also endlessly curious about the world around him.

Throughout his life, Leonardo filled thousands of pages of notebooks with drawings and ideas. He studied the human body by examining dead bodies, and his drawings of muscles, bones, and the heart were far more accurate than any others at the time. He watched birds for hours to understand how they flew, and he designed flying machines, a kind of parachute, and even an early version of a helicopter. He also drew plans for bridges, weapons, and machines that used water power.

Interestingly, Leonardo often wrote in his notebooks from right to left, so that his writing could only be read easily in a mirror. Nobody knows exactly why. Some think it was to keep his ideas secret, while others think it was simply easier for him, since he was left-handed.
Many of his inventions were never built in his lifetime, because the technology didn't exist yet. But his notebooks show a mind that was centuries ahead of its time.

title: Discoveries by Accident
paragraphs: We often imagine that great scientific discoveries come from years of careful planning. But some of the most important inventions in history happened completely by accident.

One of the most famous examples is penicillin, the first antibiotic. In nineteen twenty-eight, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming went on vacation and left some dishes of bacteria in his laboratory. When he came back, he noticed that a mold had grown on one of them. Around the mold, the bacteria had died. Fleming realized that the mold was producing something that killed bacteria. Penicillin has since saved millions of lives.

The microwave oven was also discovered by chance. In the nineteen forties, an engineer called Percy Spencer was working with radar equipment when he noticed that a chocolate bar in his pocket had melted. He was curious, so he put some popcorn kernels near the machine, and they started to pop. A few years later, the first microwave oven was sold.

Other accidental inventions include the sticky notes that many people use in offices. A scientist was trying to create a very strong glue, but he made one that was very weak instead. For years, nobody knew what to do with it. Then a colleague realized it was perfect for making bookmarks that wouldn't fall out of his book.

However, these discoveries were not just luck. Each of these people noticed something unusual and was curious enough to investigate it. As the scientist Louis Pasteur once said, "Chance favors the prepared mind."

title: The Shy Actor
paragraphs: When Oliver was a child, he was so shy that he hid behind his mother whenever visitors came to the house. At school, he never put up his hand in class, even when he knew the answer. Talking to strangers made his heart race and his face turn red.

So everyone was surprised when, at the age of fifteen, he signed up for the school drama club. Even Oliver wasn't sure why he did it. Maybe he was tired of being invisible. At the first meeting, he sat at the back and hoped nobody would notice him. But the teacher, Mrs. Clark, asked everybody to read a few lines from a play.

When it was Oliver's turn, his voice shook. But then something strange happened. As he read the words of the character, he forgot about himself. He wasn't shy Oliver anymore. He was an angry king. His voice grew louder and stronger. When he finished, the room was silent, and then everybody clapped.

Over the next few years, Oliver acted in every school play. He discovered that on stage, playing another person, he felt free in a way he never felt in real life. Offstage, he was still quiet, but he became a little more confident every year.

Today, Oliver is a professional actor who has performed in theaters all over the country. In interviews, he often says that he is still a shy person. "Acting didn't cure my shyness," he explains. "It just gave me a place where my shyness didn't matter."

title: Why Are the Bees Disappearing?
paragraphs: Bees may be small, but they play a huge role in our lives. When they fly from flower to flower collecting food, they carry pollen with them. This process, called pollination, allows plants to produce fruit and seeds. About a third of the food we eat, including apples, almonds, tomatoes, and coffee, depends on bees and other pollinating insects.

In recent decades, however, scientists and farmers have noticed a worrying trend. In many parts of the world, the number of bees is falling. Some beekeepers have lost a large part of their colonies in a single winter. Wild bees, which most people never notice, are also in decline.

There is not one single cause. One of the main problems is the use of pesticides, chemicals that farmers use to kill insects that damage their crops. Some pesticides harm bees as well, affecting their ability to find their way home. Another problem is the loss of habitat. As cities grow and farms get bigger, there are fewer wild flowers and fewer places for bees to live. Diseases, parasites, and climate change make the situation worse.

Fortunately, there are many things that can help. Some countries have banned the most harmful pesticides. Farmers are being encouraged to leave strips of wild flowers at the edges of their fields. And ordinary people can help too.

Planting flowers that bees like, such as lavender or sunflowers, can make a real difference, even on a small balcony. Avoiding chemicals in the garden and leaving some areas a little wild also gives bees a place to live. Every small garden can become a stop on a bee's journey.

title: Tips for a Job Interview
paragraphs: For many people, a job interview is one of the most stressful experiences in life. You only have a short time to show an employer that you are the right person for the job. The good news is that, with some preparation, you can feel much more confident.

The first step is to research the company. Read its website carefully, find out what it does, and look for recent news about it. Interviewers are often impressed when candidates know something about the company and can explain why they want to work there. It shows that you are genuinely interested and not just looking for any job.

Next, think about the questions you might be asked. Many interviews include common questions, such as "Tell me about yourself" or "What are your strengths and weaknesses?" Practice your answers out loud, perhaps with a friend. Prepare some examples from your experience that show your skills. For instance, if you say you are good at solving problems, describe a time when you actually solved one.

On the day of the interview, plan to arrive about ten minutes early. Dress appropriately for the type of company. Body language is important too. Smile, make eye contact, and try to sit up straight. If you don't understand a question, it is perfectly fine to ask the interviewer to repeat it.

Finally, prepare one or two questions of your own to ask at the end. You might ask about the team, the training, or the next steps in the process. And after the interview, it is a good idea to send a short email to thank the interviewer for their time.

title: Saving Handwriting
paragraphs: In many schools today, children spend more time typing on keyboards and tablets than writing by hand. Some schools have even stopped teaching joined-up handwriting altogether. After all, most adults today rarely write anything by hand except a shopping list. So is handwriting still important?

Many researchers believe it is. Several studies have shown that writing by hand helps us learn and remember better than typing. When we type, we can write very quickly, almost copying every word we hear. But when we write by hand, we are slower, so we have to think about what is important and put the ideas into our own words. This extra mental effort helps the brain to process and remember the information.

Handwriting also seems to be important for young children who are learning to read. When children form letters by hand, they activate parts of the brain that are connected to reading. Children who learn to write letters by hand often recognize them more easily than children who learn by typing.

However, others argue that keyboard skills are more useful in the modern world. Most jobs require people to type quickly and accurately, and computers make it easy to edit and share work. For children with certain learning difficulties, typing can also make writing much easier.

Perhaps the answer is that both skills are valuable. Many experts suggest that children should learn to write by hand first and then learn to type. And for adults, taking notes by hand in meetings or lectures might be an easy way to remember more.

title: A Cafe Full of Cats
paragraphs: The first cat cafe opened in Taiwan in nineteen ninety-eight. The idea was simple: customers could drink coffee and eat cake while playing with cats who lived in the cafe. It quickly became popular, especially in Japan, where many people live in small apartments where pets are not allowed. Today, there are cat cafes in cities all over the world.

Visiting a cat cafe is a unique experience. Customers usually pay an entrance fee and are asked to wash their hands and follow some rules.
