You mustn't wake a sleeping cat, pick one up without permission, or feed them human food. The cats are free to move around as they like. Some come to sit on visitors' laps, while others ignore everybody and sleep on high shelves.

Many people visit cat cafes because spending time with animals helps them relax. Research shows that stroking a cat can reduce stress and lower blood pressure. For people who love cats but can't have one at home, it is the next best thing.

In some countries, cat cafes also help homeless cats. The cats in these cafes come from animal shelters, and visitors can adopt them if they want. This gives the cats a comfortable place to live while they wait for a new family, and it helps them to get used to people.

However, not everybody likes the idea. Some animal welfare groups worry that cats may feel stressed by constant attention from strangers. Good cat cafes take this seriously. They limit the number of visitors and give the cats quiet areas where people are not allowed.

title: The Land of the Midnight Sun
paragraphs: Imagine looking out of your window at midnight and seeing bright sunshine. For people who live in the far north of countries like Norway, Sweden, and Finland, this is a normal part of summer. For several weeks around the end of June, the sun never sets. This is known as the midnight sun.

It happens because the Earth is tilted. During the summer, the northern part of the planet is tilted toward the sun, so areas near the North Pole receive sunlight for twenty-four hours a day. In the far north of Norway, the sun doesn't set at all from the middle of May until the end of July.

For visitors, the midnight sun is a magical experience. People go hiking at two in the morning, play golf at midnight, or simply sit outside and enjoy the golden light. But it can also be difficult. Many people find it hard to sleep when it is light all night, and hotels often have special thick curtains to block out the sun.

In winter, the opposite happens. For weeks, the sun doesn't rise at all. This period is called the polar night. It isn't completely dark all day, because there is a blue light around midday, but it is very cold and dark for most of the time. Some people feel tired and sad during these months.

But winter has its own beauty. The long, dark nights are the best time to see the northern lights, when green and purple lights dance across the sky. Many people say it is one of the most beautiful sights in nature.

title: Inside the Teenage Brain
paragraphs: Parents of teenagers often complain that their children are moody, take silly risks, and can't get out of bed in the morning. For a long time, people thought this was just a normal part of growing up. But scientists now know that the teenage brain is going through a period of enormous change.

Until recently, scientists believed that the brain finished developing in childhood. Thanks to modern brain scans, we now know that it continues to develop until people are in their mid twenties. The part of the brain that changes last is at the front. This area is responsible for planning, controlling impulses, and thinking about the consequences of our actions.

Meanwhile, the parts of the brain that control emotions and rewards are very active during the teenage years. This helps to explain why teenagers often react strongly to their emotions and why they enjoy excitement and new experiences. It also explains why they care so much about what their friends think. Studies show that teenagers take more risks when they are with friends than when they are alone.

Teenagers' sleep patterns also change. Their body clock shifts, so they naturally feel sleepy later at night and want to wake up later in the morning. This is why many teenagers struggle to get up early for school. Some schools have started classes later in the morning, and they have seen improvements in students' grades and mood.
Understanding these changes can help parents and teachers be more patient. Teenage behavior is not always about being difficult. Often, it is simply a brain in the middle of a major rebuild.

title: The Cost of Cheap Clothes
paragraphs: Today, it is possible to buy a T-shirt for less than the price of a sandwich. Clothes shops update their collections every few weeks, and many people buy new clothes much more often than their parents did. This trend is known as fast fashion. It has made fashion cheaper and more accessible, but it also has a hidden cost.

Producing clothes uses enormous amounts of water and energy. Making a single pair of jeans can require thousands of liters of water, mostly to grow the cotton. Many clothes are also made from synthetic materials, such as polyester, which come from oil. When these clothes are washed, they release tiny plastic fibers that end up in rivers and oceans.

Because clothes are so cheap, people often wear them only a few times before throwing them away. In some countries, the average person throws away tens of kilos of clothing every year. Most of it ends up in landfill sites or is burned. Only a small amount is recycled into new clothes.

There are also concerns about the people who make our clothes. Many factories are in countries where workers are paid very low wages and work long hours in poor conditions. Some terrible accidents in factories have shocked the world and led to calls for change.

However, more people are now looking for alternatives. Secondhand clothes shops and online markets have become very popular, especially among young people. Some people are learning to repair their clothes, and some brands now offer to take old clothes back and recycle them. Buying fewer, better quality clothes and wearing them for longer may be the simplest solution of all.

title: The Mystery of the Mary Celeste
paragraphs: In December eighteen seventy-two, the crew of a British ship saw another ship sailing strangely in the Atlantic Ocean, between Portugal and the Azores islands. It was moving slowly and seemed to have no direction. When they went closer and climbed on board, they discovered that there was nobody on it.

The ship was called the Mary Celeste. It had left New York about a month earlier, carrying a cargo of alcohol to Italy. On board were the captain, Benjamin Briggs, his wife, their two-year-old daughter, and seven sailors. But now, all of them had disappeared.

The strangest thing was that the ship was in good condition. There was plenty of food and water on board, and the passengers' personal possessions were still there. The cargo was almost complete. However, the ship's small lifeboat was missing, and some of the instruments for navigation had gone. It looked as if the crew had left in a hurry.

Nobody ever discovered what happened to the people on board, and the mystery has inspired many theories. Some people suggested that pirates had attacked the ship, but nothing valuable had been stolen. Others imagined sea monsters or giant waves. One popular theory is that alcohol from the barrels leaked and produced gas, and the captain feared an explosion. He may have ordered everybody into the lifeboat, planning to return when it was safe, but then lost contact with the ship.
The famous writer Arthur Conan Doyle wrote a story inspired by the ship, which made it even more famous. Today, the Mary Celeste remains one of the greatest mysteries of the sea.

title: Why Gardening Is Good for You
paragraphs: For many people, gardening is simply a hobby, a way to grow some vegetables or make the outside of their house look nice. But research shows that gardening has surprising benefits for both our physical and mental health.

First, gardening is good exercise. Digging, carrying bags of soil, pulling weeds, and pushing a lawn mower all use our muscles and raise our heart rate. An hour of gardening can burn as many calories as a gym session. And because it doesn't feel like exercise, many people do it for longer and more regularly than they would go to the gym.

Gardening is also good for the mind. Spending time outside in green spaces reduces stress and anxiety. Some scientists believe that a type of bacteria found in soil may even help to improve our mood. In several countries, doctors now sometimes recommend gardening to patients who are suffering from depression or loneliness. This is sometimes called "green prescribing."

Community gardens can be especially helpful. In these gardens, neighbors share a piece of land and grow food together. They give people the chance to meet others, share skills, and feel part of a community. For older people who live alone, they can be an important source of friendship.

Finally, growing your own food can encourage healthier eating. Children who help to grow vegetables are more likely to eat them. And there is a special pleasure in picking a tomato that you have grown yourself, still warm from the sun. You don't need a big garden to start. A few pots of herbs on a windowsill are enough.

title: The Professional Sleeper
paragraphs: When people talk about dream jobs, they usually mean something exciting, like being a pilot or a famous actor. But some people have jobs that are far more unusual. One of the strangest is the job of a professional sleeper.

Some hotels employ people to test their beds. These testers spend the night in different rooms and write reports about how comfortable the beds are, whether the room is quiet, and how dark it gets at night. They might also check the pillows, the temperature of the room, and even how easy it is to find the light switch in the dark.

Mattress companies also pay people to sleep. Testers might be asked to try a new mattress for several weeks and describe how they feel when they wake up. Do they have back pain? Do they feel too hot? Their opinions help the company improve its products.

Sleep scientists need volunteers too. In sleep laboratories, researchers attach small sensors to people's heads and bodies to measure their brain activity, heart rate, and breathing while they sleep. These studies help scientists understand sleep problems and develop new treatments. Some studies last for several weeks, and participants are paid for their time.

It might sound like the easiest job in the world, but it isn't always relaxing. Testers have to pay close attention and write detailed notes, and sleeping in a strange bed with wires on your head is not easy. One former tester said that, ironically, the hardest part of the job was falling asleep.

title: The Honest Waiter
paragraphs: It was the end of a long, busy Friday night, and Carlos was cleaning the tables in the small Italian restaurant where he worked. He was tired, his feet hurt, and he still had to take two buses to get home. As he lifted a napkin from the last table, he found a thick black wallet.

He opened it to look for a name. Inside, there was a driver's license, several credit cards, and a large amount of cash, more money than Carlos earned in a month. For a moment, he just stood there, holding it. He thought about his rent, which was late, and the new shoes his daughter needed for school.

Then he looked at the license again. He remembered the man: an older gentleman who had eaten alone, very quietly, and had been very polite. Carlos closed the wallet and gave it to his manager. Together, they found a business card inside with a phone number and called it.

The man came back to the restaurant half an hour later. He was shaking with relief. He explained that the money was to pay for his wife's medical treatment the next morning. He tried to give Carlos some of the money as a reward, but Carlos refused. "I just did the right thing," he said.

Two weeks later, the man returned with his wife, who was now feeling much better. He told Carlos he owned a small company and was looking for an honest person to manage his office. Carlos started his new job the following month. He still visits the restaurant every Friday.

title: How the Internet Began
paragraphs: Today, it is difficult to imagine life without the internet. We use it to work, study, shop, chat with friends, and watch films. But the internet is surprisingly young. Many people who are alive today remember a world without it.

The internet began in the late nineteen sixties as a project of the United States military. Researchers wanted to create a network of computers that could continue working even if part of it was destroyed. In nineteen sixty-nine, the first message was sent between two computers at universities in California. The plan was to send the word "login," but the system crashed after just two letters. So the first message ever sent on the internet was "lo."

During the nineteen seventies and eighties, the network grew slowly. It was mainly used by scientists and universities to share information. Using it was complicated, and you needed special knowledge to find anything.

The big change came in nineteen eighty-nine, when a British scientist called Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web. He created a system of pages connected by links, which anyone could read using a program called a browser. He decided not to make money from his invention, so that everybody could use it for free.

In the nineteen nineties, the web spread rapidly. Companies created websites, email became common, and people began shopping online. Then came smartphones, social media, and video streaming. Today, more than five billion people use the internet. In just a few decades, it has changed almost every part of our lives.

title: The Power of a Short Nap
paragraphs: In many cultures, taking a nap in the afternoon is a normal part of the day. In others, it is seen as a sign of laziness. But scientists who study sleep say that a short nap can have real benefits for our health and our work.

Most people feel a little sleepy in the early afternoon, usually between one and three o'clock. This is not only because of lunch. It is part of our natural body clock. Many experts believe that a nap at this time of day can improve concentration, memory, and mood.

The length of the nap is important. A nap of about twenty minutes is often called a "power nap." It is long enough to make you feel more alert, but short enough that you don't fall into deep sleep. If you sleep for longer, for example an hour, you might wake up feeling confused and even more tired than before. This feeling is called sleep inertia.

Some companies have started to see the benefits of napping. They provide quiet rooms or special chairs where employees can rest for a short time during the day. Some research suggests that a short nap can make workers more productive and less likely to make mistakes.

However, napping is not for everyone. People who have trouble sleeping at night are often advised to avoid naps, because they can make it harder to fall asleep later. A useful trick for a power nap is to drink a cup of coffee just before lying down. The caffeine takes about twenty minutes to work, so you wake up feeling doubly refreshed.

title: The Camel Library
paragraphs: In many rural parts of Kenya, there are no libraries, and books are very expensive. Villages are often far apart, and the roads are rough or don't exist at all. For children who live there, getting access to books can be almost impossible. So the country found an unusual solution: a library carried by camels.

The camel library service began in the nineteen nineties in the northeast of the country. Each camel can carry boxes containing hundreds of books. The camels travel from village to village with a librarian and a helper, often walking for hours through hot, dry land. Camels are perfect for this job, because they can go a long time without water and can walk where cars cannot.

When the camels arrive in a village, the librarian spreads mats on the ground under a tree and lays out the books. Children and adults gather around to choose what they want to read. They can borrow books for about two weeks, until the camels return. Many villages have nobody else to bring them reading materials, so the camels' visits are a special event.

The library has had a big impact. Teachers say that children who use it read better and do better at school. It has also encouraged adults to learn to read. In some places, the camels carry solar-powered computers as well as books.

Of course, there are challenges. Sometimes the camels get sick or the weather is too hot to travel. There are also not always enough books in local languages. But for thousands of children, the camel library opens a door to a much bigger world.

title: Unusual Festivals Around the World
paragraphs: Every country has its own festivals, but some of them are truly unusual. Across the world, people celebrate in ways that might seem very strange to visitors.

In a small town in Spain, thousands of people gather every August for La Tomatina, the world's biggest food fight. For one hour, they throw ripe tomatoes at each other until the streets are completely red. Fire trucks then wash the streets clean. The festival started in nineteen forty-five, possibly after a fight between young people at a parade, although nobody knows the exact story.

In England, there is a festival where people chase a large round cheese down a very steep hill. The cheese can reach speeds of over a hundred kilometers an hour, so nobody actually catches it. The first person to reach the bottom of the hill wins the cheese. Every year, several people get injured, but the tradition continues.

In Thailand, the town of Lopburi holds a special festival for the monkeys that live there. People prepare huge tables of fruit, vegetables, and sweets just for the monkeys, to thank them for bringing tourists and good luck to the town. The monkeys climb all over the tables and eat everything.

In India and Nepal, people celebrate the spring festival of Holi by throwing brightly colored powder and water at each other. Streets fill with music, dancing, and clouds of pink, yellow, and green. Holi celebrates the end of winter and the victory of good over evil. On this day, social differences are forgotten, and everybody plays together.

title: Swimming Against the Odds
paragraphs: In nineteen twenty-six, a nineteen-year-old American called Gertrude Ederle walked into the cold, gray water on the coast of France. Her goal was to swim across the English Channel to England, a distance of about thirty-four kilometers. At that time, only five people had ever done it, and all of them were men.

Many people believed that women were not strong enough for such a challenge. One newspaper even wrote that women should accept that they would always be the weaker sex in sport. Gertrude had already won Olympic medals in swimming, but this was something different. The water was freezing, the currents were strong, and there were jellyfish. The year before, her first attempt had failed when her coach pulled her out of the water.

This time, she was determined. She covered her body in grease to protect herself from the cold and wore special goggles that she had designed herself. As she swam, the weather got worse, and strong winds made the waves very rough. Her team on a nearby boat begged her to give up. "What for?" she shouted back, and kept swimming.

After fourteen hours and thirty-nine minutes, she walked out of the sea onto an English beach. Not only was she the first woman to swim the Channel, she had beaten the men's record by almost two hours.

When she returned to New York, around two million people came out to welcome her with a huge parade. Gertrude's swim changed many people's ideas about what women could achieve. Her record lasted for more than twenty years.

title: The Science of First Impressions
paragraphs: They say you should never judge a book by its cover. But when we meet new people, most of us do exactly that. Research shows that we form a first impression of another person in a very short time, sometimes in less than a tenth of a second.

In that short moment, our brain makes quick judgments about whether a person is friendly, trustworthy, or confident. These judgments are based on many small details: their facial expression, their clothes, the way they stand, and the sound of their voice. We are usually not aware that we are doing this. It happens automatically.

This ability probably developed because it helped our ancestors survive. Thousands of years ago, people needed to decide very quickly whether a stranger was a friend or an enemy. Today, we use the same system in very different situations, such as job interviews, business meetings, and first dates.

The problem is that first impressions are often wrong. We may judge someone as unfriendly simply because they are nervous, or trust someone because they are attractive. Our first impressions can also be influenced by stereotypes and prejudices. And once we have formed an opinion, we tend to notice things that support it and ignore things that don't.

So what can we do? Psychologists suggest giving people a second chance and trying to get to know them better before making a final judgment. And if you want to make a good first impression yourself, the advice is simple: smile, make eye contact, and show genuine interest in the other person. Most people respond warmly to someone who seems interested in them.

title: The Floating Markets of Thailand
paragraphs: In many countries, people do their shopping in supermarkets or street markets. But in parts of Thailand, some markets take place on the water. At floating markets, sellers paddle small wooden boats along the canals, offering fruit, vegetables, flowers, and freshly cooked food to customers on the banks or in other boats.

For hundreds of years, canals were the main roads in central Thailand. Many people lived in houses built over the water, and boats were the easiest way to travel and to trade. Farmers brought their products to markets by boat, and families did their shopping without ever stepping on land. As roads and cars became more common in the twentieth century, many of these markets disappeared.

Today, some floating markets have become popular tourist attractions. The most famous ones, near Bangkok, are often crowded with visitors taking photos and buying souvenirs. Some travelers feel that these markets have lost their traditional character. But there are still smaller markets where local people do their everyday shopping.

Visiting a floating market early in the morning is an unforgettable experience. Women in wide straw hats sell piles of mangoes, bananas, and coconuts from their boats. Others cook noodle soup on small stoves right on the water and pass the bowls up to customers with long poles. The air is full of the smell of grilled meat and sweet coconut.
If you visit, try to go early, before the tour buses arrive. And don't forget to try the mango with sticky rice, a delicious local dessert that tastes even better when you eat it beside the water.

title: Is Cold Water Good for You?
paragraphs: Every winter, in many countries, groups of people gather at lakes, rivers, and beaches and jump into the freezing water. To most people, this sounds like a terrible idea. But cold water swimming has become increasingly popular, and many people say it has changed their lives.

When you get into very cold water, your body reacts immediately. Your heart rate increases, and you start breathing very fast. This is called cold shock, and it can be dangerous, especially for people with heart problems. That is why experts say you should never jump straight in, but enter the water slowly and stay for only a short time at first.

So why do people do it? Many swimmers say that cold water makes them feel energetic and happy for hours afterward. Scientists think this may be because cold water causes the body to release chemicals that improve our mood. Some people believe that regular cold swimming helps them cope with stress and feel less anxious. There is also some evidence that it might strengthen the immune system, although more research is needed.

For many swimmers, the social side is just as important. Cold water swimming groups are often very friendly communities. Members encourage each other, share hot drinks after their swim, and become close friends.

If you want to try it, it is important to be careful. Never swim alone, choose a safe place, and get out of the water before you start shivering badly. Having warm clothes ready is essential. Some people prefer to start more gently by ending their normal shower with thirty seconds of cold water.

title: Never Too Old
paragraphs: Most people think of running marathons as something for young, fit athletes. But in two thousand eleven, a man called Fauja Singh changed many people's ideas about age when he finished a marathon in Toronto at the age of one hundred.

Fauja was born in a village in India. As a child, he was weak and couldn't walk properly until he was five years old. He spent most of his life as a farmer. He had never run a race. Then, in his eighties, his life changed completely. His wife and his son died, and he was heartbroken. He moved to London to live with another son and began to feel lonely and sad.

To deal with his sadness, he started running. At first, he ran short distances, but he soon discovered that he loved it. At the age of eighty-nine, he ran his first marathon in London. He finished it in a little over six and a half hours, and he went on to run several more.

When people asked him about his secret, Fauja always gave simple answers. He ate a light vegetarian diet, drank plenty of water and tea, and went to bed early. He also said that being happy and avoiding negative people was very important. "I don't think about the past," he once said. "I think about the next race."

Fauja's achievements made him famous around the world. He carried the Olympic torch in London and appeared in advertisements for a sports company. More importantly, he became an inspiration to older people everywhere, showing that it is never too late to start something new.

title: The Story of Tea
paragraphs: After water, tea is the most popular drink in the world. Every day, people drink billions of cups of it. But the history of tea goes back thousands of years, and it has had a surprising influence on world events.

According to an old Chinese legend, tea was discovered around five thousand years ago by an emperor called Shen Nong. He was boiling water under a tree when some leaves fell into his pot. He tasted the water and found it delicious and refreshing. Whether or not this story is true, we know that people in China were drinking tea at least two thousand years ago. At first, it was used mainly as a medicine.

Tea spread from China to Japan, where Buddhist monks drank it to stay awake during long periods of meditation. Over time, the Japanese developed a special tea ceremony, a slow and careful way of preparing and serving green tea that is still practiced today.

Tea arrived in Europe in the seventeenth century, and it quickly became very fashionable, especially in Britain. At first, it was very expensive, and only rich people could afford it. To meet the growing demand, the British began growing tea in India and Sri Lanka, which are now among the largest tea producers in the world.

Tea has even played a role in politics. In seventeen seventy-three, American colonists who were angry about British taxes threw hundreds of boxes of tea into the harbor in Boston. This event, known as the Boston Tea Party, was one of the events that led to the American Revolution.

title: The School That Banned Phones
paragraphs: Two years ago, the high school in our town made a big decision. Students would no longer be allowed to use their phones during the school day. Every morning, they had to put their phones in special locked bags, which they could only open when they left school in the afternoon.

At first, many students were angry. Some said it was unfair and that they needed their phones in case of an emergency. Parents were also worried at the beginning. But the school explained that students could always use the phone in the office, and that parents could call the school if there was a problem.

After a few weeks, teachers noticed some big changes. Students concentrated better in class, and they were less distracted. During breaks, instead of looking at their screens, they talked to each other, played games, and went outside. The library became busy again. Some teachers said the atmosphere in the school felt calmer and friendlier.

There were other benefits too. Cases of online bullying during school hours fell, because students couldn't send messages or take photos of each other. Some students said they felt less pressure, because they didn't have to keep checking social media all day. By the end of the first year, exam results had also improved slightly.

Not everybody is convinced. Some people argue that young people need to learn to use technology responsibly, and that banning phones doesn't teach them how to do that. But in our town, most students now say they don't mind the rule. As one fifteen-year-old put it, "It's actually a relief to have a break."

title: The Missing Painting
paragraphs: The painting had been stolen sometime between midnight and six in the morning. When the museum guard arrived for his morning shift, he found an empty space on the wall where a small but very valuable landscape had hung for fifty years. There was no sign of a break-in. The alarm had not gone off.

Detective Sarah Moss walked slowly around the room. The window was locked from the inside. The door had been opened with a key. Only four people had keys to the museum: the director, the two night guards, and the cleaner. Sarah decided to interview all of them.

The director was shocked and upset. He had been at a dinner party all evening, and many people had seen him there. The first night guard, a young man called Ryan, said he had checked the room at two o'clock, and the painting had been there. The cleaner said she had finished work at ten and gone straight home. The second guard, an older man called Peter, had been sick and had not come to work that night.

Sarah thought for a long time. Then she asked Ryan a simple question. "You said you checked the room at two o'clock. How did you know the painting was there?" Ryan looked confused. "I saw it," he said. "I turned on the light." Sarah smiled. "That's strange," she said, "because the lights in that room have been broken for a week. The director told me."
Ryan's face went white. Later that day, the police found the painting hidden in his apartment. He had planned to sell it to a collector abroad.

title: Venice and the Rising Sea
paragraphs: Venice is one of the most beautiful cities in the world. Built on more than a hundred small islands in a lagoon in northern Italy, it has canals instead of streets and boats instead of cars. Every year, millions of tourists come to admire its palaces, churches, and bridges. But Venice is in serious danger.

The city has always flooded from time to time, especially in autumn and winter. When strong winds and high tides combine, seawater rises and pours into the streets and squares. Locals call this "acqua alta," which means high water. In the past, this happened occasionally. Today, it happens much more often, and the floods are getting worse.

There are two main reasons. First, the city is slowly sinking. For many years, factories pumped water from under the ground, which made the land sink faster. Second, sea levels are rising because of climate change. Together, these changes mean that the water is getting closer and closer to the city.

To protect Venice, Italy has built a huge system of barriers at the entrances to the lagoon. When a dangerous tide is expected, the barriers rise from the seabed and block the water. The project took many years and cost billions of euros, and it has already prevented several floods.

But the barriers cannot solve every problem. If sea levels continue to rise, they will need to be closed more often, which could harm the lagoon's environment. Venice also faces other challenges, such as huge numbers of tourists and a falling population. Many people are asking how the city can survive in the future.

title: The Joy of Missing Out
paragraphs: You have probably heard of FOMO, the "fear of missing out." It is the anxious feeling that other people are having more fun or more interesting experiences than you. Social media makes this feeling very common. When we see photos of friends at parties, on vacations, or at concerts, we can easily feel that our own lives are boring.

In recent years, some people have started talking about the opposite: JOMO, the "joy of missing out." Instead of trying to do everything and be everywhere, people who practice JOMO choose to slow down and enjoy the present moment. They say no to some invitations without feeling guilty. They spend an evening at home reading, cooking, or simply resting, and they enjoy it.

The idea is simple, but it can be surprisingly difficult. Many of us feel pressure to stay busy all the time. We worry that if we say no to an event, people will forget about us, or we will miss something important. But psychologists say that constantly trying to keep up can lead to stress, tiredness, and dissatisfaction.

Practicing JOMO doesn't mean avoiding people or never going out. It means making conscious choices about how to spend your time and energy. It means focusing on what really matters to you, instead of what you think you should be doing.

Some simple ways to start include turning off notifications on your phone, spending less time on social media, and planning some free evenings with nothing to do. You may discover that missing out is not something to be afraid of. Sometimes, it is exactly what you need.

title: The Real Dracula
paragraphs: Count Dracula, the vampire who drinks human blood, is one of the most famous characters in literature. He first appeared in a novel by the Irish writer Bram Stoker in eighteen ninety-seven. But many people don't know that the name Dracula comes from a real historical person, a prince who lived in the fifteenth century.

His name was Vlad the Third, and he ruled a region called Wallachia, which is now part of Romania. His father was known as Vlad Dracul, a name that comes from the word for "dragon." So Vlad the Third became known as Dracula, which means "son of the dragon."

Vlad lived in a violent time, when his small country was often at war with the powerful Ottoman Empire. He was famous for his cruel methods of punishing enemies and criminals. His most terrible habit was killing his enemies by putting them on tall wooden stakes, which gave him the nickname "Vlad the Impaler." Stories about his cruelty spread across Europe.
However, in Romania, Vlad is not only remembered as a monster. Some people see him as a national hero who defended his country against invaders and fought against corruption.

Historians are not sure how much Bram Stoker actually knew about Vlad. He probably borrowed the name after reading about it in a book, but his vampire character has little in common with the real prince. Today, thousands of tourists visit Bran Castle in Romania, which is often called "Dracula's Castle." Ironically, there is no strong evidence that Vlad ever lived there.

title: Is It Too Late to Learn a Language?
paragraphs: Many adults would like to learn a new language, but they believe it is too late. They have heard that children learn languages easily, while adults find it much harder. Is this true? The answer, according to researchers, is more complicated than most people think.

It is true that young children have some advantages. If they grow up hearing a language, they usually learn to speak it without a foreign accent. Their brains are very good at recognizing new sounds, and they are not afraid of making mistakes. They also have a lot of time to practice, often hours every day.

But adults have their own advantages. They already know how language works, so they can understand grammar rules and use them more quickly. They can use dictionaries, apps, and books. They also have more experience of learning in general, and they can plan their studies and stay motivated. Some studies show that adults actually learn faster than children in the early stages of learning a language.

The biggest difference is often not the brain, but the situation. Children are usually surrounded by the language, while adults are busy with work and family and have less time to practice. Adults are also more likely to feel embarrassed when they make mistakes, which can stop them from speaking.

So what is the best advice for adult learners? Practice a little every day, rather than a lot once a week. Listen to the language as much as possible, through music, podcasts, and films. And most importantly, don't be afraid to make mistakes. Every mistake is a step toward speaking better.

title: The Town That Adopted Strangers
paragraphs: On the morning of September eleventh, two thousand one, about forty airplanes were flying over the Atlantic Ocean toward the United States when the American government closed its airspace. The planes were told to land immediately at the nearest airport. Many of them were sent to a small town in Canada called Gander.

Gander had a population of about nine thousand people. Suddenly, around seven thousand passengers and crew from all over the world arrived at its small airport. They were tired, frightened, and confused, and many didn't know what had happened. They would have to stay in Gander for several days.

The people of Gander responded with incredible generosity. Schools, churches, and community centers were turned into temporary shelters. Families opened their homes to strangers, offering them beds, showers, and meals. Local bakeries and restaurants cooked huge amounts of food for free. Pharmacists provided medicine, and residents brought clothes, blankets, and toys for the children. Some passengers were even taken on trips to see the local area.

Many passengers later said that the kindness they experienced in Gander was something they would never forget. Strong friendships formed between the passengers and the local people, and some of them still visit each other today. Several passengers created scholarships for students in the town to say thank you.

The story of Gander became so well known that it was turned into a successful musical called "Come From Away," which has been performed around the world. It reminds audiences that even on one of the darkest days in recent history, ordinary people chose kindness.

title: The Invention of Photography
paragraphs: Today, most of us carry a camera in our pocket and take dozens of photos every day. But taking a picture was not always so easy. The very first photograph that still exists took around eight hours to make.

That photograph was taken in eighteen twenty-six or eighteen twenty-seven by a French inventor called Joseph Nicephore Niepce. He placed a metal plate covered in a special chemical inside a box with a small hole, and pointed it out of a window at his house. The light slowly changed the chemical on the plate, creating a blurry image of the buildings and trees outside. Because it took so long, the sun moved across the sky, and both sides of the buildings appear to be lit.

A few years later, another Frenchman, Louis Daguerre, developed a much faster method. His photographs, called daguerreotypes, took only a few minutes and were very sharp. They became extremely popular, and people lined up in studios to have their portraits taken. However, they still had to sit completely still for a long time, which is why people in old photographs rarely smile.

Over the following decades, photography became faster, cheaper, and easier. In eighteen eighty-eight, an American company introduced a small, simple camera that anybody could use, with the slogan "You press the button, we do the rest." Photography was no longer just for professionals.
The arrival of digital cameras and then smartphones changed everything again. Today, people take more photos every few minutes than were taken in the entire nineteenth century.

title: In Search of Silence
paragraphs: When was the last time you experienced complete silence? For most people who live in cities, it is almost impossible to remember. Traffic, construction work, music, voices, and the sound of our phones surround us almost all the time. Some scientists believe that this constant noise is having a negative effect on our health.

Research has shown that long-term exposure to noise, especially traffic noise, can increase stress, disturb our sleep, and even raise the risk of heart disease. Children who go to schools near airports or busy roads sometimes have more difficulty concentrating and learning to read. Noise pollution is now considered one of the biggest environmental health problems in Europe.

On the other hand, silence seems to be good for us. In one study, scientists found that two minutes of silence was more relaxing for the body than listening to calm music. Other studies suggest that silence may help the brain to process information and think more clearly.

Because of this, some people are now actively looking for quiet places. Some travel to remote areas in nature, such as deserts or mountains, where they can escape all human sounds. In some cities, libraries and parks have created special quiet zones. A few organizations even certify "quiet parks" where natural sounds are protected.

You don't need to travel far to find a little more silence in your life, though. You could turn off the television when you are not watching it, take a walk without headphones, or spend a few minutes each morning sitting quietly before you check your phone. Even small moments of quiet can help you feel calmer.

title: The Dog Who Waited
paragraphs: In nineteen twenty-four, a professor at the University of Tokyo called Hidesaburo Ueno adopted a small white puppy. He named the dog Hachiko. The two became very close. Every morning, Hachiko walked with the professor to Shibuya train station, and every afternoon, the dog waited at the station for him to come home from work.

One day in May nineteen twenty-five, the professor did not come home. He had suffered a sudden illness at work and died. Hachiko waited at the station that evening, but his owner never appeared. The next day, the dog went back to the station at the same time and waited again.

Hachiko continued to do this every day for nearly ten years. At first, some station workers were not kind to him. But in nineteen thirty-two, a newspaper published a story about the loyal dog, and he became famous across Japan. People started bringing him food, and visitors came from far away to see him. Teachers and parents told children about Hachiko as an example of loyalty.

Hachiko died in nineteen thirty-five, still waiting near the station. A bronze statue of him had been placed there a year earlier, and he was present at the ceremony. Today, the statue is one of the most famous meeting places in Tokyo, and thousands of people walk past it every day.

Hachiko's story has inspired books and films in many countries. In two thousand fifteen, the University of Tokyo created a new statue showing Hachiko finally being reunited with his owner, jumping up happily to greet him.

title: How to Be a Good Listener
paragraphs: Most of us think we are good listeners. But in reality, many people don't really listen when others are talking. Instead, they are thinking about what they want to say next, checking their phone, or waiting for a chance to tell their own story. Good listening is a skill that can improve our relationships at home and at work.

The first step is to give the other person your full attention. Put your phone away and look at them. This simple action shows that you respect them and care about what they are saying. Try not to interrupt, even if you think you know what they are going to say. Let them finish their thoughts.

Good listeners also show that they are listening. You can nod, smile, or make small sounds like "mm" or "I see." Asking questions is very helpful too, especially open questions like "How did you feel about that?" or "What happened next?" These questions encourage people to say more and show that you are interested.

Another useful technique is to repeat back what you have heard in your own words. For example, you might say, "So you're saying that you felt ignored by your boss?" This helps you check that you have understood correctly, and it makes the other person feel understood.

Finally, resist the urge to give advice immediately or to turn the conversation toward yourself. Often, people don't want solutions. They simply want somebody to listen. As the saying goes, we have two ears and one mouth, so perhaps we should listen twice as much as we speak.

title: Rescue on the Mountain
paragraphs: Anna and her brother Mark had been planning their hike for months. The trail was long and challenging, but they were both experienced walkers. They set off early in the morning under a clear blue sky, carrying plenty of water, food, and warm clothes.

By the early afternoon, they had reached the top. The view was breathtaking. They could see lakes and valleys stretching for kilometers in every direction. They ate their lunch on a rock and took photos. But as they began to walk down, the weather suddenly changed. Dark clouds appeared, and within minutes, thick fog covered the mountain. They could hardly see the path in front of them.

Then Mark slipped on a wet rock and fell. When he tried to stand, he cried out in pain. His ankle was badly injured, and he couldn't walk. Anna tried to call for help, but there was no signal. She knew they couldn't stay where they were for long, because the temperature was dropping fast.

Anna made a difficult decision. She wrapped Mark in all their warm clothes and a survival blanket, gave him most of the water, and marked the spot with her bright red jacket. Then she walked carefully down the mountain until she found a signal and called the mountain rescue team.

Two hours later, a rescue team found Mark, cold but safe. They carried him down on a stretcher. At the hospital, the doctor told them that Anna's quick thinking had probably saved his life. Mark's ankle healed, and the following summer, they climbed the mountain again, this time checking the weather forecast twice.

title: The Rise of Emojis
paragraphs: Today, billions of people use emojis every day. These small pictures of faces, animals, food, and objects have become a normal part of the way we communicate, especially in text messages and on social media. But where did emojis come from, and are they changing the way we use language?

The first set of emojis was created in Japan in the late nineteen nineties by a designer called Shigetaka Kurita. He was working for a mobile phone company and wanted to create a simple way for people to express emotions in short messages. His first set contained one hundred and seventy-six simple images, including a smiling face, a heart, and the sun. Today, some of them are kept in the collection of a famous museum in New York.

Emojis became popular around the world when smartphones started to include them in the early two thousand tens. Now there are thousands of different emojis, and new ones are added every year. Anybody can suggest a new emoji, but it has to be approved by an organization that sets international standards for computer text.

Emojis are useful because written messages can easily be misunderstood. Without seeing someone's face or hearing their voice, it can be hard to tell if they are joking, angry, or serious. A simple smiling face can make a message feel friendlier.

However, emojis can also cause confusion. Some emojis look different on different phones, and people from different cultures may understand them in different ways. A thumbs up, for example, is positive in many countries but can be rude in others. Like any language, emojis need to be used with care.

title: A Farm in the Middle of the City
paragraphs: When we think of farms, we usually imagine green fields, tractors, and cows in the countryside. But in cities around the world, a new kind of farming is growing quickly. Urban farms are appearing on rooftops, in empty buildings, and even underground.

One of the most interesting types is vertical farming. Instead of growing plants in fields, vertical farms grow them indoors, in tall stacks of shelves. The plants grow under special LED lights that replace sunlight, and their roots sit in water full of nutrients rather than in soil. Computers carefully control the temperature, light, and water.

Vertical farms have several advantages. They can produce a lot of food in a very small space, and they can grow crops all year round, whatever the weather outside. Because they are indoors, they don't need pesticides, and they use much less water than traditional farms. And since they are located in cities, the food doesn't have to travel long distances to reach the shops, so it is fresher.

However, vertical farms also have problems. The lights and computers use a lot of electricity, which is expensive and can be bad for the environment unless the energy comes from renewable sources. At the moment, vertical farms are mainly used to grow salad leaves and herbs, which grow quickly. It is much more difficult to grow foods like wheat or potatoes in this way.

Other urban farms are simpler. In many cities, community groups grow vegetables on empty land or keep bees on rooftops. As the world's cities continue to grow, these projects may become an important part of feeding their populations.

title: How Habits Work
paragraphs: Every day, we do hundreds of things without really thinking about them. We brush our teeth, make coffee, check our phones, and take the same route to work. Researchers believe that around forty percent of our daily actions are habits, not conscious decisions.

Habits form because our brains like to save energy. When we repeat an action many times in the same situation, the brain starts to do it automatically. Scientists describe habits as a loop with three parts. First, there is a cue, something that triggers the habit, such as feeling bored or arriving home. Then there is the routine, the action itself, like eating a snack. Finally, there is the reward, the good feeling that makes the brain want to repeat the action.

Understanding this loop can help us change our habits. Experts say that it is very difficult to simply stop a bad habit. It is easier to keep the same cue and reward but change the routine. For example, if you always eat cookies when you feel tired in the afternoon, you could try going for a short walk instead. The cue, tiredness, is the same, and the reward, a short break and a bit of energy, is similar.

Building good habits works in a similar way. It helps to start very small. If you want to exercise more, begin with five minutes a day rather than an hour. Linking a new habit to an existing one also helps, for example doing a few stretches right after you brush your teeth in the morning.
Most importantly, be patient. Research suggests that it usually takes about two months for a new behavior to become automatic.

title: Exploring the World on Wheels
paragraphs: When Sarah was twenty-three, a car accident left her unable to walk. She had always loved traveling, and at first, she thought her adventures were over. Simple things like getting on a bus or entering a restaurant suddenly became major challenges. For more than a year, she hardly left her hometown.

Then a friend invited her on a trip to Spain. Sarah was nervous, but she decided to go. The trip was not easy. Some streets were too steep, some hotels said they were accessible but had steps at the entrance, and the airline damaged her wheelchair. But she also discovered that most problems had solutions, and that many people were happy to help.

That trip changed her life. Over the next ten years, Sarah visited more than forty countries. She has traveled through deserts, visited ancient temples, and even gone diving in the ocean with a specially trained instructor. She started writing a blog about her experiences, giving practical advice to other travelers with disabilities.

Her blog now has thousands of readers. She reviews hotels, museums, and tourist attractions, and she explains exactly how accessible they really are. She has also worked with tourism companies to help them improve their services for disabled visitors.

Sarah says the biggest barriers are often not physical but in people's minds. "People assume I can't do things," she says. "Sometimes I assumed it too. But almost everything is possible if you plan carefully and are willing to try." Her message to others is simple: don't let anybody, including yourself, decide what you can't do.

title: How Color Changes Taste
paragraphs: Imagine drinking a glass of orange juice that is colored bright blue. Would it taste the same? Most people would say yes. But scientists have discovered that the color of our food has a surprisingly strong influence on how we think it tastes.

In one famous experiment, wine experts were given white wine that had been colored red with a flavorless dye. When they described it, they used words that are normally used for red wine, such as "berry" and "chocolate." Their eyes had tricked their sense of taste. Other experiments have shown that people think drinks taste sweeter when they are red or pink, and more sour when they are green or yellow.

The color of the plate also matters. In some studies, people ate less food when the color of the plate was very different from the color of the food. Desserts served on white plates were rated as sweeter and more delicious than the same desserts on black plates.

This happens because taste is not only about our tongue. When we eat, our brain combines information from all our senses, including sight, smell, and even sound. Before we taste anything, our brain has already made predictions based on how the food looks. If the food looks fresh and ripe, we expect it to taste good.

Food companies know this very well, and they spend a lot of money choosing the right colors for their products and packages. Chefs also think carefully about color when they present their dishes. So the next time you eat, remember that you are tasting with your eyes as well as your mouth.

title: The Recycled Orchestra
paragraphs: Cateura is a poor neighborhood in Paraguay that was built next to a huge landfill site. Many families there earn a living by collecting and selling recyclable materials from the trash. For the children who grow up there, opportunities are limited, and many leave school early to work.

In two thousand six, an environmental technician named Favio Chavez started working at the landfill. He was also a musician, and he decided to offer free music lessons to local children. But there was a problem. He only had a few instruments, and they were too expensive for the families to buy. A violin cost more than a house in the neighborhood.

Then a local trash picker called Nicolas Gomez had an idea. He started making instruments from the materials he found in the landfill. He made violins from old metal cans and pieces of wood, a cello from an oil can, and flutes from old water pipes. He even used forks and coins to make some parts. The instruments looked strange, but they sounded surprisingly good.

With these instruments, the children formed an orchestra. They practiced classical music, as well as popular songs. Their story was shared online and in a documentary film, and soon the Recycled Orchestra was invited to perform in concert halls around the world. They have played in Europe, Asia, and North America, and they even performed with famous rock bands.

For the young musicians, the orchestra has changed their lives. It has given them confidence, new skills, and the chance to travel. As their founder likes to say, "The world sends us garbage. We send back music."

title: Should We Eat Insects?
paragraphs: For many people in Europe and North America, the idea of eating insects is disgusting. But for about two billion people around the world, insects are a normal part of their diet. In countries such as Thailand, Mexico, and Ghana, people eat fried crickets, roasted grasshoppers, and ant eggs as tasty snacks or meals.

Some experts believe that insects could play an important role in feeding the world in the future. The world's population is growing, and producing enough meat for everybody is becoming a serious problem. Raising cows, pigs, and chickens requires huge amounts of land, water, and food, and it produces a lot of greenhouse gases.

Insects are much more efficient. They need far less space and food than other animals to produce the same amount of protein. Crickets, for example, need about twelve times less food than cows to produce the same amount of protein. Insects also produce much fewer greenhouse gases. And they are very nutritious, full of protein, vitamins, and minerals.

So why don't more people eat them? The main reason is cultural. Many people simply find the idea unpleasant. To solve this problem, some companies are turning insects into powder and using it to make products like pasta, protein bars, and cookies. In this form, the insects can't be seen, and many people say they can't even taste the difference.

Insect farming is still a small industry, and there are questions about safety and how to produce insects on a large scale. But who knows? In twenty years, a cricket burger might be as normal as a beef burger.

title: Alone in Space
paragraphs: In nineteen sixty-nine, millions of people around the world watched on television as Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin became the first humans to walk on the Moon. But there was a third astronaut on the mission who never set foot on the Moon. His name was Michael Collins.

While Armstrong and Aldrin were on the surface, Collins stayed in the command module, flying in orbit around the Moon. His job was to keep the spacecraft ready to bring his two colleagues back. If something went wrong on the surface, he would have to return to Earth alone.

Every two hours, as the spacecraft traveled around the far side of the Moon, Collins lost all radio contact with Earth. For about forty-eight minutes each time, he was completely cut off from the rest of humanity. At those moments, he was further from other people than any human had ever been. Some newspapers later called him "the loneliest man in history."

But Collins said he didn't feel lonely at all. In his book, he wrote that he felt awareness, anticipation, and even joy. He enjoyed the silence, and he described the experience of seeing the stars without the light of the Earth as beautiful.

After the mission, many people asked him if he was disappointed that he didn't walk on the Moon. He always said no. He felt that he had been an important part of the team and was proud of what they had achieved together. Collins later became the director of the National Air and Space Museum in Washington.

title: The Midnight Feast
paragraphs: It was the last night of summer camp, and the twelve girls in Cabin Seven had been planning their midnight feast for a week. They had saved candy from the camp shop, hidden cookies under their beds, and someone's mother had sent a whole chocolate cake in the mail.

The rules were very clear: lights out at ten o'clock, and nobody was allowed to leave the cabins at night. The camp counselor, a strict young woman called Miss Turner, walked around the cabins every hour with a flashlight. But at midnight, when everything was quiet, the girls crept out of bed and gathered in the middle of the cabin floor.

They spread out a blanket and laid out all the food. They whispered and giggled as they shared the cake. Somebody started telling a ghost story, and just at the scariest moment, there was a loud knock on the door. Everybody screamed. The door opened slowly, and a bright light shone into the room. It was Miss Turner.

The girls froze. They were sure they were in terrible trouble. Miss Turner looked at the blanket, the cake, and the twelve frightened faces. Then, to everybody's surprise, she sat down on the floor. "Is there any cake left?" she asked. "When I was your age, I stayed in this very same cabin. We had a midnight feast on the last night too."
They talked and laughed until two o'clock in the morning. Many years later, the girls still remembered that night as the best night of camp, and Miss Turner as their favorite counselor.

title: Five Ways to Beat Stress
paragraphs: Stress is a normal part of life. A little stress can even be useful, because it gives us energy and helps us concentrate when we have a deadline or an important exam. But when stress continues for a long time, it can damage our health. It can cause headaches, sleep problems, and stomach problems, and it can make us more likely to get sick.

The first way to reduce stress is to move your body. Exercise is one of the most effective ways to fight stress. It doesn't have to be intense. A brisk walk, a bike ride, or some gentle yoga can help your body release tension and improve your mood.

Second, pay attention to your breathing. When we are stressed, we often breathe quickly and shallowly. Taking slow, deep breaths can calm the nervous system. One simple method is to breathe in for four seconds, hold your breath for four seconds, and breathe out for four seconds. Repeating this for a few minutes can make a big difference.

Third, talk to someone. Sharing your worries with a friend, a family member, or a professional can make problems feel smaller. Often, simply putting your feelings into words helps you see the situation more clearly.

Fourth, take a break from screens. Constant emails, news, and social media can make us feel overwhelmed. Try to have some time each day without your phone. And fifth, make time for things you enjoy, whether it is reading, cooking, listening to music, or spending time in nature. These moments of pleasure are not a luxury. They are essential for good health.

title: The Island of Cats
paragraphs: Off the coast of Japan, there is a small island called Aoshima. Fewer than ten people live there, and most of them are old. But the island is far from empty. It is home to well over a hundred cats, and it has become famous around the world as "Cat Island."

The cats were originally brought to the island many years ago to control the mice on the fishing boats. At that time, Aoshima had a busy fishing community of about nine hundred people. But over the years, young people left the island to find work in the cities, and the population fell sharply. Meanwhile, the cats, with no natural predators, kept on multiplying.

Today, the cats are everywhere. They sleep on walls, sit on boats, and wait near the harbor for the arrival of the small ferry that brings visitors from the mainland. As soon as tourists step off the boat, dozens of cats come running toward them, hoping for food.

The island has no shops, restaurants, or hotels, so visitors must bring their own food and water. There are also rules to protect the cats and the residents. Visitors are asked not to leave any food behind and to be quiet and respectful.

Some residents enjoy the attention, while others find the crowds of tourists tiring. In recent years, animal welfare groups have worked with the islanders to give the cats medical care and to stop the population from growing too large. For cat lovers, a day trip to Aoshima is like a dream come true.

title: The Woman Who Calculated the Stars
paragraphs: In nineteen sixty-two, the American astronaut John Glenn was preparing to become the first American to orbit the Earth. The mission was very dangerous, and the calculations for his flight had been made by new electronic computers. But Glenn didn't completely trust the machines. Before the flight, he made a special request: he wanted a woman called Katherine Johnson to check the numbers by hand.

Katherine Johnson was a brilliant mathematician. Born in West Virginia in nineteen eighteen, she showed an incredible talent for numbers from a very young age. She finished high school at fourteen and university at eighteen. But as an African American woman at that time, she faced many barriers. Schools and workplaces were segregated, and women were rarely given important jobs in science.

In nineteen fifty-three, she started working at the organization that later became NASA. She was one of a group of women who worked as "human computers," doing complex calculations by hand. Her skill quickly made her stand out. She calculated the paths of spacecraft, including the flight that took the first American into space.

When Glenn asked for her, Katherine spent days checking the computer's calculations. She confirmed that they were correct, and the mission was a success. Later, she also worked on the calculations for the missions that took astronauts to the Moon.

For many years, her work was not widely known. But in two thousand fifteen, she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom, one of the highest honors in the United States. A year later, a popular film called "Hidden Figures" told her story to the world.

title: Why Do We Laugh?
paragraphs: Laughter is one of the most human things we do. Babies start laughing when they are just a few months old, long before they can speak. And people laugh in every culture in the world. But why do we laugh, and what is it for?

Most people think we laugh mainly because something is funny. But research shows that this is not quite true. In one study, scientists listened to people's conversations in public places and recorded when they laughed. They found that most laughter did not follow jokes at all. People laughed at ordinary comments, like "See you later" or "I know what you mean."

This suggests that laughter is mainly a social signal. It shows other people that we are friendly, that we agree with them, and that we feel comfortable with them. In fact, we are about thirty times more likely to laugh when we are with other people than when we are alone. Laughter is also contagious. When we hear other people laughing, we often start laughing too, even if we don't know why.

Laughter has benefits for our health as well. When we laugh, our body releases chemicals called endorphins, which make us feel good and can even reduce pain. Laughter can also reduce stress hormones and relax our muscles.

Interestingly, humans are not the only animals that laugh. Apes like chimpanzees make laughing sounds when they play and tickle each other. Scientists have even discovered that rats make tiny squeaking sounds, too high for humans to hear, when they are tickled. Laughter, it seems, is a very old part of our nature.

title: Lost in Tokyo
paragraphs: On my first trip to Japan, I made a mistake that I will never forget. On my second day in Tokyo, I decided to explore the city alone. I took a train to a district I had read about, walked around for a few hours, and then realized I had no idea where I was. My phone battery was dead, and I couldn't read any of the signs.

I started to panic. It was getting dark, and the streets were busy with people rushing home from work. I tried to ask a few people for directions, but they didn't speak English, and I didn't speak Japanese. I showed them the name of my hotel, which I had written on a piece of paper, but they just shook their heads politely.

Then an elderly man stopped and looked at my piece of paper. He didn't speak English either, but he smiled and made a sign for me to follow him. I was a little nervous, but I didn't have much choice. We walked to a train station, where he bought two tickets and got on the train with me.

We traveled for about twenty minutes. Then he led me out of the station and through several streets until we arrived in front of my hotel. I was so grateful that I wanted to give him some money or buy him dinner, but he refused. He simply bowed, smiled, and walked back toward the station.
I never learned his name. But whenever I see a tourist who looks lost in my own city, I remember that man, and I stop to help.

title: Living Without Trash
paragraphs: The average person in Europe produces around five hundred kilos of household waste every year. But some families have managed to reduce their waste to almost nothing. They follow a lifestyle known as "zero waste," and their entire year's trash can fit into a single small jar.

One of the most famous examples is Bea Johnson, a French woman living in California. In two thousand eight, she and her husband decided to change their lifestyle. They wanted to live more simply and protect the environment. Over time, they found ways to avoid almost all packaging and single-use items.

Their approach is based on five simple rules, in this order: refuse, reduce, reuse, recycle, and rot. First, they refuse things they don't need, such as free pens, plastic bags, and advertising leaflets. Then they reduce the number of things they own. They reuse items whenever possible, for example by taking their own cloth bags and glass jars to the shops. They recycle what they cannot refuse, reduce, or reuse, and they turn food scraps into compost for the garden.

The family says that living this way has many benefits. They save a lot of money, because they buy less and avoid packaged products. Their home is much less cluttered, and they spend less time cleaning and shopping.

Of course, it isn't easy for everybody. Not all towns have shops where you can buy food without packaging, and it requires time and planning. But even small changes, like carrying a reusable water bottle or saying no to plastic bags, can make a real difference.

title: The Teacher Who Believed in Me
paragraphs: At the age of fifteen, I was close to leaving school. My grades were terrible, I often skipped lessons, and most of my teachers had given up on me. At home, things were difficult. My parents had just separated, and nobody seemed to notice how unhappy I was.

Then a new English teacher arrived at our school. Her name was Ms. Rivera. On her first day, she asked us to write a short story about anything we wanted. I wrote about a boy who ran away to the sea. It was messy and full of mistakes, but I put everything I felt into it.

The next week, Ms. Rivera asked me to stay after class. I expected to be in trouble again. Instead, she handed me back my story covered in notes. "This is really good," she said. "You have a gift for writing. Have you ever thought about developing it?" Nobody had ever told me I was good at anything.

From that moment, things began to change. Ms. Rivera lent me books and encouraged me to enter a writing competition. She let me stay in her classroom at lunchtime to write when I didn't want to be around other people. Slowly, I started attending more lessons, and my grades improved in other subjects too.

Today, I work as a journalist, and I have written two books. A few years ago, I went back to my old school to give a talk. Ms. Rivera was in the audience. When I thanked her publicly, she cried. One person's belief can change a whole life.

title: The Sharing Economy
paragraphs: In the past, if you wanted to stay in a city for a few days, you would book a hotel. If you needed to get across town, you would take a taxi. Today, many people use apps that connect them directly with ordinary people who can offer these services. This new way of doing business is often called the sharing economy.

The idea is simple. Many people own things that they don't use all the time, such as a spare room, a car, or tools. Through online platforms, they can rent these things to others and earn some extra money. Some apps let people rent out their homes to travelers, while others allow drivers to use their own cars as taxis. There are even apps for sharing parking spaces, clothes, and dogs.

For customers, the sharing economy often offers lower prices and more choice. Travelers can stay in local neighborhoods instead of tourist areas and experience a city more like a resident. For providers, it can be a flexible way to earn money and make better use of their possessions.

However, the sharing economy has also caused problems. In some popular cities, so many apartments are rented to tourists that there are fewer homes available for local people, and rents have gone up. Taxi drivers have protested, saying that app drivers don't have to follow the same rules. There are also concerns about workers' rights, because many app workers are not employees and don't receive benefits like sick pay or vacations.
Many cities are now introducing new laws to control the sharing economy. The challenge is to keep its benefits while protecting the people affected by it.

title: Why Reading Fiction Is Good for You
paragraphs: In a world full of television, video games, and social media, reading novels might seem old-fashioned. But scientists are discovering that reading fiction has surprising benefits for our brains and our relationships with other people.

One of the most interesting findings is that reading fiction may help us understand other people better. When we read a novel, we see the world through the eyes of the characters. We learn about their thoughts, feelings, and motivations. Some studies suggest that people who read a lot of fiction are better at understanding what others are thinking and feeling. This ability is known as empathy.

Reading is also good exercise for the brain. When we read, we have to concentrate, imagine scenes and characters, and remember complicated plots. Brain scans have shown that reading a story activates many different parts of the brain, including areas connected with movement and the senses. When we read about a character running, the parts of our brain that control running become more active.

Reading can also reduce stress. In one study, just six minutes of reading reduced stress levels more than listening to music or going for a walk. Losing ourselves in a good book allows us to escape our worries for a while.

Finally, regular reading may help to protect the brain as we get older. Studies suggest that people who read and do other mentally challenging activities throughout their lives may keep their memory sharper in old age. So the next time someone tells you that reading novels is a waste of time, you can tell them it is good for your health.

title: The Unexpected Gift
paragraphs: Jenny had only met her great-aunt Margaret twice, both times when she was a little girl. She remembered an old woman with sharp eyes and a strange sense of humor who lived alone in a big house by the sea. So she was very surprised when a lawyer called to tell her that Margaret had died and left her something in her will.

"What did she leave me?" Jenny asked. The lawyer hesitated. "A key," he said, "and a letter. She asked that you open the letter at her house." Curious, Jenny took a train to the small coastal town the following weekend.

The house was old and full of dusty furniture. Jenny sat in the kitchen and opened the letter. "Dear Jenny," it began. "When you were six, you told me you wanted to be a painter. You were the only person in the family who ever liked my paintings. The key opens the room at the top of the house. Everything in it is yours."

Jenny climbed the narrow stairs and unlocked the door. The room was full of light from a huge window that looked out over the sea. There were dozens of canvases, brushes, and tubes of paint. And on the walls were beautiful paintings of the coast, the sky, and the sea in every kind of weather.

Jenny had given up painting years ago to work in an office. She stood in the room for a long time, looking at the paintings. Then she picked up a brush. A year later, she moved into the house, and she has been painting there ever since.

title: Racing to the Sky
paragraphs: For most of human history, the tallest buildings in the world were religious buildings, such as churches, temples, and pyramids. The Great Pyramid of Giza in Egypt held the record for nearly four thousand years. But in the late nineteenth century, a new type of building began to change city skylines forever: the skyscraper.

Two inventions made skyscrapers possible. The first was the use of steel frames, which were strong enough to support very tall buildings without needing extremely thick walls. The second was the safe elevator. Before this, nobody wanted to climb more than a few floors of stairs. The first skyscrapers appeared in Chicago and New York in the eighteen eighties.

In the early twentieth century, there was a competition between cities and companies to build the tallest building. In New York, the Chrysler Building and the Empire State Building were completed within a year of each other. The Empire State Building was the world's tallest building for almost forty years.

Today, the tallest building in the world is the Burj Khalifa in Dubai, which is more than eight hundred meters tall. Building it required solutions to many new problems. At that height, the wind is extremely strong, so the building was designed in a special shape to reduce its effects. Its elevators are among the fastest in the world.

Even taller buildings are being planned. But some architects question whether we need them. Very tall buildings are expensive to build and use a lot of energy. Some cities prefer to grow in other ways, with lower buildings, green spaces, and good public transportation.

title: Walking Around the World
paragraphs: In nineteen seventy, a young American called Dave Kunst set off from his home in Minnesota with his brother John and a mule named Willie Makeit. Their plan was to walk all the way around the world. Nobody had ever done it before, and many people thought it was impossible.

The brothers walked across the United States, then flew across the Atlantic and continued walking through Europe and Asia. Along the way, they collected money for a children's charity. Everywhere they went, people were curious about the two men and their mule. They were often invited into people's homes for meals and given a place to sleep.

But the journey also had terrible moments. In Afghanistan, the brothers were attacked by robbers. John was killed, and Dave was seriously injured. It took Dave four months to recover. Many people expected him to give up and go home. Instead, he decided to continue the walk, both for himself and in memory of his brother.

He continued with another brother, Pete, and later walked alone. He crossed India and then flew to Australia, where he walked across the vast, hot desert. During this part of the journey, he met a teacher called Jenny, who drove a car behind him with supplies for many weeks. They later got married.

In October nineteen seventy-four, more than four years after he had left, Dave walked back into his hometown. He had walked about twenty-three thousand kilometers and worn out twenty-one pairs of shoes. He was the first person ever confirmed to have walked around the world.

title: Why We Are Losing the Night Sky
paragraphs: For most of human history, people could look up on a clear night and see thousands of stars and the bright band of the Milky Way stretching across the sky. Today, most people who live in cities have never seen it. The reason is light pollution: the artificial light from streetlights, buildings, cars, and advertisements that brightens the night sky.
