For centuries, people had little understanding of the disease. The name malaria comes from the Italian words for "bad air," because people believed it was caused by the unhealthy air near swamps. It was not until the late nineteenth century that scientists discovered the role of parasites and mosquitoes.

One of the simplest and most effective tools in the fight against malaria is the insecticide-treated bed net. Mosquitoes that carry malaria usually bite at night, so sleeping under a net provides strong protection. Millions of nets have been distributed in affected countries, and they have helped to save countless lives. Spraying the inside walls of homes with insecticide and providing fast diagnosis and treatment have also been important.

However, the battle is far from won. In some regions, mosquitoes have developed resistance to common insecticides, and parasites have become resistant to some drugs. Climate change may allow mosquitoes to spread into new areas.

In recent years, there has been a major breakthrough: the first vaccines against malaria. After decades of research, the World Health Organization recommended a malaria vaccine for children in two thousand twenty-one, followed by a second vaccine two years later. They are not perfect, but they can significantly reduce the number of severe cases and deaths. Scientists are also experimenting with other innovative approaches, including genetically modified mosquitoes that cannot transmit the parasite. Many experts now believe that eliminating malaria in our lifetime is a realistic goal.

title: The Beauty of Broken Things
paragraphs: In most cultures, when a precious bowl or cup breaks, we either throw it away or try to repair it so that the damage is as invisible as possible. In Japan, however, there is a traditional art that takes a completely different approach. It is called kintsugi, which means "golden joinery," and it involves repairing broken pottery with lacquer mixed with powdered gold.

The result is striking. Instead of hiding the cracks, kintsugi highlights them, turning them into shining golden lines that run across the surface of the object. The repaired piece is often considered more beautiful and valuable than it was before it broke. Each piece becomes unique, because no two objects break in exactly the same way.

According to one popular story, kintsugi began in the fifteenth century, when a Japanese military ruler broke his favorite tea bowl. He sent it to China to be repaired, but it came back held together with ugly metal staples. Unhappy with the result, he asked Japanese craftsmen to find a more attractive method, and kintsugi was born. Whether or not this story is true, the technique became highly valued, and some collectors were even accused of breaking pottery deliberately so that it could be repaired with gold.

The process is slow and requires great skill. The lacquer used comes from the sap of a tree and must be applied in several thin layers, each of which needs to dry for days or even weeks. A single repair can take a month or more to complete.

Kintsugi is closely connected to Japanese philosophy. It reflects the idea of wabi-sabi, which finds beauty in imperfection, simplicity, and the passage of time. It also relates to the idea of mottainai, a sense of regret at waste.

In recent years, kintsugi has become popular around the world, not only as a craft but as a metaphor. Many people find in it a powerful message about life: that our scars and failures do not need to be hidden, and that the experiences that break us can become part of what makes us strong and unique. In a culture that often values perfection and replaces broken things without a second thought, kintsugi offers a different way of seeing damage.

title: Are We Sleeping Less Than Ever?
paragraphs: Sleep experts generally recommend that adults get between seven and nine hours of sleep every night. Yet surveys in many countries suggest that a large proportion of people regularly sleep less than this. Some researchers have described insufficient sleep as a global public health problem, with serious consequences for our health, safety, and productivity.

Modern life presents many obstacles to good sleep. Long working hours, commuting, and the pressure to be constantly available make it hard for many people to get to bed early. Artificial light, especially the blue light emitted by phones, tablets, and computers, can interfere with the production of melatonin, a hormone that helps regulate our sleep cycle. Caffeine, alcohol, and irregular schedules can also disrupt sleep.

The effects of sleep deprivation go far beyond feeling tired. In the short term, lack of sleep impairs concentration, memory, and decision-making. It makes us more irritable and less able to cope with stress. Studies have shown that staying awake for around twenty hours can affect our performance as much as drinking alcohol. Drowsy driving is a major cause of road accidents.

In the long term, chronic lack of sleep has been linked to a wide range of health problems, including obesity, diabetes, heart disease, and depression. Sleep also appears to play a role in clearing waste products from the brain, and some research suggests that poor sleep over many years may increase the risk of dementia.

Teenagers are particularly affected. During adolescence, the body's internal clock shifts, so teenagers naturally tend to fall asleep and wake up later. Early school start times force many of them to wake up before their bodies are ready, leaving them chronically tired. Some school districts that have moved their start times later have reported improvements in attendance, grades, and mood.

Fortunately, there are many ways to improve sleep. Experts recommend going to bed and getting up at the same time every day, even on weekends. Keeping the bedroom dark, cool, and quiet, avoiding screens for an hour before bed, and limiting caffeine in the afternoon can all help. Perhaps most importantly, we need to stop seeing sleep as a waste of time and start treating it as an essential part of a healthy life.

title: Mapping the Ocean Floor
paragraphs: For most of human history, the bottom of the ocean was a complete mystery. Many people imagined it as a vast, flat, featureless plain covered in mud. In the nineteen fifties, an American geologist and cartographer named Marie Tharp proved them dramatically wrong, and in doing so, she helped to transform our understanding of the planet.

Tharp worked at a research institute at Columbia University in New York. At the time, women were not allowed to join research voyages, so she could not go to sea herself. Instead, her colleague Bruce Heezen collected data from ships that measured the depth of the ocean using sound waves. Tharp's job was to turn thousands of these measurements into maps.

It was painstaking work, done entirely by hand. But as she plotted the data from the Atlantic Ocean, Tharp noticed something extraordinary. Running down the middle of the ocean was a huge mountain range, and along its center was a deep valley, or rift. She concluded that the ocean floor was splitting apart along this line.

This idea supported a theory known as continental drift, which proposed that the continents slowly move across the surface of the Earth. At the time, most geologists rejected the theory. When Tharp showed her findings to Heezen, he dismissed them as "girl talk." It took him almost a year to accept that she was right.

Tharp and Heezen continued to map the ocean floor for many years. Their work revealed a global system of ridges and valleys running through all the world's oceans, like the seams on a baseball. In nineteen seventy-seven, they published a famous map of the entire ocean floor, painted by an Austrian artist, which showed underwater mountains, valleys, and plains in remarkable detail.

Their discoveries provided key evidence for the theory of plate tectonics, which is now the foundation of modern geology. It explains earthquakes, volcanoes, and the formation of mountains. For many years, Tharp received little recognition, and credit for the discovery often went to male scientists. Today, she is celebrated as one of the most important scientists of the twentieth century, a woman who mapped a hidden world she was never allowed to visit.

title: The Advantages of a Bilingual Brain
paragraphs: More than half of the world's population speaks at least two languages. For many people, switching between languages is a natural part of daily life, whether they speak one language at home and another at work, or use several languages with friends from different backgrounds. In recent decades, researchers have become increasingly interested in how bilingualism affects the brain.

For much of the twentieth century, many educators believed that raising children with two languages could cause confusion and slow down their development. Some parents who had immigrated to a new country were even advised to stop speaking their native language to their children. Today, this view has largely been abandoned. Research has shown that bilingual children reach the same language milestones as monolingual children, although they may know slightly fewer words in each language at first.

One of the most interesting areas of research concerns what are known as executive functions. These are mental skills that help us plan, focus our attention, and switch between tasks. When bilingual people speak, both of their languages appear to be active in the brain at the same time. To speak in one language, they must constantly suppress the other. Some researchers believe that this constant practice strengthens the brain's control systems.

Several studies have found that bilingual people perform better on certain tasks that require switching attention or ignoring distractions. There is also some evidence that bilingualism may help to protect the brain in old age. Studies of older adults have suggested that bilingual people may develop symptoms of dementia several years later than monolingual people, even though they do not avoid the disease altogether.

However, these findings are not universally accepted. In recent years, some researchers have failed to reproduce the bilingual advantage in carefully controlled experiments. They argue that other factors, such as education, income, and cultural background, may explain some of the differences observed in earlier studies.

Even if the cognitive benefits turn out to be smaller than once thought, few people doubt the social and cultural advantages of speaking more than one language. Bilingualism allows people to communicate with a wider range of people, to access different cultures and ways of thinking, and to maintain a connection with their family heritage.

title: Solving Crimes with Science
paragraphs: In popular television dramas, forensic scientists solve crimes in a matter of minutes. A single hair or a drop of blood is analyzed with impressive machines, and the identity of the criminal appears on a screen just before the commercial break. Real forensic science is rarely so fast or so certain, but it has nonetheless transformed the way crimes are investigated.

One of the oldest forensic techniques is fingerprint analysis. In the late nineteenth century, scientists discovered that the patterns of ridges on our fingertips are unique to each individual and remain the same throughout life. Fingerprints were soon being used by police forces around the world. Today, computer databases can compare a fingerprint found at a crime scene with millions of records in seconds.

The most important breakthrough in modern forensics, however, came in the nineteen eighties with the development of DNA profiling. Every person, except identical twins, has a unique DNA code. By analyzing DNA from blood, saliva, skin cells, or hair left at a crime scene, scientists can link a suspect to a crime with a high degree of probability. DNA evidence has helped to convict criminals in cases that had remained unsolved for decades.

Equally significantly, DNA evidence has been used to prove the innocence of people who were wrongly convicted. In the United States alone, hundreds of prisoners have been released after DNA tests showed they could not have committed the crimes for which they were imprisoned. Some had spent more than twenty years in prison.

Forensic science is not infallible, though. Evidence can be contaminated, samples can be mixed up, and results can be misinterpreted. Some techniques that were once considered reliable, such as comparing the marks left by teeth, have been criticized for lacking a solid scientific basis. Experts warn that juries may place too much trust in scientific evidence, partly because of the way it is presented in television shows.

New technologies continue to emerge. Investigators can now analyze tiny amounts of DNA and even use family history databases to identify unknown suspects through their relatives. These advances raise important questions about privacy and the balance between solving crimes and protecting individual rights.

title: The Pigeon Who Saved Two Hundred Soldiers
paragraphs: In October nineteen eighteen, during the final months of the First World War, a group of more than five hundred American soldiers found themselves trapped behind enemy lines in the Argonne Forest in France. Surrounded by German troops, short of food and water, and running out of ammunition, they were in a desperate situation. Their commander, Major Charles Whittlesey, had only one way to communicate with headquarters: carrier pigeons.

Carrier pigeons were widely used in the war because they could find their way home over long distances, even through smoke and gunfire. Radio technology was still unreliable, and telephone lines were easily cut. Soldiers would write messages on small pieces of paper, place them in tiny containers attached to the birds' legs, and release them.

On the second day, the situation became even worse. American artillery, unaware of the soldiers' exact position, began firing shells that landed directly on them. Whittlesey sent pigeon after pigeon with messages explaining where they were, but the birds were shot down. Only one pigeon remained, a bird named Cher Ami, which means "dear friend" in French.

Whittlesey wrote a short, urgent message: "We are along the road parallel to two seven six point four. Our own artillery is dropping a barrage directly on us. For heaven's sake, stop it." The message was attached to Cher Ami's leg, and the bird was released.

As Cher Ami flew up, German soldiers opened fire. The pigeon was hit and fell, but then managed to rise again and continued flying. Around twenty-five minutes later, it arrived at its base, about forty kilometers away. It had been shot through the chest, had lost an eye, and its leg, still carrying the message, was hanging by only a few tendons. The artillery fire was stopped, and the surviving soldiers, about two hundred in total, were eventually rescued.

Army doctors worked hard to save Cher Ami's life, and even carved a small wooden leg for the bird. Cher Ami was awarded a French military medal for heroic service and became a celebrity. After the bird died the following year, its body was preserved, and it can still be seen today at a museum in Washington.

title: Farming Without Plowing
paragraphs: For thousands of years, farmers have prepared their fields in the same basic way: by turning over the soil before planting seeds. Plowing buries weeds, loosens the earth, and mixes in fertilizers. It has long been seen as essential to good farming. But a growing number of farmers around the world are now abandoning the plow altogether, in a practice known as no-till farming.

The problem with traditional plowing is that it can damage the soil. Turning over the earth exposes it to wind and rain, which can wash or blow away the fertile top layer. This erosion is a serious problem in many parts of the world. In the nineteen thirties, a combination of intensive plowing and severe drought in the American Midwest led to the Dust Bowl, when huge clouds of soil were blown across the country and thousands of farming families were forced to leave their land.

Plowing also disrupts the complex ecosystem that lives in healthy soil, including earthworms, fungi, and countless microorganisms. These creatures help to create the structure of the soil and recycle nutrients. In addition, plowing releases carbon stored in the soil into the atmosphere as carbon dioxide, contributing to climate change.

In no-till farming, seeds are planted directly into the remains of the previous crop using special machines that cut narrow slots in the ground. The stems and leaves left on the surface act as a protective layer, reducing erosion and helping the soil to retain moisture. Many no-till farmers also plant "cover crops," such as clover or rye, between their main crops to keep the soil covered all year round.

Supporters say that no-till farming improves soil health, saves fuel and labor, and can help farms become more resilient to droughts. Over time, some farmers have reported higher yields and lower costs.

However, the method has its challenges. Without plowing to control weeds, many no-till farmers rely heavily on herbicides, which raises environmental concerns of its own. The transition can also be difficult, and yields may fall during the first few years while the soil adjusts. Nevertheless, the practice is spreading, and many experts believe that caring for soil will be one of the keys to feeding the world in a changing climate.

title: Feeling Like a Fraud
paragraphs: Imagine being promoted at work, winning an award, or getting into a top university, and instead of feeling proud, being convinced that it was all a mistake. You worry that you are not really as talented as people think, that you succeeded only because of luck, and that sooner or later, everybody will discover the truth. If this sounds familiar, you may have experienced what psychologists call imposter syndrome.

The term was first used in the nineteen seventies by two psychologists, Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes, who noticed that many highly successful women they studied believed they were not intelligent and had fooled everyone around them. Since then, research has shown that the feeling is very common among both men and women. Some studies suggest that around seventy percent of people experience it at some point in their lives.

People with imposter feelings often attribute their successes to external factors, such as luck, timing, or the help of others, while blaming their failures on their own lack of ability. As a result, success does little to increase their confidence. Many respond by working extremely hard to avoid being "found out," which can lead to stress, anxiety, and burnout. Others avoid new challenges altogether, fearing that they will not be able to cope.

Interestingly, imposter syndrome is particularly common among high achievers. Even famous people, including the writer Maya Angelou and the physicist Albert Einstein, are reported to have described feeling like frauds. It is also often experienced by people who are different from most of their colleagues, for example the first person in their family to go to university, or one of the few women in a male-dominated field.

There is no simple cure, but several strategies can help. The first is to recognize the feeling and to understand that it is common. Talking openly with friends, colleagues, or mentors often reveals that many others feel the same way. Keeping a record of achievements and positive feedback can help people see their successes more objectively.

It can also be helpful to change the way we think about competence. Nobody knows everything, and making mistakes is a normal part of learning. Accepting that we can be capable without being perfect may be the first step toward feeling that we truly deserve our success.

title: The Art of Remembering
paragraphs: Every year, competitors at memory championships perform feats that seem almost impossible. Some memorize the order of a shuffled deck of fifty-two playing cards in less than twenty seconds. Others can recall hundreds of random numbers or the names and faces of dozens of strangers after studying them for just a few minutes. Remarkably, most of these memory champions insist that they were born with perfectly ordinary memories. Their secret is a set of techniques that are thousands of years old.

The most famous of these is the method of loci, also known as the memory palace. According to legend, it was invented by the ancient Greek poet Simonides. He was attending a banquet when he was called outside. While he was away, the roof of the hall collapsed, killing everyone inside. The bodies were so badly damaged that they could not be identified. But Simonides found he could remember who had been sitting where, by picturing the room in his mind. This experience made him realize that memory is closely connected to places.

The technique works like this. First, you imagine a place that you know well, such as your home or your route to work. Then, you mentally place the things you want to remember at specific locations along the way. To recall the information later, you simply take a mental walk through the place and see what you left there.

The key is to make the images as vivid, strange, and memorable as possible. If you need to remember to buy milk, eggs, and bread, you might imagine a river of milk flowing through your front door, a giant egg sitting on your sofa, and loaves of bread falling from the kitchen ceiling. The more unusual the image, the easier it is to recall.

Scientists believe the technique works because our brains evolved to be extremely good at remembering spaces and visual images. For our ancestors, remembering where to find food and water was essential for survival. Remembering lists of abstract information, however, was not.

Brain-scan studies have shown that memory champions use areas of the brain associated with spatial memory when they memorize. In one experiment, ordinary people who trained with the method of loci for six weeks significantly improved their memory, and the improvement lasted for months. It seems that with the right techniques, almost anyone can become a better rememberer.

title: Walking Between the Towers
paragraphs: On the morning of the seventh of August, nineteen seventy-four, people on their way to work in Lower Manhattan began to stop and stare upward. Four hundred meters above the street, a tiny figure was walking on a wire stretched between the roofs of the two towers of the World Trade Center, which had only recently been completed. The man on the wire was a twenty-four-year-old French street performer named Philippe Petit.

Petit had dreamed of this walk for years, ever since he saw a picture of the towers in a magazine at a dentist's office, before they were even built. Preparing for it took him more than six years. He practiced on wires in fields in France, studied the buildings carefully, and made several secret visits to the towers, sometimes disguised as a construction worker or a journalist.

The walk itself was completely illegal. On the night before, Petit and his team of friends hid in the towers with their equipment. During the night, they used a bow and arrow to shoot a fishing line from one tower to the other. Using this line, they pulled across ropes and then the heavy steel cable that Petit would walk on. The work took hours, and several times the team came close to being discovered by security guards.

Shortly after seven o'clock in the morning, Petit stepped onto the wire. For about forty-five minutes, he crossed back and forth between the towers eight times. He walked, knelt, lay down on the wire, and even saluted the crowds below. Police officers waited on the roofs, but they could do nothing until he decided to come back.

When he finally stepped off the wire, he was arrested. However, the public reaction was so enthusiastic that the charges were soon dropped, on the condition that he give a free performance for children in Central Park. The walk made him world famous.

Decades later, after the towers were destroyed in the attacks of two thousand one, Petit's walk took on a new meaning. A documentary about the event won an Academy Award, and many people saw his daring performance as a celebration of beauty, courage, and the human spirit in a place now associated with tragedy.

title: Social Media and Mental Health
paragraphs: Over the past fifteen years, social media has become an integral part of daily life for billions of people, particularly young people. Many teenagers spend several hours a day on platforms where they share photos, watch videos, and follow the lives of friends and celebrities. During the same period, rates of anxiety and depression among adolescents have risen significantly in several countries. Many people have concluded that social media is to blame. But is the evidence really that clear?

Some researchers argue strongly that social media is harming young people's mental health. They point out that the rise in mental health problems began around the early two thousand tens, roughly when smartphones became widespread. They suggest that social media encourages constant comparison with others, who often present idealized versions of their lives. Seeing carefully edited images of attractive, successful, and happy people may make users feel inadequate. Social media can also expose young people to cyberbullying and harmful content, and time spent online may replace sleep, exercise, and face-to-face social contact.

Other researchers urge caution. They note that many studies on the topic show only a correlation between social media use and poor mental health, which does not prove that one causes the other. It is possible that young people who are already unhappy spend more time online, rather than the other way around. Some large studies have found that the overall link between screen time and well-being is relatively small. Furthermore, social media is not the same for everyone. For some young people, particularly those who feel isolated, online communities can provide valuable support and a sense of belonging.

What most experts agree on is that how people use social media may matter more than how much they use it. Passive scrolling and comparing oneself with others seems to be more harmful than actively communicating with friends. Using social media late at night appears to be especially damaging, because it disrupts sleep.

In response to public concern, some governments are considering or introducing new rules, such as minimum age limits for social media accounts or restrictions on phones in schools. Technology companies have introduced features designed to protect younger users. Meanwhile, many parents and teenagers are trying to find a healthier balance, deciding consciously when, why, and how they go online.

title: The House on Ash Lane
paragraphs: When Laura and her husband bought the house on Ash Lane, the real estate agent mentioned, with an embarrassed smile, that some people in the village believed it was haunted. Laura laughed. She was a science teacher and did not believe in ghosts. Besides, the house was beautiful, spacious, and surprisingly cheap.

The first strange thing happened on their third night. Laura woke at three in the morning to the sound of a piano playing softly downstairs. They did not own a piano. When she went down, heart pounding, the living room was silent and empty. The next morning, she told herself it had been a dream.

But over the following weeks, the incidents continued. Doors that she was sure she had closed were found open. The smell of pipe tobacco drifted through the hallway, although nobody in the family smoked. Her daughter, who was six, began talking about "the old man in the garden" who waved at her from beneath the apple tree.

Laura, determined to find a rational explanation, began to investigate. At the local library, she found newspaper articles about the house's previous owner, a retired music teacher named Edward Cole, who had lived there alone for forty years. He had been known for his kindness to local children and for the piano lessons he gave for free in his living room. He had died in the house, peacefully, about ten years earlier.

One afternoon, while clearing out the attic, Laura's husband found a box of old sheet music and a photograph of Mr. Cole sitting at a piano, smiling, with a pipe in his hand. Beneath the photograph was a note in shaky handwriting: "For whoever lives here next. Please let the children play."

That weekend, on an impulse she could not fully explain, Laura bought a secondhand piano and placed it in the living room where Mr. Cole's had once stood. Her daughter began taking lessons. Laura never heard the music at night again, and the smell of tobacco faded. She still does not believe in ghosts. But every spring, when the apple tree blossoms, she finds herself glancing at the garden and smiling, just in case.

title: The Long Journey of Your Morning Coffee
paragraphs: For many people, the day does not really begin until they have had their first cup of coffee. Coffee is one of the most widely traded agricultural products in the world, and the global coffee industry is worth hundreds of billions of dollars every year. Yet the journey from a coffee farm to your cup is long and complex, and the money is shared very unequally along the way.

Most of the world's coffee is grown in a band of tropical countries near the equator, including Brazil, Vietnam, Colombia, Ethiopia, and Indonesia. Around twelve and a half million farms produce coffee, and the great majority of them are small family farms, often less than a few hectares in size. Coffee plants take several years to produce their first crop, and the fruit, known as coffee cherries, is often picked by hand.

After harvesting, the cherries are processed to remove the fruit and dry the seeds, which we call coffee beans. The beans are then sorted, packed, and shipped across the world, usually to be roasted in the countries where they will be consumed. Roasting transforms the green beans into the brown, aromatic beans we recognize, and it is at this stage, and later in cafes and shops, that much of the value is added.

According to some estimates, coffee farmers typically receive only a small fraction of the price a consumer pays for a cup of coffee in a cafe in Europe or North America. The rest goes to traders, roasters, retailers, and cafes. In addition, the price that farmers receive can vary dramatically from year to year, depending on the weather in major producing countries and the activity of financial markets. When prices fall, many small farmers struggle to cover their costs.

Climate change presents a further threat. Coffee plants, particularly the popular arabica variety, are sensitive to changes in temperature and rainfall. Some studies suggest that the area suitable for growing coffee could shrink significantly in the coming decades.

Various initiatives aim to make the coffee trade fairer and more sustainable, including fair trade certification, which guarantees farmers a minimum price, and direct trade relationships between roasters and farmers. Consumers who are willing to pay a little more for their coffee can help to support these efforts.

title: How the Sandwich Got Its Name
paragraphs: The sandwich is one of the most popular foods in the world. Every day, millions of people eat sandwiches for lunch, whether a simple combination of cheese and bread or an elaborate creation with many layers. It is so familiar that few people stop to wonder where it came from or why it has such an unusual name.

According to the most popular story, the sandwich was named after John Montagu, the fourth Earl of Sandwich, an English aristocrat who lived in the eighteenth century. The legend says that the earl was a passionate gambler who did not want to leave the card table to eat a proper meal. He asked his servants to bring him slices of meat between two pieces of bread, so that he could eat with one hand while continuing to play. Other gamblers began to ask for "the same as Sandwich," and the name stuck.

Historians, however, are not sure that this story is accurate. It comes mainly from a travel book written by a French author, who may have been repeating gossip. The earl's biographers have suggested that he was more likely eating at his desk while working, since he held a number of demanding government positions, including a role in charge of the navy.

What is certain is that the idea of eating food between pieces of bread is much older than the earl. People in many cultures had been doing so for centuries. In ancient times, a Jewish teacher is said to have eaten lamb and bitter herbs between pieces of flatbread during Passover. In medieval Europe, people often ate their food on thick slices of stale bread called trenchers, which served as plates. In the Middle East and India, flatbreads have long been used to wrap meat and vegetables.

What the earl did, perhaps, was to give a name and a fashionable reputation to a very old way of eating. Interestingly, the earl is also remembered in another way. The explorer James Cook named the Sandwich Islands, now known as Hawaii, in his honor.

Today, every culture seems to have its own version of the sandwich, from the Vietnamese banh mi to the Mexican torta and the Italian panini. It is a simple invention that has truly conquered the world.

title: The Right to Repair
paragraphs: Have you ever had a smartphone with a battery that no longer lasted a full day, a washing machine that stopped working just after its warranty expired, or a printer that was cheaper to replace than to repair? If so, you are not alone. Many modern products are difficult or expensive to repair, and as a result, millions of devices are thrown away every year. A growing movement known as the right to repair is campaigning to change this.

Supporters of the right to repair argue that people who buy a product should have the ability to repair it themselves or take it to an independent repair shop of their choice. In practice, however, manufacturers often make this difficult. Some products are glued together, making it almost impossible to replace parts such as batteries without damaging the device. Spare parts, repair manuals, and special tools may not be available to the public. In some cases, devices contain software that prevents them from working properly if a part has been replaced by someone other than an authorized technician.

Manufacturers argue that these restrictions exist for good reasons. They say that repairs carried out by untrained people could be dangerous, for example if a battery is damaged and catches fire. They also want to protect their intellectual property and maintain the security and quality of their products.

Critics believe that the real motivation is often financial. If customers cannot easily repair their devices, they are more likely to pay high prices for official repairs or simply buy a new product. This contributes to a huge environmental problem. Electronic waste is one of the fastest-growing types of waste in the world, and only a small proportion of it is properly recycled. Producing new devices also requires large amounts of energy and raw materials, some of which are mined in difficult conditions.

The movement has achieved some important successes. The European Union and several American states have introduced laws requiring manufacturers to make spare parts and repair information available for a number of years. Some companies have started selling repair kits to the public. Many supporters believe this is only the beginning, and that in the future, products will be designed from the start to be repaired, upgraded, and reused.

title: Malala's Voice
paragraphs: In October two thousand twelve, a fifteen-year-old girl named Malala Yousafzai was traveling home from school on a bus in the Swat Valley in northern Pakistan. A gunman stopped the bus, asked, "Who is Malala?" and then shot her in the head. Two of her friends were also injured. The attack shocked the world. But the girl the gunman had tried to silence would go on to become one of the most powerful voices for education on the planet.

Malala had grown up in a family that valued education. Her father ran a school, and she loved learning. However, in two thousand seven, an extremist group took control of much of the valley where she lived. They banned many activities, including watching television and listening to music, and they began destroying schools, particularly schools for girls. They announced that girls would no longer be allowed to attend school.

Malala refused to stay silent. At the age of eleven, she began writing an anonymous blog for a British news organization, describing her life under the extremists and her fear that she would not be able to continue her education. Later, she began to speak publicly, giving interviews to journalists and appearing on television. Her courage made her well known in Pakistan, and it also made her a target.

After the attack, Malala was flown to a hospital in Birmingham, in England, where she underwent several operations. Against the odds, she survived and recovered. Rather than being frightened into silence, she continued her campaign with even greater determination. On her sixteenth birthday, she gave a speech at the United Nations in New York, declaring that "one child, one teacher, one book, and one pen can change the world."

In two thousand fourteen, at the age of seventeen, Malala became the youngest person ever to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. She used the prize money to help fund a school for girls. She also founded an organization that works to ensure that every girl in the world can receive twelve years of free, safe, quality education.

Today, many millions of girls around the world are still out of school, because of poverty, conflict, discrimination, or early marriage. Malala's story is a reminder of both how much remains to be done and how much difference one determined person can make.

title: The Chemistry in Your Kitchen
paragraphs: Every time we cook, we are performing a series of chemical experiments. Heat, acids, salt, and time transform the appearance, texture, and flavor of our ingredients in ways that can seem almost magical. Understanding a little of the science behind cooking can help explain why certain techniques work and can make us better cooks.

One of the most important chemical reactions in the kitchen is the Maillard reaction, named after the French scientist who first described it in the early twentieth century. When foods containing proteins and sugars are heated to high temperatures, they react to produce hundreds of new compounds that create brown colors and rich, savory flavors. The Maillard reaction is responsible for the delicious crust on a grilled steak, the golden color of toasted bread, and the aroma of roasted coffee. It happens most effectively when the surface of the food is dry, which is why chefs often recommend drying meat before frying it.

A different process, called caramelization, occurs when sugar itself is heated. As sugar breaks down, it turns brown and develops complex flavors that can be nutty, buttery, or slightly bitter. This is what happens when onions are cooked slowly until they become sweet and golden.

Eggs provide another fascinating example of kitchen chemistry. Egg whites contain proteins that are tightly folded. When eggs are heated, these proteins unfold and bond together, turning the liquid into a solid. When egg whites are whisked, air bubbles are trapped in a network of proteins, creating the light foam used in meringues and mousses.

Acids also play an important role. A squeeze of lemon juice can brighten the flavor of a dish, and acidic marinades can help to tenderize meat. In some dishes, such as ceviche, which is popular in Latin America, raw fish is "cooked" by soaking it in citrus juice, which changes the structure of its proteins without any heat at all.

Even salt does more than simply make food taste salty. It can reduce bitterness, enhance sweetness, and draw moisture out of vegetables. As many cooks know, the difference between a dull dish and a delicious one is often just a pinch of salt. Cooking, it seems, is both an art and a science.

title: The Bookshop at the End of the Street
paragraphs: When the big chain bookstore opened in the shopping center, everyone expected Arthur Bell's little shop to close within a year. It had stood at the end of Mill Street for more than half a century, a narrow building with a crooked sign and a window display that changed with the seasons. Arthur, who had inherited it from his mother, was seventy-three, and many people assumed he would welcome the excuse to retire.

He didn't. Instead, he did something nobody expected. He started reading aloud. Every Saturday morning at ten o'clock, he sat in an armchair at the back of the shop and read a chapter of a novel to anyone who wanted to listen. At first, only two or three people came, mostly elderly neighbors who had known him for decades. Then a young mother brought her children. Then a group of students came, curious about the old man who was reading Dickens to an audience of strangers.

Within a few months, the Saturday readings had become an event. People arrived early to get a seat. Arthur chose books carefully, mixing classics with adventure stories and the occasional mystery. He did all the voices, sometimes badly, and the audience laughed and gasped in the right places. Afterward, people lingered, drinking tea from mismatched cups and talking about books. Many of them bought something before they left.

Then, one winter, Arthur fell ill. The shop stayed closed for three weeks, and the people of Mill Street realized how much they had come to depend on it. When he finally returned, thinner and walking with a stick, he found a surprise waiting. A group of regular visitors had organized a schedule of volunteers to help him run the shop. A retired teacher offered to do the accounts. Teenagers from the local school redesigned the window display. A carpenter fixed the crooked sign.

The chain store in the shopping center closed five years later, a victim of online shopping. Arthur's bookshop is still open. He no longer reads every week, but the readings continue, led by the volunteers, some of whom first came as children. And there is always an empty armchair at the back of the shop, kept for Arthur, in case he feels like reading one more chapter.

title: How Small Nudges Change Our Behavior
paragraphs: Governments and organizations have traditionally tried to change people's behavior in two main ways: by making rules and by offering financial rewards or punishments. If they want people to drive more safely, they introduce speed limits and fines. If they want people to save energy, they offer tax benefits. But in recent decades, a different approach has become increasingly popular. It is known as nudging.

The idea was popularized by the economist Richard Thaler and the legal scholar Cass Sunstein in a book published in two thousand eight. A nudge is a small change in the way choices are presented that encourages people to behave in a certain way, without forbidding any options or significantly changing financial incentives. The key insight is that human decisions are strongly influenced by context, habits, and mental shortcuts, often in ways we are not aware of.

One of the most famous examples involves retirement savings. In many countries, workers had to actively choose to join a pension plan, and many never did, even though it was in their interest. When some employers changed the system so that workers were automatically enrolled, unless they chose to leave, participation increased dramatically. People are strongly influenced by default options, because changing them requires effort.

Nudges can take many forms. Placing fruit at eye level in a school cafeteria and moving desserts to a less visible position can encourage children to eat more healthily. Sending letters to people who are late paying their taxes, telling them that most people in their area pay on time, has been shown to increase payments. Painting lines on roads that make drivers feel they are going faster can encourage them to slow down.
Several governments have set up special teams to apply these ideas to public policy. Supporters argue that nudges are cheap, effective, and respect people's freedom of choice.

However, nudging has also attracted criticism. Some people argue that it can be manipulative, because it influences people without their full awareness. Others point out that the same techniques can be used by companies to encourage people to spend more money or share personal data. There are also concerns that nudges are sometimes used as an easy alternative to more substantial measures. Like any tool, it seems, the power of nudging depends on how, and by whom, it is used.

title: Recording a Disappearing World
paragraphs: In the late nineteen sixties, an American musician and naturalist named Bernie Krause began recording the sounds of wild places. Over the following decades, he traveled to forests, deserts, wetlands, and oceans around the world, capturing thousands of hours of audio. His recordings form one of the largest archives of natural soundscapes ever created. But listening back to them today, Krause has noticed something deeply disturbing: many of the places he recorded have fallen silent.

Krause developed the idea that every healthy habitat has its own unique acoustic signature, which he called a biophony. Just as instruments in an orchestra play in different ranges so that each can be heard, he observed that different species tend to use different frequencies and time slots for their calls. Insects might occupy high frequencies, birds the middle range, and frogs and mammals lower sounds. Together, they create a complex, layered sound in which each species has its place.

When a habitat is damaged, this acoustic structure changes. In one striking example, Krause recorded a forest in California before and after a selective logging operation. Visually, the forest looked almost the same after the work, since only certain trees had been removed. Acoustically, however, it was transformed. The rich chorus of birds that he had previously recorded was reduced to a few scattered voices.

Krause estimates that a large percentage of the habitats in his archive are now either completely silent or so altered that their original soundscapes can no longer be heard. The causes include deforestation, agriculture, urban expansion, pollution, and climate change.

His work has inspired a growing field of research known as soundscape ecology. Scientists now use automated recorders placed in forests, reefs, and other habitats to monitor biodiversity over long periods. Listening to an ecosystem can reveal changes that might be missed by visual surveys, such as the return of a species after restoration or the gradual decline of insects.

Krause's recordings are also a reminder of what we stand to lose. For many listeners, hearing the voice of a vanished forest is a powerful emotional experience, more moving than any statistic. As he once said, a picture may be worth a thousand words, but a soundscape is worth a thousand pictures.

title: Breaking the Four-Minute Barrier
paragraphs: For much of the first half of the twentieth century, many athletes, coaches, and even doctors believed that it was physically impossible for a human being to run a mile, about one thousand six hundred meters, in less than four minutes. The best runners in the world had come close, but the barrier seemed unbreakable. Some experts warned that anyone who attempted it might seriously damage their health.

On the sixth of May, nineteen fifty-four, a twenty-five-year-old British medical student named Roger Bannister set out to prove them wrong. Bannister was an amateur athlete who trained around his demanding studies, often running for less than an hour a day. He approached the challenge scientifically, studying his own body and carefully planning his training.

The race took place at a small athletics track in Oxford. The weather was poor, with strong winds and rain, and Bannister almost decided not to run. Shortly before the start, the wind dropped. With the help of two friends who acted as pacemakers, setting a fast speed for the first laps, Bannister completed the four laps of the track. On the final lap, he ran alone, pushing himself to the limit.

When he crossed the line, he collapsed, almost unconscious. The crowd waited anxiously for the time to be announced. The announcer began, "The time was three," and the rest of his words were drowned out by the cheering of the crowd. Bannister had run the mile in three minutes and fifty-nine point four seconds.

What happened next is perhaps even more remarkable. Just forty-six days later, an Australian runner named John Landy broke Bannister's record. Within a few years, dozens of runners had run a mile in under four minutes. Today, the record stands at more than fifteen seconds faster than Bannister's time, and many high school students have run under four minutes.

The story is often used to illustrate the power of belief. Once athletes saw that the barrier could be broken, it no longer seemed impossible, and they were able to achieve the same result. Of course, improvements in training, tracks, and nutrition also played a role. But Bannister's achievement remains a powerful symbol of how human limits are often set as much by the mind as by the body.

title: The Hidden Cost of Next-Day Delivery
paragraphs: It has never been easier to shop. With a few taps on a smartphone, we can order almost anything, from books and clothes to groceries and furniture, and in many cities, it will arrive the next day or even within a few hours. For consumers, fast delivery is extremely convenient. But the systems that make it possible have significant costs that are often invisible to the people who benefit from them.

One of these costs is environmental. Fast delivery often means that vans travel with only partial loads, making more frequent trips to deliver individual packages to different addresses. This increases traffic, air pollution, and carbon emissions, particularly in urban areas. Many products are also wrapped in large amounts of packaging, much of which is not recycled. In addition, online shoppers tend to return a high proportion of their purchases, especially clothes, and some returned items are simply thrown away because it is cheaper than checking and repackaging them.

There are also human costs. Behind every quick delivery is a large workforce of warehouse employees and delivery drivers who work under intense pressure. In some warehouses, workers are expected to pick and pack hundreds of items per hour, and their movements are tracked by computer systems. Delivery drivers may have to complete a large number of deliveries in a single shift, leaving little time for breaks. Many are self-employed and lack the protections of regular employees.

Fast delivery also affects local communities. Small independent shops often struggle to compete with large online retailers that can offer lower prices and faster delivery. When local shops close, town centers can lose their character and their sense of community.

None of this means that online shopping is necessarily bad. For people who live far from shops, have limited mobility, or simply have busy lives, it can be invaluable. Some studies even suggest that well-organized delivery can produce lower emissions than many people driving to shops individually.

However, many experts believe that consumers could reduce some of the negative effects by making small changes. Choosing slower delivery options when speed is not necessary, combining orders, collecting parcels from local pickup points, and buying from local shops whenever possible can all help to make our shopping habits more sustainable.

title: A Diary from the Past
paragraphs: The diary had been hidden under a loose floorboard in the bedroom for almost a century. Ben found it by accident while replacing the old carpet in the house he had just bought. It was a small leather notebook, stiff and spotted with age, and on the first page, in careful handwriting, was written: "The private diary of Elsie Thornton, aged fourteen, nineteen twenty-four."

That evening, Ben sat on the floor of the empty room and began to read. Elsie wrote about her school, her strict father, her best friend Dora, and her dream of becoming a doctor, which her family considered ridiculous for a girl. She described the price of candy, the arrival of the first motor car in the street, and a boy called Albert who worked at the bakery and always gave her the largest bun.

As the months passed in the diary, the tone changed. Elsie's mother became ill, and Elsie had to leave school to look after her and her younger brothers. She wrote less often, and her entries became shorter and sadder. The last entry, written two years after the first, said only: "Mother died today. I will not be a doctor now. Perhaps one day someone else will be, for me."

Ben closed the diary and sat in silence for a long time. He could not stop thinking about the girl who had once slept in this room and whose dreams had been abandoned so young. Over the next few weeks, he began to search local records. He discovered that Elsie had married Albert from the bakery, had four children, and had lived in the same town until her death in nineteen eighty-six.

Eventually, he traced one of her granddaughters, a woman named Helen, who lived only an hour away. When Ben called her and explained what he had found, there was a long silence on the line. Then Helen began to cry. "My grandmother never talked about her childhood," she said. "And I am a doctor. I always wondered why she was so proud of me."

Ben gave Helen the diary. A few months later, he received a letter from her. Inside was a photograph of a small brass plaque, newly placed in the waiting room of the clinic where Helen worked. It read: "In memory of Elsie Thornton, who wanted to heal people."

title: How Colors Affect Our Minds
paragraphs: Why are so many fast-food restaurants decorated in red and yellow? Why do banks often use blue in their logos? Why are hospital walls frequently painted in soft greens and pale blues? Many people believe that colors have a powerful influence on our emotions and behavior, and businesses spend considerable sums of money choosing exactly the right shades. But what does scientific research actually tell us about the psychology of color?

Some effects are well documented. Red, for example, tends to attract attention, which is one reason why it is used for warning signs, stop lights, and sale signs in shops. Several studies have suggested that red can increase arousal and may make people react more quickly. In sport, some research has found that athletes wearing red were slightly more likely to win in certain combat sports, perhaps because the color is associated with dominance and aggression, although these findings have been debated.

Blue, on the other hand, is often associated with calm, stability, and trust. It is consistently one of the most popular favorite colors in surveys across many different countries. This may explain why it is so common in the branding of banks, technology companies, and social media platforms, which want to appear reliable.

However, many popular claims about color are less well supported. The idea that painting a room a particular color can dramatically change people's mood or productivity, for example, has produced mixed results in research. One famous case involved a shade of pink that was claimed to reduce aggression in prisoners. Early reports were enthusiastic, but later studies failed to confirm the effect.

One of the main challenges is that the meaning of colors is strongly influenced by culture and personal experience. In many Western countries, white is associated with purity and weddings, while in parts of East Asia, it is traditionally associated with mourning and funerals. Red symbolizes danger in some contexts, but luck and celebration in China. A person who had a bad experience in a green room may feel differently about the color than someone who associates it with a happy childhood garden.

Context also matters. The same red that seems exciting on a sports car may feel alarming on a medical report. Psychologists therefore caution against simple rules. Color certainly affects us, but its effects are complex, subtle, and deeply shaped by where and how we encounter it.

title: Should Zoos Still Exist?
paragraphs: For many people, a visit to the zoo is a cherished childhood memory. Seeing an elephant, a lion, or a giraffe up close can be an unforgettable experience. Zoos attract hundreds of millions of visitors around the world every year. Yet in recent decades, a growing number of people have begun to question whether it is right to keep wild animals in captivity at all.

Critics of zoos argue that even the best enclosures cannot replicate the complexity of an animal's natural habitat. Elephants, for example, can walk many kilometers a day in the wild and live in large, close-knit family groups. Some marine mammals, such as orcas, travel enormous distances in the ocean. In captivity, some animals display repetitive behaviors, such as pacing back and forth or swaying, which scientists consider signs of stress or boredom. Critics also point out that many zoos still keep animals mainly for entertainment rather than for genuine conservation purposes.

Supporters of modern zoos, however, argue that the best institutions have changed dramatically. Many have replaced small cages with larger, more natural enclosures and provide activities to keep animals mentally and physically stimulated. They argue that zoos play a vital role in conservation. Through carefully managed breeding programs, zoos have helped to save several species from extinction, including the California condor and the Arabian oryx, both of which were later reintroduced into the wild.

Zoos also contribute to scientific research, providing opportunities to study animal behavior, health, and reproduction that would be difficult in the wild. Many fund conservation projects in the animals' native countries, protecting habitats and training local scientists. And supporters argue that by allowing people to see animals in person, zoos inspire visitors, particularly children, to care about wildlife and the environment.

Between these two positions, many experts take a middle view. They suggest that zoos should focus on species that can thrive in captivity and that genuinely benefit from conservation programs, while gradually phasing out the keeping of animals that suffer most, such as elephants and large marine mammals. Some argue that resources should increasingly be directed toward protecting animals in their natural habitats, perhaps through sanctuaries and wildlife reserves.
The debate is likely to continue. What is clear is that the role of zoos is changing, and that the question of how humans should share the planet with other species has never been more urgent.

title: The Lost Art of Letter Writing
paragraphs: There was a time when letters were the main way that people separated by distance kept in touch. Families exchanged news across oceans, lovers poured their feelings onto paper, and friendships were maintained over decades through regular correspondence. Today, most of us communicate through instant messages and emails, and many young people have never written or received a personal letter. Something valuable, some argue, has been lost.

Letters have played an important role in history. Much of what we know about the lives and thoughts of famous people comes from their correspondence. The letters of writers, artists, scientists, and politicians reveal their private doubts, their humor, and their relationships in ways that official documents cannot. The painter Vincent van Gogh, for example, wrote hundreds of letters to his brother Theo, which provide extraordinary insight into his art and his struggles with mental illness.

Ordinary people's letters are equally precious. Historians use letters written by soldiers, immigrants, and workers to understand how people experienced major events. A letter from a soldier to his mother during a war can communicate the reality of that experience more powerfully than any history book.

Part of the special value of a letter lies in its physical nature. Handwriting is personal and unique. A letter can be held, kept in a drawer, and reread years later. Many people treasure letters from parents or grandparents long after they have died, finding comfort in the familiar shape of their writing.

Letter writing also encourages a different kind of communication. Because writing by hand takes time and effort, people tend to think more carefully about what they want to say. Letters are often longer, more reflective, and more personal than digital messages. The delay between sending and receiving a letter also creates a sense of anticipation that instant messaging cannot match.

Interestingly, there are signs of a small revival. Some people have rediscovered the pleasure of writing letters, joining pen pal programs or sending handwritten cards to friends. Research suggests that receiving a handwritten thank you note has a much greater emotional impact than people expect. In a world of constant digital communication, a letter in the mailbox may have become more special than ever.

title: The Year Without a Summer
paragraphs: In April eighteen fifteen, Mount Tambora, a volcano on the island of Sumbawa in what is now Indonesia, erupted with extraordinary violence. It was the most powerful volcanic eruption in recorded history. The explosions could be heard more than two thousand kilometers away, and the top of the mountain was blown off, reducing its height by more than a kilometer. Tens of thousands of people on the surrounding islands were killed, either directly by the eruption or by the starvation and disease that followed.

But the effects of Tambora were not limited to Indonesia. The eruption threw enormous quantities of ash and gas high into the atmosphere. Among these gases was sulfur dioxide, which formed tiny droplets that spread around the globe and reflected some of the sun's light back into space. As a result, global temperatures fell.

The following year, eighteen sixteen, became known in Europe and North America as "the year without a summer." In parts of the northeastern United States, snow fell in June, and frosts continued throughout the summer, destroying crops. In Europe, constant rain and cold temperatures led to failed harvests. Food prices rose dramatically, and many people faced hunger. There were riots in several countries, and thousands of people emigrated in search of better conditions.

The strange weather also had some unexpected cultural consequences. In the summer of eighteen sixteen, a group of young English writers was staying in a villa near Lake Geneva in Switzerland. Because of the constant storms, they were forced to spend much of their time indoors. To entertain themselves, they decided to hold a competition to see who could write the most frightening story. One of them, eighteen-year-old Mary Shelley, began writing a story that would become the novel "Frankenstein," one of the most famous works of horror fiction ever written.
Some historians have also suggested that the dramatic, colorful sunsets painted by artists during this period may have been influenced by the volcanic particles in the atmosphere.

At the time, nobody connected the bad weather with a volcano on the other side of the world. It was only in the twentieth century that scientists understood the link. Today, the story of Tambora is studied as a powerful example of how events in one part of the world can affect the climate and lives of people everywhere.

title: Letters to a Prisoner
paragraphs: It began with a mistake. Grace, a seventy-eight-year-old widow who lived alone in a small town, had signed up for a pen pal program at her local library, expecting to correspond with a student overseas. Instead, due to a mix-up with the forms, she received a letter from a man named Marcus, who was serving a twelve-year sentence in a prison three hundred kilometers away.

Her first instinct was to throw the letter away. Her daughter, when she heard about it, told her to do exactly that. "You don't know what he did," she said. "He could be dangerous." But Grace had read the letter twice, and something in it had touched her. Marcus wrote about the small window in his cell, the birds he watched every morning, and the fact that nobody had written to him in four years.

She wrote back. She told him about her garden, her late husband, and the crossword puzzles she did every evening. She did not ask about his crime, and he did not mention it. Over the following months, their letters grew longer. Marcus told her about the books he was reading in the prison library and the courses he had begun to take. Grace sent him newspaper clippings and, once, a pressed flower from her garden.

In his tenth letter, Marcus finally told her why he was in prison. He had been involved in a robbery when he was twenty-two, and a man had been seriously injured. He wrote that he thought about that man every day and did not expect her to forgive him. Grace read the letter many times. Then she wrote back: "I am not the person you need to ask for forgiveness. But I am still here."

Their correspondence continued for six years. When Marcus was released early for good behavior, the first place he went was Grace's house. He was nervous, holding a bunch of flowers, unsure if she would want to see him in person. She opened the door, looked at him for a long moment, and then invited him in for tea.

Marcus now works as a gardener and volunteers with a charity that supports prisoners returning to society. He visits Grace every Sunday. Her daughter, who was so worried at the beginning, now says that Marcus is the most reliable person she knows.

title: Why Cities Need Trees
paragraphs: As cities grow, they tend to become warmer than the surrounding countryside. Concrete, asphalt, and brick absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night, while cars, air conditioners, and factories produce additional heat. This phenomenon, known as the urban heat island effect, can make cities several degrees hotter than nearby rural areas. As the climate changes and heatwaves become more frequent and intense, finding ways to cool cities has become an urgent priority. One of the simplest and most effective solutions is to plant more trees.

Trees cool their surroundings in two main ways. First, they provide shade, preventing sunlight from heating streets, buildings, and people. Second, they release water vapor through their leaves, a process that cools the air around them, much like sweating cools the human body. Studies have shown that streets with plenty of trees can be significantly cooler on hot summer days than streets without them.

The benefits of urban trees go far beyond cooling. Trees absorb carbon dioxide and can help to filter some pollutants from the air. Their roots absorb rainwater, reducing the risk of flooding during heavy storms. They provide homes and food for birds, insects, and other wildlife, increasing biodiversity in urban areas.

Trees also appear to have significant benefits for human health and well-being. Research has linked access to green spaces with lower levels of stress, better mental health, and increased physical activity. In one well-known study, hospital patients who had a view of trees from their window recovered more quickly after surgery and needed fewer painkillers than patients whose windows faced a brick wall. Some studies have even found that neighborhoods with more trees have lower crime rates, although the reasons are complex.

Despite these benefits, trees in cities face many challenges. Space is limited, roots can damage sidewalks and pipes, and trees can be expensive to plant and maintain. In many cities, wealthier neighborhoods have many more trees than poorer ones, which means that the residents who most need cooling often have the least access to it.

Many cities have now launched ambitious programs to plant hundreds of thousands or even millions of new trees. Experts emphasize that it is important not only to plant trees, but to choose the right species, plant them in the right places, and care for them over the long term.

title: Amelia Earhart's Final Flight
paragraphs: In the nineteen twenties and thirties, aviation was still a new and dangerous adventure, and pilots who set records became international celebrities. Among the most famous was Amelia Earhart, an American who broke barriers not only in the sky but also in the way society viewed women.

Earhart took her first flight in nineteen twenty, as a passenger in a small plane at an air show in California. By the time she landed, she later said, she knew she had to fly. She took lessons, worked several jobs to pay for them, and bought her first airplane. In nineteen thirty-two, she became the first woman to fly alone across the Atlantic Ocean, a dangerous journey of almost fifteen hours during which she faced strong winds, ice on her wings, and mechanical problems.

Earhart used her fame to promote aviation and to encourage women to pursue careers that were considered unsuitable for them. She wrote books, gave lectures across the country, and helped to found an organization for female pilots. She believed that women should have the same opportunities as men in every field.

In nineteen thirty-seven, she set out on her most ambitious challenge yet: to become the first woman to fly around the world near the equator. With her navigator, Fred Noonan, she flew from California across the United States, South America, Africa, and Asia. After about a month, they had completed more than two thirds of the journey and arrived in New Guinea.

The next stage was one of the most difficult: a flight of more than four thousand kilometers across the Pacific Ocean to Howland Island, a tiny piece of land barely two kilometers long. On the second of July, they took off. Many hours later, a ship waiting near the island received radio messages from Earhart saying that they could not see the island and were running low on fuel. Then the messages stopped.

Despite one of the largest search operations in history, neither Earhart nor Noonan, nor their plane, was ever found. Their disappearance remains one of the great mysteries of the twentieth century. Some believe they crashed into the ocean and sank. Others think they may have landed on another remote island and survived for a time. Expeditions continue to search for answers. Whatever happened, Earhart remains a powerful symbol of courage and independence.

title: Why Schools Should Teach Failure
paragraphs: In many education systems, success is measured by grades, test scores, and rankings. Students are rewarded for getting the right answers and penalized for mistakes. As a result, many young people grow up deeply afraid of failure. They avoid difficult challenges, choose subjects they know they will do well in, and feel devastated when they receive a disappointing mark. Some educators now argue that schools should do more to teach students how to fail, and how to learn from failure.

Research on learning suggests that mistakes are not only inevitable but essential. When we make a mistake and then correct it, we often remember the correct information better than if we had gotten it right the first time. Some studies have found that students who struggle with a difficult problem before being shown the solution understand the topic more deeply than students who are simply taught the solution directly. Psychologists call these "desirable difficulties."

The way students think about failure also matters. As psychologist Carol Dweck has shown in her research on mindsets, students who believe that intelligence can grow with effort are more likely to persevere when they face difficulties. Students who believe that intelligence is fixed tend to see failure as proof that they are not smart, and they may give up more quickly.

Some schools have begun to introduce activities designed to change students' attitudes toward failure. Teachers may share stories of their own mistakes, celebrate interesting errors in class, or give students challenging projects in which there is no single correct answer. Some schools have even held "failure weeks," during which students and staff discuss their failures openly and reflect on what they learned.

Critics caution that such approaches must be handled carefully. Simply telling students that failure is good can feel hollow, especially for students who face real consequences when they fail important exams. Learning from failure requires support, feedback, and opportunities to try again. Without these, failure can simply be discouraging.

Nevertheless, many employers say that resilience, creativity, and the ability to learn from mistakes are among the most important skills they look for. In a rapidly changing world, where many problems have no easy solutions, the ability to fail well may be as valuable as any academic knowledge.

title: How Elephants Communicate
paragraphs: Elephants are among the most intelligent and social animals on Earth. They live in complex family groups led by an older female, known as the matriarch, who guides the group to food and water and protects its members from danger. To maintain these close relationships, elephants rely on a sophisticated system of communication, much of which humans cannot hear.

Elephants produce a wide range of sounds, including trumpets, roars, barks, and rumbles. Many of their rumbles are at frequencies so low that they are below the range of human hearing. These low-frequency sounds, known as infrasound, can travel several kilometers, allowing elephants to stay in contact with members of their group even when they are far apart, or to find mates over long distances.

Remarkably, elephants may also be able to detect vibrations through the ground. Researchers believe that elephants can sense low-frequency rumbles traveling through the earth with sensitive cells in their feet and trunks. This could allow them to receive messages from distant elephants or detect approaching danger, such as a herd running away from predators.

Elephants also communicate through touch, using their trunks to greet, comfort, and reassure each other. They have been observed caressing distressed companions and wrapping their trunks together in what appears to be a gesture of affection. Scent plays an important role too, providing information about an elephant's identity and condition.

In recent years, scientists have made an even more surprising discovery. A study of wild African elephants in Kenya found evidence that elephants may address each other with unique calls, something like individual names. When researchers played recordings of calls originally directed at a specific elephant, that elephant responded more strongly than when it heard calls directed at others. Very few animals are known to do this, and it suggests that elephants may be capable of abstract thought.

Elephants are also known for their remarkable memory. Matriarchs remember the locations of water sources during droughts and can recognize the calls of many other elephants. They have also been observed behaving in ways that suggest they mourn their dead, touching and staying near the bodies of family members.

Understanding how elephants communicate is not only fascinating but also important for their conservation. As human settlements expand, conflicts between people and elephants are increasing. Knowledge of elephant behavior can help to design better ways of protecting both.

title: The Forgotten Sense
paragraphs: Among our five senses, smell is often considered the least important. Many people say that if they had to lose one sense, smell is the one they would choose. Yet scientists are increasingly discovering that our sense of smell is far more powerful and influential than we tend to believe.

For many years, it was widely claimed that humans could distinguish only around ten thousand different smells. This number was based on an old estimate that was never properly tested. In a study published in two thousand fourteen, researchers suggested that humans may in fact be able to distinguish more than a trillion different odors. While this figure has also been debated, it is clear that our noses are much more sensitive than previously thought.

Smell is closely connected to the parts of the brain that process emotion and memory. Unlike our other senses, information about smells travels almost directly to these regions. This is why a particular smell, such as freshly baked bread or a certain perfume, can instantly bring back vivid memories from many years ago, often accompanied by strong emotions. This phenomenon is sometimes called the Proust effect, after the French writer who described how the taste and smell of a small cake dipped in tea brought back memories of his childhood.

Smell also plays a crucial role in taste. Much of what we think of as flavor actually comes from our sense of smell. When we have a cold and our nose is blocked, food often tastes bland. Without smell, we can still detect basic tastes such as sweet, salty, sour, and bitter, but we lose the rich complexity of flavors.

The importance of smell became particularly clear during the recent pandemic, when millions of people temporarily or permanently lost their sense of smell. Many reported that the experience had a much greater effect on their lives than they had expected. They lost enjoyment of food, felt disconnected from their surroundings, and some even experienced depression. They also became more vulnerable to dangers such as gas leaks, smoke, and spoiled food.

Researchers are now exploring whether changes in our sense of smell might help to detect diseases early. Some studies suggest that a decline in the ability to smell can be an early sign of conditions such as Parkinson's disease. Far from being a minor sense, smell may offer a valuable window into our health and our minds.

title: Will Robots Take Our Jobs?
paragraphs: Throughout history, new technologies have transformed the world of work. The invention of the steam engine, electricity, and computers all destroyed some jobs while creating many new ones. Today, advances in artificial intelligence and robotics are raising the question once again: will machines take our jobs?

Some studies have produced alarming predictions. A widely cited study from the University of Oxford in two thousand thirteen estimated that nearly half of jobs in the United States were at high risk of being automated in the coming decades. Since then, the rapid development of AI systems that can write texts, generate images, and analyze data has led some experts to argue that even highly skilled professions may be affected.
